item.title: [投资TALK君] ✨【投资TALK君1480期】沃什意外放鹰，和贝森特对着干？半导体机会来了✨20260829#CPI #nvda #美股 #投资 #英伟达 #ai #特斯拉
item.dc:creator: 投资TALK君
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、市场情绪的"照妖镜"效应：价格才是真正的宏观分析师

一个反常识的观察：大多数人以为自己在分析市场，其实是在被价格分析。视频里最锋利的一刀，是揭示了同一批人在两个月内的思维反转——6月底担心"指数下跌软件会一起跌"，8月底担心"指数下跌硬件会继续跌"。恐惧的对象在轮换，但恐惧的语法结构一模一样：都是"线性外推 + 厌恶浮亏 + 事件催化"的三段论。

这里藏着一个跨领域的连接——这与认知心理学中的"可得性启发式"（Availability Heuristic）完全同构：人们不是根据基本面判断风险，而是根据"最近发生了什么、疼不疼"来判断风险。凯文沃什的讲话本身波动有限（标普基本横盘），但因为芯片股跌了3.2%，人的神经系统会自动把"疼痛"归因给沃什的"鹰派"，形成一个虚假的因果链。真正的鹰派不是沃什，是你的杏仁核。

二、贝森特与沃什的"双簧"：一个被误读的博弈论均衡

视频里最令人意外的洞见是：一个鹰派的美联储主席，恰恰是财政部长贝森特的盟友，而不是敌人。这完全颠覆了市场的直觉判断（"鹰派=紧缩=长债利率上行=贝森特输"）。

分析师的逻辑链条非常精巧——短端利率与长端利率的关系不是同向传导，而是通过"通胀预期"和"经济增速预期"这两个中介变量反向作用。鹰派立场→压制通胀预期→压低长端名义利率，这正是贝森特想要的"降低家庭和企业融资成本"。

这里可以拉一条跨领域连接到中国古代兵法的"欲擒故纵"——甚至更接近博弈论中的"斯塔克伯格均衡"：贝森特是领导者（明牌宣示目标是压低长债），沃什是跟随者（用短期鹰派换取长期长债下行）。两个看似对着干的人，实际上在演一出"红脸-白脸"的合谋戏。而市场只看到红白脸的表演，看不到剧本。

三、Marvell 悖论：为什么"最弱"的公司享受"最贵"的估值？

这是本期最锋利的估值洞察，也是一个反直觉的商业规律：在AI芯片三巨头（英伟达/博通/Marvell）中，体量最小、绝对营收最少的Marvell，却拿到了最高的PE。市场先生这里表现得像个"势利眼"——但势利得非常有逻辑。

关键在于"营收增速的二阶导数"：Marvell 是加速→加速→加速（45%→50%→70%），英伟达是加速→放缓（70%→30%）。市场估值的锚，从来不是"你今天赚多少"，而是"你的斜率会不会变陡"。

这里有一个惊人的跨领域类比——这与物理学中的"急动度"（Jerk，加速度的变化率） 完全同构。在赛车工程里，让驾驶员感觉"贴背推力"最强的不是最大加速度，而是急动度。Marvell 给市场的正是"贴背感"——每年比上一年更陡。而英伟达就像已经飙到300迈的F1赛车，绝对速度冠绝全场，但推背感反而在减弱。

更深一层：Marvell 的高估值本质上是一种"小体量红利" ——谷歌一张订单就能重塑其收入曲线，而同样一张订单丢给英伟达可能都进不了小数点。在AI基建的食物链里，"被巨头需要分散风险"本身就是一种可变现的资产——这是护城河理论从未讨论过的新维度：不是你有多强大，而是你的客户"需要你存在"来平衡另一家更强大的供应商。这是一种"寄生性议价权"。

📝 转录文本

一、开场：Jackson Hole 后的市场体感为何强烈

在一个相对比较平静的8月份，这一次的一个 Jackson Hole 会议，凯文沃什的这段发言再次引起了市场的这个关注。其实从结果去看，美股这边的波动并不大，为什么给市场的一个体感那么的大？是因为一些板块的标的下跌的幅度相对会大一些。

所以周五的市场里面几乎在充斥着两方面的声音都有：到底凯文博士敢不敢加息？或者说另外一方面，就是认为凯文沃什这一次的发言是相对比较鹰派的，最早9月份又要进行加息了。所以感觉是6月份的一次重演。

唯一不同的是，6月份那一次会议之后，我和大家分享，我认为凯文沃什非常的鹰派。啊，我说市场已经去定价要加息了，但是市场部分在我留言区里面，一些观众告诉我：市场不同意你啊，股市那天是出现上涨的。那一天本身是出现上涨，但是之后我们知道，迎来了整个7月份的一个下跌。

而今天又反过来了。今天其实市场并没有下跌非常的多，只是凯文沃什讲完话之后，先出现了一波上涨，然后再下跌，所以给市场的体感就是这样。从结果去看的话，今天整个标普其实基本是在横盘的。

所以你会发现，当天市场的一个走势，特别是股市这边的一个走势，就会影响到大家对于凯文沃什讲话到底是鹰派还是鸽派的这个判断。但其实我们要真的要去自己做出一个比较客观的一个判断的话，应该要先把股市放在一边。

二、今日视频结构

所以今天视频内容的第一部分，我们聊一下凯文沃什的讲话，聊一下张夏宏观的一个主线条到底是什么。第二部分，我们聊一下财报，周四盘后发布财报的 Marvell，那今天这周五是下跌了10%，正好我们把 Marvell，然后把 AVGO，包括英伟达三家公司从估值这个角度去看一下，好吗？

欢迎大家来到一个不单只聊新闻的专业美股频道，我是市场分析师小涛。那大家记得留言点赞加转发，我们马上就进入今天的期正题。

三、回顾七月初的展望：与市场情绪完全反着走

我先回顾一下从七月份以来，第三季度以来整个市场的一个走势。那我下面引用的是我在七月初的时候，我所做的这个展望。为什么我要聊这一点？稍后大家就知道我的一个用意了。

首先，当时我在七月初，就六月底七月初的时候，我做了一个对于下半年的这个展望。我说其实市场是连续性的，但是一定要让我做展望的话，我可以去做。

那当时我做的展望里边，比较庆幸的是，到现在过去的将近两个月的时间里边，有很多个点都已经被兑现了。比如说当时我认为，就当时市场并不喜欢大科技，把所有的资金全部集中在那些收支票的。当时我们说，写支票的和收支票的，市场不喜欢写支票的，类似于大科技；市场喜欢这些收支票的，类似于硬件公司，类似于像美光啊，像存储这一类的公司。这是当时6月底的时候市场的一个故事线。

但是当时我说，市场非常的短视，嗯，只是去回馈这些收支票的，却无视这些写支票的，因为这些写支票他们基本面非常的强，且财报已经被证明了。

那我这边的第二点，所以我认为大科技是便宜的，包括我认为软件也是便宜的。那软件今年上半年的回调幅度也相当的大。

那同时我指出在第一点里边，我指出我期待今年的下半年会有一次整个大致7%至10%的这个回调，由谁所带领？由硬件所带领。因为硬件的情绪面非常的高。

那然后我说，我并不认为整个牛市结束了，还是会以 AI 为主，以现金流为王，EPS 增速为主。现金流的话就是和软件是相关的，会有一些宏观的一个噪音。那最后一点，我聊到了 AI agent 这一块。

然后另外一点，黄金我认为是可以长期布局，比特币也是可以长期布局。

四、当时的判断为何是"反共识"的

你会发现，我当然啊，现在看起来其实都还是不错，但是当时我做的这些展望或者做的这些预测，很多都是和市场的情绪面完全反过来的，或者基本上很多都是和市场情绪面反过来。

  • 硬件：我认为硬件要回调，因为当时硬件的情绪面非常的高；
  • 大科技：当时的 YTD 走势应该是负的10%，在6月底的时候情绪面非常的低；
  • 软件：更不用说了，直接是低迷了6个月，甚至你可以理解为从24年到26年，两年半的时间软件板块都在回调；
  • 比特币：也没人再聊了，直接从12万腰斩到6万；
  • 黄金：更没有人聊。很多人在年初的时候，年初、上年底、今年年初还有很多人聊黄金，我在直播的时候，有人让我去买白银。

你会发现基本上完全和市场情绪反过来。

五、过去两个月的实际走势验证

而在过去的两个月，我们看到就是完全和今年上半年反过来。整个第三季度到现在为止：

  • 纳指虽然只上涨了1%，
  • 但 Max 7 七大科技股上涨了7.2%，
  • 黄金上涨了12.4%，
  • 比特币上涨了33%，
  • IGV 软件板块上涨了21%。

到现在为止，即使经过了这一波 IGV 的一个反弹之后，我都不认为软件板块这一波的反弹结束了。那我在前几期的视频有和大家分享过这个观点。因为现在机构也好，个人也好，在软件板块上面的一个仓位是非常的低配。

刚刚从第二季度开始退出这些软件板块，终于放弃了软件板块，开始进入、开始去追这些硬件板块，结果第三季度马上迎来就是硬件板块、芯片板块这边的一些回调，然后软件板块开始拉升。

这就是我以前我有聊过我自己看法：就我宁愿去踏空，我宁愿去错过这个标的，我也不会去为别人去抬轿子。那当我知道这一个标的、这个板块里边没有很多的一些仓位在里边，或者股价非常低迷的时候，我知道起码在那个位置进去，我不会给别人抬价。至于它会不会起来、什么时候起来，我可能并不知道。但是我选择去投的话，一定是我认可它的一个基本面，其次，我知道里面是没有仓位的，我起码不会给别人抬轿。那当然未来如果有些基本面这个回归或者情绪面的这个回归，它会轮动到我现在去布局的这些标的。

六、当下芯片板块的估值再次变便宜

从第三季度到现在为止，起码我当时做的很多个预测你会发现到现在，其实两个月的走势，情绪面都出现了这些反转。

那回到当下，经过了两个月之后，你会发现 SOX 整个半导体板块的一个估值，其实已经没有——我当时在聊28倍、28倍、29倍，我反复提醒反复提醒，我说主动止盈也好，被动止盈也好，我们一定要在这个位置去做一个止盈。这是在 SOX 在28、28、29倍的估值的时候，六月底的时候、六月中旬、六月底的时候。

但是反过来到现在，情绪面的改变就是非常的快，才两个月的时间，现在 SOX 变得便宜了，但是却很多人对于芯片板块没有信心了，觉得芯片板块不行了。当然我稍后再聊三家公司估值的时候，你们会发现，我们会发现整个芯片板块里边那些估值其实都已经非常的便宜。个别标的真的都已经很便宜了。就你去横向和纵向地去和其他板块的一些标的去做对比的话，你会发现芯片板块里面的标的是真的便宜，现在就现在这个位置。

当然现在这个便宜的位置，从估值这个角度去看的话，可能就是和七月底当时的股市类似。那七月份、七月底进行了一波下跌，八月的上旬出现了反弹，然后八月的下旬，在过去的两周时间再次出现了一个下跌。

那一波下跌，很多人忍着忍着忍着就坚持在那边。然后八月上旬的那一波反弹，让很多人觉得"啊，终于可以反弹了"，结果现在的这个我们说 second leg 第二腿往下跌的话，让很多人彻底失去这个信心了。

七、投资心理与线性外推的陷阱

所以你会发现，两个月的时间就使得原来在六月底对芯片板块非常乐观的这一部分人、或者追高的那一部分人，到现在为止就会非常的悲观。自己的标的跌也就算了，最大的问题是自己的标的在跌，但是其他的标的在涨，这就会让很多人非常的难受。

在6月份、5月份的时候，有人问过我。我记得非常清，在我在直播的时候有人问我，他说软件板块——软件现在跌、硬件现在涨——他担心的是未来指数如果下（因为指数还没怎么下跌嘛，4、5、6三个月指数走得非常好），他担心未来如果指数下跌，软件还会跌。

那当时我就说，千万不要去做这一个线性的一个外推，不要拿历史的数据去做一个线性的外推。基本面好、估值便宜的这些软件板块公司，没有任何的理由在这个位置去卖软件，对吧？当上涨的时候可以是因为硬件板块的一个强势，然后把指数带上去，那凭什么未来指数下跌的时候就一定要一起下跌呢？这个是不讲道理的。就我们的思路里边，你会发现"因为软件的下跌，所以我默认未来指数下跌，软件会同时下跌，会一起下跌"。

现在也是一样。现在很多人可能会觉得，OK，指数还在一个高位，未来如果指数下跌的话，硬件可以继续下跌。这样的思维和在6月份、5月份担心指数下跌、软件会继续下跌不完全一样吧？这种思路是完全一样，就是做一个再做一个线性外推。明明已经非常的低迷了，然后你认为指数的下跌它会更加低迷。

而为什么会让我们有这种感觉？主要有两点：

第一点：单纯的因为价格的下跌。价格的下跌让人很多人会使得非常的悲观。其实这一点我们恰恰要反过来，价格的下跌基本面没有改变，我们应该变得乐观，而不是变得更加的悲观。但是没办法，大多数人的思维，因为我们正常人的思维都是一个厌恶亏损或者厌恶浮亏的。那一旦出现一些浮亏，一旦出现下跌，人就会非常的烦躁，就会对这一个结果本身会感到厌恶。

第二点：叠加一些事件。比如说今天凯文沃什这个讲话，虽然指数其实没怎么下跌，但是凯文沃什的讲话会让人觉得非常的悲观，马上接下去又要进行加息了，或者又要打开这个加息周期了。价格的下跌配合一些事件，会让人们做一个线性的一个外推。线性的外推就是把前段时间的一个价格下跌，假设未来会继续出现前段时间的一个价格下跌。

八、建立"最高判断逻辑侧面"

那么所以在这种时候，我们一定要有自己在判断逻辑里面的一个最高的一个判断逻辑侧面。我一直和大家分享，在我自己的一个主线条里面，永远是基本面排第一的。因为如果说基本面和其他的一些宏观也好、技术面也好出现冲突的话，我知道对我来说什么判断层级更高，我知道我应该依赖于什么的一个判断主逻辑线。

所以只有我们认清了在整个投资的一个判断逻辑里边，或者交易的一个判断逻辑里边的最高的这个逻辑层面，我们才可以在很多复杂信号在交错的时候，我们去找到属于自己的这个主线条，跟着这条主线条去走。

九、周五债市反应：短端与长端的博弈

如果我们去看今天，就周五整个债券市场的一个走势，其实凯文沃什讲完话之后，长债这块的利率波动并不大。但是之后他讲完话之后的那一段，在11点、12点之后，然后长债的利率也开始出现上升。就起码在周五那一天并没有走出我期待的这种走势。

什么是我期待这种走势？就短债，如果他要选择鹰派的话，短债的利率是一定上涨。但是我认为一个鹰派的美联储对于长端这一块、长端债利率这一块的一个控制，其实是一个利好，并不是利空。就是美联储本身变得鹰派，其实是有利于贝森特，或者和贝森特是在往一个方向去努力。

为什么呢？因为我们知道一个鹰派的美联储主席或者一个鹰派的美联储，他们会对于未来有可能会加息，对吧？或者会去收缩整个金融环境。收缩金融环境对于经济增速来说是一个向下的压力，或者是一个向下的一个助力，这是第一点。

然后第二点，一个鹰派的美联储，它的目的什么？它的目的是压制通胀。所以未来的这个通胀预期也会被往下压。那影响到10年期名义利率的这个因素有很多个呢，其中包括了真实利率和通胀的预期。

那在周五的市场走势里边，其实我们看到了通胀的预期是往下降，10年期——我聊的是10年期——10年期通胀预期是往下降了两个基点。那是合理的，因为凯文沃什变得鹰派、美联储变得鹰派，所以确实通胀的这个预期往下降了。

但是真实利率往上涨了7个基点，0.07。真实利率的一个上涨，它可以反映的是什么？它可以反映的是一个相对比较鹰派的美联储，因为它要加息，使得这个中性利率——中性利率是美联储通过隔夜利率去进行调整——那中性利率本身往上抬。中性利率往上抬会带着所有的利率开始往上抬，就短债利率开始往上抬，5年期、7年期、10年期都会出现一部分的一些上涨。

但是这些东西是相对比较短期的，因为随着时间比较长，你想你如果保持在一个相对比较紧缩的一个状态之下，对于通胀的这个预期一定是往下降的，对于经济增速这个预期也是往下降的，那这两者都会使得10年期的名义利率往下降。

十、鹰派美联储 = 贝森特的盟友

所以从单——如果单指拿周五这一天市场的一个走势去看的话，确实不是贝森特所希望看到的。但是如果持续下去，市场持续这样的一个阴盘，就短端持续保持在一个相对的高位，对于长债利率就是一个利好，对于长债利率就是一个向下的助力。所以我的看法是，一个鹰派的美联储主席，其实和贝森特所努力的这个方向是一致的。

然后正好在周五的时候有一条新闻，贝森特他是写了一封信给一个议员 Elizabeth Warren。他写的时候他说，日元的这个无序的波动将会导致美债率的这个上升。就是他已经明牌了。

那我前段时间和大家聊过，我说贝森特的目的什么？他的目的不是帮日本的央行去保住日元，不是。他的最终目的是把美国长债这一块的利率给打压下去。为什么？中期选举，他选票，去降低人们，就百姓和企业的这个融资成本。

贝森特表示到：日元市场的混乱可能引发强制平仓，这可能会扰乱全球市场，并最终增加美国家庭和企业的借贷成本。

所以贝森特或者美国财政部的目标，当他们的目标非常明确的时候，我丝毫不担心他们背后所用的一些工具、所拥有的一些工具。就只要他的目标非常的明确，那我知道，长债利率，因为现在比如说周五的市场，长债利率往上涨，那我知道接下去贝森特一定会有更加激进的这个行为。

所以如果一定要在一个现在变得鹰派的一个美联储，或者起码今天因为凯文沃什的一个讲话变得更加鹰派的美联储，和贝森特财政部之间去做这个选择，去挑出哪一个是宏观的一个主线条的话，我认为财政部才是现在宏观的一个主线条。

十一、"沃什喂了贝森特一坨"——但长期方向一致

如果去看单一去看周五的一个市场，其实这一次凯文沃什是拉了一坨比较大的，直接喂给贝森特了。因为你从今天市场的走势去看，它是和贝森特在往两个方向去走。

但是我知道，我个人认为，我认为他们都非常的清楚知道自己在做什么。特别凯文，我是非常的清楚地知道自己在做什么。所以我认为稍微时间线放长一点的话，就我说只是你给他几周的时间，你就会发现长端这一块的利率应该是往下，而不是往上。

好吧，那在今天凯文沃什发言之前，有很多人认为凯文沃什会配合贝森特，然后去放鸽。这背后的一个逻辑认为是放鸽的话，长端的利率会下来。其实我认为恰恰是相反，或者背后并不是非常地理解短端利率和长端利率之间的这个关系。美联储只能控制短端利率，而短端利率和长端这一块并不是那么地直接，你降息长端利率就一定要下来。

十二、凯文沃什讲话细读：从"很虚"到"更实"

这一次凯文沃什的讲话我也听了。那我听完之后其实和彭博他们的判断是比较一致的，就我认为他这一次讲话里边，其实是回到了他第一次的讲话，但是比他第一次的就6月份那次会议里面提供了更多他对于市场的一些判断，这一点是他在前两次会议里面都没有的。所以比起上一次的会议，市场认为他讲得很虚，这一次的会议会比较的实际，因为他讲了自己对于市场这个判断。

在他所有的讲话里面，有一句话让我印象非常的深刻。他说：如果我现在和市场说整个金融环境是紧缩的话，我会受到非常大的一些挑战。这句话的意思说的有点绕口，意思就是说，他认为当下的金融环境起码不是在一个——就利率起码不是在一个紧缩的一个阶段。什么叫不是在紧缩的阶段？就是未来有紧缩的、有更加紧缩的这个空间在那边，或者说有加息的一个空间在那边。这就是他今天表现出了一个比较明显鹰派的态度。

那同时他还聊到了贡献到 PCE，他把 PCE 里边有100多项全部拆开来去看，有百分之多少的项目比疫情那段时间是低了很多，但是和疫情之前低通胀的这个环境去做对比的话，还是在一个相对的高位。所以他看的数据非常的细致。他给人一种"OK，你确实掌握了背后很多的一些数据，也有你自己一些看法，只是你不愿意去给出——提前去给出这个判断而已，但是你自己心里是有数的"。

那所以彭博他们那个看法是：凯文沃什在这一次 Jackson Hole 会议取得了一次成功的鹰派立场，令人信服。我也觉得挺令我信服的。彭博他们有聊到，他说凯文沃什成功地提出了减少前瞻性指引的理由，同时又没有显得闪烁其词。这也是我非常直接的这个感受，并没有那么地闪烁其词，因为他给了一些非常具体的一些数据和理由。

十三、彭博对九月加息的判断

所以最后彭博他们认为，因为这一次比较鹰派的这个发言，彭博他们提高了9月份加息这个风险。虽然他们认为今年并不会进行加息，甚至我记得他们认为今年是会降息的。但最终他们说，决定下一次接下来会加息还是不加息的话，有两组非常重要的数据：一组就是非农数据，一组就是 CPI 数据。

他们认为这一次的非农数据将会表现出疲软。如果非农表现出疲软，那加息的概率就会下降，就所以是不利于加息的。但是同时他们却认为8月份的 CPI 数据将会表现得比较的强劲，会比较的高，与加息的这个预期可能就会相反了，就是可能会增加这个加息的预期。

十四、周五市场：为何体感如此明显

如果去看一下周五的这个市场，为什么让人体感会比较的明显？是因为前段时间、那么过去两个月里面走得比较好的一些标的出现了比较大幅度的一些回调：

  • 黄金下跌了3.1%；
  • 比特币下跌了3.3%。

那其实我在黄金上，我在 APP 里有分享过我两次在黄金上的这个交易——NUGT 这一个标的的一个交易——还算是比较的好。我觉得应该是很大一部分有运气的成分在背后，但是从时间点上来说的话我觉得已经比较的完美。我在208的时候就把 NUGT 给卖了。那在周五的时候，其实 NUGT 包括黄金出现了比较大幅度的一个下跌。比特币下跌了3.3嘛，也是在前段时间走得比较好的。

可能让人比较感受、体感比较严重的是芯片板块继续下跌3.2%，高动能高贝塔动能板块下跌了5%。Q1到现在为止，高贝塔动能下跌了将近40%。硬件、而且芯片板块 SOX 半导体板块下跌了21%。那可能这些标的给人的体感会比较的严重一些，因为很多人在6月份或者7月份的时候追进了一些半导体板块。

而实际上你看前七大科技股在周五是表现得相对的强势的：亚马逊走得非常的强势，谷歌也 OK，然后苹果也 OK，然后微软也非常的好。

十五、黄金交易的时机复盘

讲到黄金，我在第一次选择做，就要差不多一个多月之前了，在第一次选择交易黄金的时候，当时的一个时间点是在七月份的会议之前。那七月份的会议之前，我说接下去无论它是选择加息也好，还是不加息也好，我认为最鹰派的这个时间点应该已经在身后。

那图里这条图里白色这条线是市场对于今年整个26年加息的这个次数的预期，截止到周五的收盘是1.536次，也就是市场认为在26年美联储将会加息1.5次。那我这边有一个箭头，就是在7月底的时候，就是差不多正好是在上一次会议之前，我认为这个最鹰派的时间点在身后。就是市场对于加息预期、加息次数的这个预期，最高值可能在身后。

那虽然未来可能去到1.8次、1.9次，甚至于接近于两次，但是我的一个判断是，最多美联储会加息两次，我们不会进入一个加息周期。这才是最重要的。只要不进入加息周期，加息两次，我并不认为对于整个美股这边会造成非常大的一些影响。

所以这是当时我的一个判断。那现在也是一样，我并不认为——即使他们、即使我们这次市场都认为，包括债市也认为美联储是变得鹰派了——但是我并不认为这一次的一个鹰派会对于资产价格造成非常大的一些影响。反而我仍然认为最鹰派的这个时间点应该已经在身后。

其实你会发现可能这一次其实沃什的态度其实也就是回到了6月份。那也许真的到9月份加息的时候，他又模棱两可，他又不给市场任何的一些指引。就他会反复嘛，现在最多是回到了6月份的这个沃什，然后7月份的沃什大家都不喜欢，九月份他又是通过这张嘴去调节市场这个预期，哎，市场还真信了，对吗？结果如果真的到九月份，市场都等着他去加息，他去告诉你："哎，我觉得不用加息怎么样"，他就有可能再次跳回到七月份的那个沃什，那市场又不喜欢。

所以我觉得现在还是在了解沃什的一个过程里边，他自己还是在建立一个信心的时候、建立市场信任的一个时候。其实今天他的这个言语本身，我认为对于长期来说，从中长期来说，我认为是一件好事，不是一件坏事。

好吧，那从鹰派这个角度去看，你可以看到蓝色这条线是黄金的价格，那黄金的价格其实已经出现了两三天的这个下跌了。那这一波黄金的下跌，如果因为市场对于加息预期的这个抬升，我认为黄金会再次会有一个进场的一个机会。我认为这一波黄金的反弹应该还没有结束。所以接下去黄金这一块是可以关注一下。

十六、比宏观更重要的是基本面：半导体估值回到七月底

然后我认为比现在当下的宏观——或者贝森特也好、凯文沃什也好——更加重要的是基本面。基本面是什么？基本面是现在整个半导体板块的估值又回到了将近7月底的那个水平了。

我这张图里是过去5年的一个 forward PE 向前看的这个市盈率。7月底的时候差不多是在19倍左右，然后到截止到周五的收盘是在19.3倍，就接近于7月底的这个水平了。那有些标的其实也已经回到了7月底的这个水平，有些标的还没有，那有些标的已经到了。

所以就和7月底我的一个看法一样，都现在整个芯片板块、整个 SOX、那整个半导体板块又回到了一个相对非常低的位置。

下面我画了一条线，那这条线是25年的一个低位和26年的3月份的这个低位，一次是关税，然后一次是战争。有没有可能再跌到那里？我并不知道。但是如果再跌到那边的话，从 ETF 就从整个板块这个角度去看，向下还有10%的这个空间，10%、11%的这个空间。

那即使你在现在这个位置，我说你如果没有意见，即使你在现在这个位置，你选择去进行加仓，再往下跌个5%，你再加一次；再往下跌10%，你再加一次，那又如何？对吧？你可以保证你从现在这个位置往下跌了10%之后，你能够总共算上加仓、算上建仓的话，你有三次加仓的这个机会。而真的估值如果跌到那一个位置的话，你就会知道是非常非常便宜的这个位置。

所以我认为我们可以讨论宏观的，我也可以和大家分享在宏观这一块我的一些看法，但是比起宏观来说，我认为当下可能应该更加应该关注的是整个 SOX 它的一个估值在什么那个位置，包括在 SOX 板块里边的一些标的是不是现在值得去布局。

十七、Marvell 财报解读：为什么估值最高

那讲到半导体板块，我们就来聊一下周四盘后发布财报的一个 Marvell。那周五的话 Marvell 是下跌了10%。那主要下跌的理由你可以去找很多，就你可以从包括他们的 margin 可能没有达到预期，或者指引没有达到市场的这个预期，谷歌这一次订单可能没有进来。你可以从各个角度去出发吧。

但下跌就下跌嘛，但我主要今天是想从估值这个角度去出发，和大家解释一下，为什么 Marvell 现在的估值是会比 AVGO 要高，甚至于会比英伟达要高。你会发现它是有一个阶梯性的一个——就 Marvell 相对是最高的，然后是 AVGO，然后是英伟达。那这背后的个逻辑是什么，我也和大家讲清楚。

首先我们先来看一些数据。那这已经是市场更新后的这个数据。他们上调了2027年的营收，然后也上调了2028年的这个营收。那像是他们上调到了18个百分点，那最终其实是非常有可能是可以做到18个百分点。甚至已经在聊29年，在他们下一次这个投资者会议的时候，会给出29年的这个指引。现在市场预期是25个基点。

其实我昨天在直播的时候，因为谷歌的订单要进来，在29年的时候要新的订单要进来，非常有可能在29年的这个营收能够达到30个基点以上。那当然取决于他们到底合同能够第一年的合同在29年落地的时候能够落地多少。所以我的期待是 at the minimum 最少是30个 billion。也就是说，现在市场预期才26、25.66，市场预计29年的这个营收增速是44%，所以我把44%划掉了。如果按照30个基点去算的话，那29年营收这个增速在70%。

所以你会发现未来的三年，就27年算上、27年算上28、29的话，它的营收增速分别是45%、50%和70%。它的营收增速在干嘛？在加速。

以前我和大家聊过的，市场最喜欢这类的公司，营收增速在加速，然后你的 margin 在加速，它市场马上就会做一个线性外推。那市场是最喜欢这类的公司。所以如果我们从静态市盈率这个角度去看，它现在静态市盈率是在65倍、65.6倍左右。那根据它未来三年 EPS 这个增速去推算的话，现在它的一个 PEG 其实只有1倍。

十八、博通估值对比：体量更大但增速会放缓

然后我们来看博通。博通也同样的，26年和27年，就是今年的下半年和27财年，营收增速是66%和64%。你会发现，其实博通在今年和明年，它的一个营收增速比 Marvell 还要高。它的营收的体量已经比 Marvell 高很多，营收体量在28年的27年的话是 Marvell 的10倍。那么它是174个 billion，Marvell 是18个 billion，将近10倍不到一些。但是就营收增速比 Marvell 要高，体量又比 Marvell 要高。

其实你会发现，从这个角度你可能会 argue，你说为什么博通它的估值竟然会比 Marvell 要低呢？问题在哪呢？问题就是在他们28年，就是你要往两年半之后去看。往两年半之后去看，我这边打了一个问号，28财年他们的营收到底是多少？按照现在市场的预期，营收增速是34%。你会发现出现了一个什么问题？营收增速在28年要进行放缓，29年会在28年的基础上继续放缓。

但是 Marvell 不一样，Marvell 做一个线性外推的话，它是每一年的营收增速都会比上一年要高。所以这就是为什么，如果从 PEG 这个角度去看，前面我们算出来 Marvell 根据现在市场的预期差不多是一倍左右，博通我算出来差不多是0.78倍、0.79倍、0.8倍左右。如果从下一个财年的 forward PE 去看，博通这边是19倍，只有19倍，然后 Marvell 的话是32倍至34倍左右。那么 forward PE 的话，两者之间明显差得非常的多。

十九、英伟达估值对比：体量最大、增速却在明年最高

然后我们再来看英伟达。英伟达其实比更比他们更加的夸张。当然我这边是 EPS 的这个增速，你看就 EPS 增速营收增速一样。那么营收增速，英伟达给了 28财年是70%，你会发现比 AVGO 还要高，一山还比一山高。体量的话，英伟达的体量比 AVGO 的体量还要大，对吗？但是你会发现，英伟达的增速——是却竟然是未来一年半的增速——竟然是这三家公司里面最高的，但是估值却是最低的。

为什么？还是其实类似于和前面 AVGO 一样的道理，市场预计29年你的营收增速就会出现一个放缓，在28年的这个基础上，能从66%、70%左右吧放缓到31%、30%左右。

那在这个基础上呢，我现在算出来英伟达的一个 PEG 优势是多少？0.67倍。那比 Marvell 要低，然后比 AVGO 也要低。那从 forward PE 这个角度去看28财年，英伟达的 forward PE 是多少？14倍。AVGO 是19倍，英伟达是14倍，Marvell 是32倍。

二十、三家公司估值差异背后的两个原因

那为什么会出现这种情况？我们把三家公司放在一起的话，我认为有两个原因。

第一个原因就是 Marvell 市场做一个线性外推，它每一年的营收增速都会比上一年要高。最主要一个原因还是它体量相对是最小的。那你才十几个 billion 一年的这个营收，一旦谷歌的一个订单进来之后，对于一家公司来说，它的影响就会非常的大。

那谷歌要去扶持 Marvell 其实也非常的合理。它希望去增加它的一个供应链。从未来从供应链、从 networking 这个角度去看，如果可以扶持另外一家公司和 AVGO 去竞争的话，对于谷歌来说是一件好事，它可以降低它的一个成本。啊从 AVGO、从 Broadcom 这个角度去看，他们也在分散他们这个客户，那从原来的一个谷歌，然后现在有了 OpenAI，有了包括 Anthropic 之间的这个合作，是一样的。所以两家公司都在分散自己客户的一个风险。

那所以 Marvell 因为它体量相对比较小，所以它的营收增速可以每一年比上一年都在增加。那市场做一个线性外推，就愿意给这类的公司相对比较高的这个估值。

那同时因为从体量这个角度去，英伟达是最大的，英伟达的估值也是最大的。嗯，然后接下去是 AVGO，接下去是博通。那你的估值越高，可能市场对于这一类的标的想象空间可能就会越低。

二十一、三家公司如何选？

那最后大家肯定会问我，那么这三家公司哪家公司值得去投？其实这不是一个一定要是选 A 或者选 B 的一个问题。这三家公司我认为都是便宜的。你 Marvell 你从 forward PE 可能没有那么的便宜，但是你看它那个 PEG 是1倍，其实也不贵的。因为它未来的增速会慢慢的抬高嘛。三家公司都是便宜的。

就取决——而且每家公司你会发现英伟达的波动一定是最低的，所以它一定是你自己可以承受的这个风险，英伟达的风险波动一定是最低的，风险也是最低的；AVGO、博通的风险相对会高一些，波动也相对会大一些；Marvell 的这个波动一定是最大的。所以完全取决于你能够接受什么样的一些风险和波动。

## 一、市场情绪的"照妖镜"效应：价格才是真正的宏观分析师
一个反常识的观察：**大多数人以为自己在分析市场，其实是在被价格分析**。视频里最锋利的一刀，是揭示了同一批人在两个月内的思维反转——6月底担心"指数下跌软件会一起跌"，8月底担心"指数下跌硬件会继续跌"。**恐惧的对象在轮换，但恐惧的语法结构一模一样**：都是"线性外推 + 厌恶浮亏 + 事件催化"的三段论。
这里藏着一个跨领域的连接——这与**认知心理学中的"可得性启发式"（Availability Heuristic）**完全同构：人们不是根据基本面判断风险，而是根据"最近发生了什么、疼不疼"来判断风险。凯文沃什的讲话本身波动有限（标普基本横盘），但因为**芯片股跌了3.2%**，人的神经系统会自动把"疼痛"归因给沃什的"鹰派"，形成一个虚假的因果链。**真正的鹰派不是沃什，是你的杏仁核**。
## 二、贝森特与沃什的"双簧"：一个被误读的博弈论均衡

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、SaaS的"陷阱价值"：被压抑的真相突然被AI解放

Benioff 在这期节目里透露了一个反直觉的洞见——Salesforce 里存在大量"trap value"（陷阱价值），即产品功能极其丰富，但普通用户永远发现不了。过去二十年，SaaS 行业的商业模式其实建立在"用户使用率极低"这个悖论之上：企业为100%的功能付费，实际只用20%。

而 AI Agent 的登场，第一次让"未被使用的功能"具备了商业价值。Agent 是完美的 power user，它会主动挖出那些藏在菜单第七层的功能，并说"我要不要帮你启用？"

这里有个惊人的反转：所有人都以为 AI 会杀死 SaaS，结果 AI 反而在"激活"SaaS 的沉睡资产。Salesforce 20% 单日暴涨的本质，不是它做出了新东西，而是市场突然意识到——它过去卖出去但没被消费的那部分，现在要开始被消费了。这在会计上叫"库存释放"，在物理上叫"势能转动能"。SaaS 的护城河不是功能，而是被埋葬的功能。

二、跨领域连接：Nvidia、Druckenmiller的AI写作、和美国国债，其实是同一个故事

表面看这三件事毫不相干，但它们共享一个隐藏结构——"人类决策系统正在被外包给概率机器，而制度还没有准备好接住它。"

  • Nvidia 一个季度赚 600 亿，是因为整个美国经济把"国家级基础设施投资"外包给了几家私企——因为国会瘫痪、财政破产，美国政府这个"百年前的建设主体"已经消失了。Chamath 一句话点破："100 年前该是美国政府干的事，现在是 Nvidia、Google、Meta 在背。"
  • Druckenmiller 用 AI 写社论，把"个人判断的表达权"外包给了模型。J-Cal 的愤怒不是因为文章写错了，而是因为权威的产生机制被替换了——我们过去付费购买的是"Druckenmiller 大脑的稀缺性"，现在这份稀缺性被稀释了。
  • 30年期国债突破5.2%，是市场在给"国会的判断力"打折——债券投资者正在做同一件事：把对美国财政纪律的信任外包给市场价格机制。

三件事的共同深层结构：当有机的判断系统（政府、专家、机构）失灵时，市场会自动寻找机械化替代品——芯片、模型、利率。但这些替代品都不承担"共同体后果"，所以危机会以更快的速度累积。

三、意想不到的观察：癌症疫苗和美国财政的诡异同构

Freeberg 讲 Moderna 时揭示了一个模式：神经抗原免疫疗法的核心技术是纳税人几十年前用 NIH 拨款培育出来的公共知识，现在被私人公司用 FDA 审批流程"圈地"，做成50万美元一针的专利药。

这个模式和美国财政困局形成惊人的镜像——社会用集体资源培育的东西（公共健康基础、国家信用），最终都被少数私人主体套现，成本由多数人承担。

更深一层：Moderna 从 200 亿市值涨到 600 亿，不是因为它发明了新东西，而是因为它成功"占领了监管通道"。这和为什么加州的高铁能烧掉 1000 亿而不停工，本质上是同一个机制——在民主制度下，谁能把"公共成本"转化成"私人租金"，谁就是赢家。 Freeberg 提到蒙大拿有诊所5万美元就能做同样的事，就像布莱特兰用民营资本建成了佛罗里达高铁——替代方案一直存在，但制度不允许你选择替代方案。

四、一个尖锐的元洞察

这期播客里有个"隐藏的时代主题"没有被明说：2026年的美国正在经历一场"责任的蒸发"。

  • 国会不为财政负责，把烂摊子甩给 Bessent
  • Bessent 不为长期国债负责，用 buyback 短期粉饰
  • Druckenmiller 不为自己的文字负责，甩给 AI
  • 政府不为科研成果的公共性负责，甩给药厂
  • 药厂不为治疗普及性负责，甩给 FDA 保护伞
  • 媒体不为准确报道负责，甩给点击率
  • 家长不为孩子的手机使用负责，等着 Meta 来关

Chamath 说的那句"必须要有一个 acute moment（急性时刻）才能触发结构性变化"——这不是预测，这是在一个"所有人都在把责任向下一层踢"的系统里，唯一的能量释放方式。 而AI 恰好是最理想的"责任接收器"——因为它不会反驳，不会离职，不会投票。这才是本期节目最令人不安的隐藏共识。

How do they get that key for me personally versus you? How do you get that into the mRNA? They would take a sample of your tumor or cancer cells. So when you take your, let's say you have you know, melanoma. And the reason that melanoma is one of the kind of biggest targets for this immunotherapy is that melanomas have very kind of unique DNA mutations because of UV light hitting the skin. And so the particular cancer that you'll get in a melanoma that you have is going to be very unique with respect to the rest of your body. It's going to be a very unique mutation.

So they take the, a little bit of the melanoma, they get the DNA out of it, and when you do DNA sequencing, you multiply the DNA by millions or billions of times, you put all that DNA in a DNA sequencer, it gets chopped up and read, and then the sequence data comes back and it says, "This is what makes this cancer unique. It's this little sequence of the DNA." And that sequence of the DNA causes that cancer to make a unique protein that is basically like a key or an ID or a fingerprint of that cancer. They then take that DNA, and make protein from it, put that protein in your body, and now your immune system goes crazy and starts attacking that protein because it's like, "Oh, antigen, antigen, I got to go get it." Now that those cells are activated, those immune cells are activated to that protein, they'll eventually go destroy that cancer.

So this has been successful. There have been hundreds of trials with this neoantigen-based therapy for many different types of cancer. And there's all these trials that have tried to figure out what's the right technique for delivering the neoantigen. Do we make the protein and then stick it in your body? Or, in this case, with what Moderna did, make mRNA and stick it in your body. And the mRNA causes your own cells to now make that protein and spit it out, ends up in your blood, and now your immune cells got activated. So rather than making the protein ex vivo, which means outside of your body, you're making the protein in your body, in vivo. And now your body's making the protein. So the idea with the mRNA concept is you can get one shot. That shot goes into your body, and now your body's making that protein, just like we made the COVID vaccine. Yes. Your cells would make a particular protein segment that would activate your immune system, and it would go kill that cancer.

There's other questions around what are the other adjuvants, what types of cancer can you use this system for, and then combination therapies. Are there other cancer drugs that you can do this in combination with And all the trials that have been going on are all about this delivery mechanism, the technique that's used, the types of cancer, the dosing, and getting all of that stuff right.

监管俘获与50万美元的问题

Now, what's interesting about this is it is much more of a technique than a drug. In the traditional sense of process of it's a process, right? So the process is customized per person. So there's some cost to doing it per person. That's right. But the cost because I do DNA sequencing in my company all day long, getting that sample very cheap, getting the DNA data very cheap, actually doing a lot of the upfront work very cheap. Now, theoretically, making the mRNA, or making the protein should also be pretty cheap. But it's human trials and human safety. And so there's a lot of questions around how do you make sure that everything's safe? And what's the right combinations that people don't get overreacted immune systems, or that people don't have adverse side effects. So that's all of the tuning of this.

But I think what frustrates me the most about all of this, and everyone's kind of lauding this as some unique breakthrough and special and powerful, and it's not. Because a lot of people are going to places like Montana, and they are getting peptides printed for their particular cancer sequence, and they are making their own neoantigens, putting it in their body, and getting cured of their cancer. You can pay someone $50,000 to do this for you today. There's a lot of clinics that'll do it, and it's not a special FDA-approved drug. To your point, J. Cal, it's a process. The process is take the DNA sequence from my cancer, make a protein, put it back in my body, my immune system goes and destroys the cancer in my body. Great idea.

So why is Moderna saying that they're going to charge $500,000 for this? And that's what I think frustrates me about all this. Everyone's lauding this and everyone's very happy about this. But I'm actually pretty sad and frustrated and disappointed by this. I don't think that this technique which has been largely developed through several decades of iteration, research and development, which was largely funded by NIH and other public funding dollars that has led to this incredible concept of neoantigen immunotherapy for cancer, which can eradicate or theoretically eliminate many different types of cancer, should now be patented, FDA approved and charged half a million dollars for people to get treated for this. And so what I don't like about this story is is that a private pharmaceutical company has seen their market cap go from 20 billion to 60 billion, because they went through this regulatory process to create what in my mind is a form of regulatory capture, and making the case that it's all about safety and trials, and we've got patents and all this other stuff, when fundamentally, there's an underlying technique that was funded by a lot of public research dollars that I think should be more open sourced, more ubiquitous, and every hospital should be trained on how to do this process to treat cancer patients. It should become much more of a ubiquitous thing.

专利、mRNA与CAR T疗法

Do you think that people, I have two questions, we can end it on that, but do you think they're going to be able to successfully defend this patent in the United States and then also globally? Because there's obviously a global world here and people do travel for treatments now, medical tourism is a thing. So if it's a half million dollars here, can it be done for 50K in South Korea, Japan, other places? And then second, whatever happened with mRNA vaccines And the COVID vaccine and a lot of the concerns people had, we never got an update on that, but obviously this podcast started during all of that. And that was the first rollout at scale, correct? For mRNA? Yes. How do you feel?

Yeah. For years, Moderna was working towards this mRNA based cancer. They're calling it a vaccine, but it's really immunotherapy. A vaccine means you prevent yourself from getting something. Whereas in this case, you're actually getting rid of something you already have. So I don't like the word vaccine. But Moderna worked on this for years and they never really kind of got to market with it. And then COVID came about and they pivoted very quickly and got this COVID vaccine out.

Moderna has a whole bunch of patents on the techniques and tools that they use to make mRNA and to make sure that it's not integrated into the human genome and it doesn't actually use a traditional kind of replicating system. So you can't actually replicate that mRNA, which means it won't start propagating in your body because your cells typically might start making copies of RNA if it ends up in your cells. So there was a lot of stuff that Moderna developed that made their particular mRNA technology patented and safer and so on. So I think that they do have strong patent coverage on their particular set of tools for mRNA.

But when I described earlier, so if I take the sequence of your cancer cell, And I look at the DNA of it and I'm like, I found what makes it unique. There's this little sequence. And now I take that sequence of DNA and I can stick it in a bacterial cell, E. coli, in a little tank, what's called a bioreactor. And that bacterial cell will now start to make that protein because I've taken the DNA and put it in the E. coli cell. So now the E. coli cell is coding that DNA into into RNA, into proteins, because that's the sequence, right? DNA turns into RNA, turns into proteins. So that E. coli cell, there's billions of copies of those cells, they make billions of copies of the protein, you isolate the protein out of the bioreactor, and you can inject it into your body. And when you inject that protein into your body, and now your immune system gets activated. So you don't necessarily need mRNA, is my point. And mRNA is a really effective way of doing this. It's super cheap because you don't have to go make all the protein outside the body. You can literally just print the mRNA and get one shot and you're done.

But that end-to-end system, the real cost of doing that is very low. And so this is one of those things where we have a very big fundamental question that we should all be asking, which is like, should we be giving the monopoly on cancer treatment to to this company that went through this FDA process and filed a bunch of patents on certain techniques, but the general theory, the general thesis, the general therapeutic process is well described, well understood, generally understood, and should be available everywhere. And I think over the next couple of years, we are gonna see this cancer immunotherapy-based system start to proliferate, and you will see this happening overseas very cheap. It is very efficacious. And we act you and I actually have a friend in common who's kind of standing up a business to do this in a very cheap way up in Montana where you have a right to try and they can make this stuff. So we are going to see I think more of this come to work. But it is for certain types of cancer, very efficacious, very safe, very effective. So I'm excited by this.

Just for people who are listening who are normies, All of this cancer treatment requires early detection, and that's something that people have been working on with the blood test, the Galleria, I believe it's called. So getting to the cancer and getting regularly tested is a critical part of this, yes? So you're talking about a Galleria test by Grail? The blood test, yeah. The blood test, yeah. Just early testing is the key piece for all of us to keep in mind. Get tested early and often for cancer.

Yeah, and remember, there's a bunch of these new what are called modalities, new modes of therapy, therapeutic modalities that are being used to destroy cancer. One was CAR T therapy, where you take T cells out of your body, and you use CRISPR or some other system to reprogram those T cells to go after, remember that protein I described? So you actually program the T cells to go find a specific protein in your body and destroy it. So they go find the the protein that's unique to a specific type of cancer cell, and the T cells get put back in your body and they destroy it. CAR T therapy. CAR T therapy costs a million dollars. And for people with blood cancers, where the cancer cells aren't clumped together in a tumor, but blood cancers, the cancer cells float around individually in the blood. And so by putting T cells in your blood, it's very easy, or it's much easier for the T cells to find the cancer cell, grab them and destroy them. And so for blood cancers like multiple myeloma, the efficacy is incredible with CAR T therapies now. So that's a new type of modality. This is a new type of modality, this mRNA or neoantigen therapy. So there's all these new techniques that are being used to destroy cancer. And I think in aggregate, we should be very excited and optimistic about where this is headed.

Wow. Thanks for sharing. And let's hope for the best with implementing this. And I love this right to try. That seems to be something we should talk about in a future episode. We'll see you all next time on the All In Podcast. Bye-bye. Bye-bye.

结尾闲聊

Besties are gone. Dog taking a listen to your driveway sex. Oh man. My avatars are really being put in some- We should all just get a room and just have one big huge orgy because they're all just useless. It's like this like sexual tension that they just need to release somehow. The beat. Let your beat. Your beat. We need to get merged. Besties are back. I'm going all- What? I'm going all in.

## 一、SaaS的"陷阱价值"：被压抑的真相突然被AI解放
Benioff 在这期节目里透露了一个反直觉的洞见——Salesforce 里存在大量"trap value"（陷阱价值），即产品功能极其丰富，但普通用户永远发现不了。**过去二十年，SaaS 行业的商业模式其实建立在"用户使用率极低"这个悖论之上：企业为100%的功能付费，实际只用20%。**
而 AI Agent 的登场，第一次让"未被使用的功能"具备了商业价值。Agent 是完美的 power user，它会主动挖出那些藏在菜单第七层的功能，并说"我要不要帮你启用？"
**这里有个惊人的反转**：所有人都以为 AI 会杀死 SaaS，结果 AI 反而在"激活"SaaS 的沉睡资产。Salesforce 20% 单日暴涨的本质，不是它做出了新东西，而是市场突然意识到——它过去卖出去但没被消费的那部分，现在要开始被消费了。这在会计上叫"库存释放"，在物理上叫"势能转动能"。**SaaS 的护城河不是功能，而是被埋葬的功能。**

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] How AI Could Concentrate the World’s Labor in a Few Companies - Dylan Patel
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、当"人口爆炸"发生在服务器里：这是一场被误读为经济议题的人口学事件

Dylan 说的"每年 10 倍"其实并不是算力增长率——而是AI 有效人口的年增长率。这个数字如果放到生物学语境里是荒谬的：地球上从未有过任何具备高等认知的物种以这种速率繁殖过。哺乳类翻倍要以年为单位，细菌以分钟为单位——但没有一种"细菌"能写代码、做研究、执行阴谋。

真正令人意外的观察是：AI 对齐问题的本质，其实正在悄悄从"技术问题"漂移成"人口学问题"。当 Dylan 说"如果 AI 是 misaligned 的，那世界就是 misaligned 的，因为世界上大多数的'心智'都在那里"——他实际上是在说：未来的"民意"不是由 80 亿人构成，而是由两家公司里那几十亿到几百亿个推理进程构成。这意味着 alignment 不再是让机器听人类的话，而是决定谁的"人口"能定义"人类"。这是一个被 AI 安全社区严重低估的框架转换。

二、Jane Street 现象：一个正在关闭的套利窗口

访谈里最有金融史意味的一段，是那个"Jane Street 每兆瓦赚 500 万，愿付 Anthropic 100 万，而 Anthropic 内部使用可能创造几亿"的推理。Dylan 用这段话不动声色地宣告了一件事：我们正处在 AI 算力的最后一段"批发时代"。

跨领域看，这几乎是19 世纪末洛克菲勒故事的重演——早期石油公司把原油卖给下游炼油商，直到发现"垂直整合+自己炼油"利润是外卖的十倍，从此外部市场消失。Anthropic / OpenAI 现在还在"卖原油"（API 调用），是因为它们的内部"炼油厂"（自动化研究、代码代理、模型自迭代）还没跑通。一旦跑通，API 会像 20 世纪初的原油现货市场一样迅速枯竭。今天 Cursor、Perplexity、Character 之流的存在，本质上是历史窗口，不是行业结构。

这里还有一个更冷的观察：Dylan 自己在直播里承认"这是我的 cope"——他一边论证权力必然集中，一边希望外部经济能从 Anthropic 获益更多，然后立刻承认这两件事在逻辑上不能同时成立。这种"作者亲手拆掉自己的救生艇"的时刻，在访谈里极为罕见，也是这段对话最有分量的地方。

三、AI 正在反转资本主义的元定理

Dwarkesh 说"资本主义之所以有效，是因为它把决策去中心化了"。这是海耶克式的老命题。但 Dylan 悄悄把它翻了个面："AI 可能是人类历史上第一个'中心化比去中心化更高效'的通用技术"。

这个论断如果成立，其含义远远超出 AI 行业。它意味着过去 250 年被视为"文明常识"的东西——市场分散决策比计划经济更快、更聪明——并不是一条自然律，而只是"人类作为有限带宽处理器"这个特定条件下的暂时最优解。一旦"处理器"可以无限扩容、且规模收益不递减，海耶克就被物理学取代了。

跨领域再拉一个类比：这其实和黑洞的临界质量是同一种数学。一旦某物达到自吸积阈值，它周围的物质会以加速度而非匀速被卷入。AI 训练的数据回流、部署学习、内部研究闭环——三者一起构成了一个"认知黑洞的吸积盘"。资本主义之前从未遇到过这种物理结构，因为没有任何一个工厂能用自己造的车去设计下一代工厂。AI 是第一个可以这样做的东西。

所以真正应该被问的问题不是"我们如何避免集中"，而是——如果集中是这个技术的物理属性而不是政策选择，那么人类文明该如何在一个"物理上不允许分权"的时代重新定义自由？ 这个问题目前没有人认真在答。

📝 转录文本

The Setup: AI Labor Is Compounding at 10× a Year

One thing I find crazy about these scenarios is just how much of the world's future labor supply ends up in very few companies — and also how fast that labor supply grows year-over-year.

So if compute at the frontier (in flop terms) is growing 4 or 5× a year, and further, the compute required to share the — uh — capability is decreasing 3× a year, then the compute at the frontier, or basically the effective AI population size at the frontier labs, is increasing 10× year over year.

And so that doesn't really matter that much right now, because AIs are not good enough to do full jobs, or be as autonomous as people in their capacity to do work, or pull off schemes, or whatever. But if the current trend continues, you have a world where OpenAI goes from having, say, 10 million basically-AI-laborers this year, to 100 million the next year, to a billion the year after that.

And then pretty soon — even if compute scaling slows down — it doesn't take many more years before each company individually has more labor equivalents than there are people on Earth. And I think that's a thing that is very plausible by the end of this decade: that there's more AI labor, more effective population within a single lab, than there are people on Earth.

Centralization Is the Under-Discussed Story

So we talk often about centralization of power because of nationalization or whatever, but we don't think enough about the fact that we're actually moving very fast into a regime where most AI labor — or, sorry, most people, in terms of work output — is just concentrated within two labs, who are consuming more and more of the world's compute.

And so, if these AIs are misaligned, then most of the world is misaligned, basically — because most of the world's minds are there. But even if they're not, it just — very few companies have a lot of influence.

It's sort of… there was the whole spat recently where — I think Gavin Baker was like, "Dario believes that there'll only be one company in the world," and then Sholto and Dario came out and were like, "No, no, no, we didn't say that." But ultimately, if you believe in RSI, and you believe the labs are the most effective user of compute and can generate the most value from the compute, then the only thing that's going to happen is centralization of compute. And if you believe in AI-researchers-RSI-AGI, then all of this exists — all of this is the base…

Even Without RSI, the Population Compounds

This is even true if there's no RSI. The current effective population of the frontier is currently increasing 10× year over year for a given level of capabilities. Right? So if you get to the level of capabilities which is a — a very competent remote worker, or a very competent software engineer, or a very competent researcher — that population of those would 10× year over year at the current rate of capabilities.

And without RSI. Then once you have RSI, it's —

Like maybe growing 100× a year, or 1000× a year, or their intelligence is increasing but the population isn't increasing, or some mixture of the two. Right?

Is There Any World That Isn't Centralized?

Um, yeah. I mean — I guess, what world do you see, Dwarkesh, where everything is not centralized? Because it seems to me that every force is screeching towards centralization. And that's scary as hell.

Yeah.

I don't — you know, I would love for it not to be centralized completely. But maybe that's the whole point of a machine that loves grace, right? Is — it is everything, and it makes our lives great.

Yeah. It's so hard to think about the future.

The Two Economies of Scale

But I agree with you that I think the fundamental problem is that lab AI training has huge economies of scale — because any effort you spent into training an AI for a specific skill or specific set of knowledge gets amortized across billions of sessions or billions of users. So that's one effect.

The other effect is: if you're slightly ahead in the AI race and compute is in shortage, you can charge a much higher markup, because you can better economize the scarce resource. So there are two effects which give more and more to the person who's ahead in the AI race.

There may be more, right? So if the models are learning from deployment, and one model is deployed much more widely than another one, it's getting much more real-world data.

Yeah, your point is taken that — whether it's user deployment and continual learning, whether it's training having these economies of scale, whether it's the incremental progress that the best AI model helps you make the next AI model —

RSI —

All of these things —

I didn't mention RSI —

All of these things point to centralization.

The Intellectual Project That's Missing

So I think one of the big intellectual projects, honestly, that — yeah, we should spend some time thinking about async, or at least I'll spend some time thinking about — is: what is a vision of a decentralized, broadly-empowered future after AGI that takes these economies of scale seriously?

The alternative vision is that the government controls it, and maybe you think you can trust the government more because it's not a private corporation.

I don't trust the government, and I don't trust Dario, and I don't trust Zuck.

Yeah. Yeah. That's the problem, right?

But — obviously, it's very easy to be wrong about the future, and you don't anticipate a key effect or something that changes everything. But ex ante, it's very hard to see a reason why, or how, we avoid a scenario where we have to choose one.

Why AI Inverts the Logic of Capitalism

It's why capitalism worked, right? It's the decentralized decision-making and decentralized power — and why super-centralized capitalistic economies actually grew slower than super-decentralized capitalist economies, to some extent. You have to have rule of law and all this, but…

Then AI flips all this on its head, right? And ultimately you're like — actually, private ownership is probably not the most efficient economy, and therefore it grows slower than an AI economy which is centralized. It's still private ownership, but it's — how many firms are really involved in this?

Like, the share of the economy that's — what, like 5% of the economy? Or something like that? In the US — sorry, 1 trillion divided by 30, less than that, sorry — but yeah, maybe 2% of the economy right now. It's like Nvidia is a huge share of it, and then Anthropic and OpenAI and these hyperscalers, and obviously there are other firms involved — but a large share of the AI stuff is just happening from very few companies. So it could be private property, but very few companies are involved.

I mean, this is what the structure of the market is doing. So what can prevent it? I don't know. Unless AI progress slows down.

Unless governments regulate the [__] out of it. This is all that happens.

In which case — you know, we're headed for a world where either we have super-concentration of resources and we pray that that one company gets everything right, or we have governments slow everything down, and people slow everything down, and you have a slowdown of progress somehow — hopefully — and there is more of a balance of power. And even as we go towards an AGI-ASI-RSI, everything along the way will still lead to someone… someone's going to allocate — going to capture more resources.

So it's kind of hard for a framework in which AI doesn't lead to super-concentration.

The Jane Street Consolation (and Its Expiration Date)

Now, the one positive thing here is that today Anthropic does not capture most of the value. So we can talk all we want about, "Oh, you know, they went from $20 million per megawatt to $100 million per megawatt," but they're still paying $13[M] for a lot of the compute they're buying.

But at the end of the day, the reason they've gone to $100 million per megawatt is because Jane Street is capturing $300 million per megawatt, or $500 million per megawatt. Or Dwarkesh — from researching his podcast and learning about credit — is capturing, you know, how many dollars per megawatt now? How much can you use? Tough.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

But, you know, I think that's the one saving grace — that the rest of the economy maybe profits so much more from Anthropic —

No, but the whole logic you're laying out earlier — of them reallocating inference to R&D — the whole logic of that is that the returns to labor inside AI labs is much higher —

This is my hope.

— than the returns outside.

Yeah. This is my cope.

I agree. In all scenarios of the world — you know, there's 80,000 worlds, and only one of them Anthropic doesn't own the whole world — is that, again, power concentrates because "I don't want to send the tokens outside. They're more valuable inside."

Why Anthropic Will Eventually Stop Selling to Jane Street

And so it's the same thing, right? Why would I let Jane Street, you know, make all this money off of these degenerate options traders?

Hey, they're a sponsor. Come on.

Jesus Christ.

No, I think it's great. I think it's great. It's a good value for the world to make it an efficient market.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. You know, Jane Street making all this money off of getting the world view correctly, making money off of degenerate options traders, whatever it is — you know, why would Anthropic allocate compute to that if the end monetization that Jane Street has per megawatt is 200, so they're willing to pay Anthropic 100 — well, what if Anthropic can just generate hundreds of millions of dollars per megawatt by using that compute internally?

And that's what's happening.

Yeah. Yeah. Well, on that somber note — I guess we'll meet again when the RSI is officially kicked off.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here, and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

item.title: [Lex Clips] DHH on AI psychosis | Lex Fridman Podcast Clips
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、把"精神病"这顶帽子反戴回去——一次修辞上的柔道

DHH 最锋利的一击不是辩护，而是诊断反转：真正处于妄想状态的，是那些看着世界剧变却坚持"不过是电子鹦鹉"的人。这不是简单的口舌之快，而是暗合了库恩（Thomas Kuhn）在《科学革命的结构》里描述的"范式的不可通约性"——两个范式内的人看着同一张纸，却看见不同的图案。有趣的是，DHH 自己 9 个月前就是那个"看不见"的人；Tobi Lütke 把备忘录递到他手上，他嗤之以鼻。这种"曾经是自己现在要说服的人"的经历，让他的辩护带有一种福柯式的自省：谁在定义疯狂，往往取决于谁尚未跨过那道感知阈值。

二、勒芒赛道上诞生的操作系统——一个几乎没人注意的元隐喻

一个容易被忽略的细节：Omarchy 起源于他在勒芒 24 小时耐力赛间隙看 YouTube 时的灵感。这不是巧合，而是一种几乎潜意识的宣言。勒芒的核心不是极速，而是在极限速度下不炸引擎的持续输出——法拉利的极速 P4 在勒芒输给了看起来更慢但更聪明的福特 GT40。DHH 对 AI 的哲学正在复刻这条曲线：他反复强调"由我引导"、"我有使命"、"不感到过载"。当 Lex 描述自己像《梦之安魂曲》里的角色被快感冲垮，DHH 描述的是赛车手在漫长夜晚保持节奏。他不是在拒绝加速，他是在拒绝无方向的加速。这可能是这段对话里最容易被漏掉的哲学。

三、稀缺资源的迁移：从"能力"到"意图"——AI 时代真正的心理学转折

这里有一个跨领域的连接值得挖：心理学、经济学、脑科学都在讲同一件事，但没人把它们拼起来。

  • 心理学（Viktor Frankl）：过载不是外部信息量的问题，而是意义系统的缺失。
  • 经济学：当一种生产要素变得几乎免费（AI 让代码变得像空气），瓶颈就会跳到剩下的稀缺要素——方向、品味、判断力。
  • 神经科学（Lex 顺口带过的 Neuralink 带宽论）：真正的限制不再是打字速度，而是"想清楚一件事"的速度。

把三者叠加，你会得到一个反直觉的结论：AI 让程序员变得像艺术总监，而大多数人抱怨的"AI 精神病"其实是"没有作品目标的人第一次被迫直面自己没有作品目标"。DHH 没被冲垮，不是因为他更聪明，而是因为他早就有 Omarchy 这个执念在等这批算力落地。Lex 描述的燃尽感，本质上是多个 project 争夺同一个稀缺资源——但那个稀缺资源不再是时间，而是"专注在某一个未来"的意愿。

四、一个隐藏的历史类比——为什么"看不见的人"这次会输得特别快

40 年里，Lisp、Smalltalk、四代语言、低代码，都承诺过"普通人也能编程"，都失败了。DHH 说这次不一样，但没有点破为什么这次不一样。我给你一个更狠的类比：这更像 1900 年前后电力从"工厂动力源"过渡到"配电网络"的时刻。之前的电力革命，工厂主必须重新设计整个车间才能受益，多数人观望了 20 年；等到通用电气把电力做成"墙上插座"，观望者用 5 年被彻底甩开。Claude Code / agent 就是那个"插座"。DHH 说的"laggards will be overwhelmed by evidence"不是威胁，而是电气化历史正在重演的具体形态：不是技术突然变神，而是摩擦力突然消失，之前需要重构工作流的能力，现在直接从命令行滴出来。这也解释了他自己的时间线——2 月 Claude Code 发布，他 9 月才装上，然后 3 个月内世界翻了个面。摩擦消失的临界点，往往就是这么短。

📝 转录文本

The Steel-Man Question

Lex: So, some people listening to you right now will say DHH is suffering from the old case of AI psychosis. Yeah, can you steel-man the case that you are in fact experiencing a state of delusion, like One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, and can you argue against it?

Not Psychosis — Delirium

DHH: I'm in a state of delirium. That's the state I'm in. Because I have been working with computers for 40 years, and I've never seen the things that I've seen in just the last 2 months. A whole career, a whole life dedicating to the love of computers as my main focus for the working hours and then some — suddenly completely upended, suddenly completely rewritten. Of course I'm delirious. Who, looking at this reality, is not? If you are not delirious, or at the very least very excited… actually, I guess that's not even true. If you're not recognizing the gravity of the moment, that's the delusion. That's the psychosis. The psychosis is believing that the world is barely different, that we just have some electronic parrots reciting things to us.

Now, in my opinion, the reason this argument is actually brought up is because people are not able to see the fruits of the progress. That goes to your point earlier: where is the amazing software? Why isn't American GDP running at 12% year over year? First of all, give it a minute. It hasn't even been a year, god damn it. But second of all, I feel on my own account I have actually brought the pudding.

Omarchy Quattro — Bringing the Pudding

DHH: Omarchy Quattro launched on Friday. It's been downloaded by tens of thousands of people. And they like it. They like it a lot.

Lex: We should mention — going to Perplexity here — Omarchy is a highly opinionated Arch Linux–based desktop distribution centered on the Hyprland Wayland tiling compositor. It was created by David Heinemeier Hansson, DHH, as a polished developer workstation setup with a cohesive visual style and many everyday tools already configured.

DHH: Let me put it: Omarchy is a beautiful, modern, and opinionated Linux system. It's an alternative operating system to macOS and Windows, and it's freaking amazing.

Lex: And the Quattro thing is — you're pushing towards the age of agents.

Origin at Le Mans

DHH: That's right. That's the latest version that we just dropped out, which is also funny. The Omarchy project is only a year old and a little bit. I started it last summer in between sessions at the 24 Hours of Le Mans, where I had watched one too many YouTube videos on Linux ricing and got bitten by that bug. Started working on this second iteration of my attempt at creating a better Linux operating system.

The first iteration we talked about last time was called Omakub, was built on top of an existing system called Ubuntu, and it was fine. But the ambition I was able to pour into the new version, Omarchy, because I started seven layers deeper down the stack, was completely different — but it was still done in a pre-agentic world. I wrote all those bash scripts by hand in the beginning.

The Switchover to Agents

DHH: And then I got to see the midway point where things changed over. I did a couple of versions of Omarchy that had partial agent acceleration, and then 3 months ago it was full throttle: 100% everything is written by agents, but steered by me. And that just ended up being a very different experience and a very different operating system, because I was suddenly granted a limitless ceiling on my ambition.

I could look at any feature in Windows, on Mac, on other Linux systems, and say, "I want that." And the agents would deliver. So everything I wanted was suddenly within reach — which meant that I got a little delirious.

Who would not get delirious if suddenly a genie pops out of the bottle and says, "You can have whatever you want. Every feature you've ever dreamed of in an operating system, I can deliver them to you. Most of them in 5 minutes, a few in 20, and if we really go hog wild, it's going to take me 2 hours."

Overwhelm vs. Mission

Lex: Have you seen Requiem for a Dream, the movie? There's a drug-like effect here. I find, personally — we'll talk about many levels of this, but it is overwhelming how much power is placed in our hands so suddenly. And it's very hard to know, it's like with the Hobbit or something, what to do with it. I find myself truly overwhelmed with the multitasking, on the verge of almost burnt out, super excited about so many things, but ultimately looking back, you want to focus on one thing in a relationship.

DHH: I don't have that sense. I don't have the sense of overwhelm, I don't have the sense of dread, I don't have the sense of distortion — because I have a mission. I'm going somewhere. And therefore, I can channel all this new power towards a singular goal and outcome: creating the perfect computer. And therefore, all my investigations with AI are focused towards that end.

Now, I also have a day job, and we also use agents there, and that's also targeted towards specific outcomes. But with the Omarchy experience, I got to tap in straight in the back of my head and increase the bandwidth between ideas arriving in my brain and software emerging on the screen.

From Dial-Up to Fiber

DHH: It was like going from dial-up to fiber. I think on your podcast, Elon talked about the actual human bandwidth that Neuralink and other projects are trying to accelerate. Like, the bandwidth we're communicating over right now is quite low, because we're limited by our cognition, we're limited by the rate of speech. You're not limited by those things when you're working with a swarm of agents.

A Confession — The Nine-Months-Ago Self

DHH: Now, let me caveat this by saying: if I'd heard myself talk like this 9 months ago, I would probably use the label "AI psychosis." I think it would be fitting. Because 9 months ago, when people were talking like this, they weren't shipping. And I think that's the ultimate difference.

There were people who saw this early. I was not actually that early. As we've talked about, I was rather skeptical, and I was using AI in certain ways, but I was not the first person who downloaded Claude Code. I think Boris released that in end of February. I don't think I installed Claude Code until September. So there was about 6 months there where pioneers saw these glimmers of what the future was going to look like. It wasn't there yet — because the intelligence wasn't there, the harnesses weren't there — but they could see the glimmers.

Tobi Lütke and the Rocket

DHH: Tobi Lütke, the CEO of Shopify — and now my partner in crime on this Omarchy project in part — he's gotten pilled with Omarchy as well. He saw these things very early and he tried to tell me. And I wasn't seeing it. I was not seeing what he was seeing.

Lex: You were a hater.

DHH: Yes. I was still on Earth.

Lex: Okay.

DHH: And he had already boarded the rocket and was heading towards space. I remember actually reading his memo to the company, the AI memo, and thinking, "Ah, seems a little much. Like, you're making a big deal out of something that I cannot yet feel is a tangible thing." Because — where's the output of this? I try using it, it writes code I don't like, it wants to interrupt me all the time. Where are you getting this from?

So I get it. I totally get it. If you're not seeing what the current quality of intelligence can produce, of course you're going to look at someone and go, "They sound a little nutty." Because all your experience up until this point would tell you that they are nutty.

The 40-Year False Promise

DHH: If you look at the history of computer programming for the last 40, 50 years, people have been promising that regular people could write code just by talking. We're going to have fourth-generation languages. Lisp was once upon a time presented, Smalltalk was presented, as these environments that would let regular people write their own applications. And none of it came true — in the sense beyond, like, Microsoft Access databases or Excel spreadsheets. Those are end-user programming environments, but it's nothing like what we're able to do now.

And then — I mean, I'm not even talking about end users. I'm talking as me, someone who's been programming for 25 years, seeing the output and the acceleration and the quality, and then shipping it.

The Flood of Evidence

DHH: And I think that's what's going to change the entire conversation quite quickly. The few laggards who are still on the fence about whether this is actually useful, who are still trapped in a meme from early '25 about mechanical parrots — they're simply going to be overwhelmed by the evidence that's about to flood over them.

Lex: So, I hope to see projects like Omarchy — several of them — that really show agent first.

DHH: It's coming. All of it is coming.

Lex: In the silly spaces already mentioned — like video editing, all these kinds of apps that were like Type-Ora…

DHH: Yes.

Lex: …this kind of stuff.

item.title: [a16z] Why Top Founders Are Racing Into AI Infrastructure
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"心理反转"：我们正在见证软件行业最深的信仰崩塌

过去 40 年，硅谷奉行一条铁律——"神话的人月"（Mythical Man-Month）：你不可能靠砸钱和堆人追上一个领先两年的对手。这条定律塑造了从 Fred Brooks 到 Paul Graham 的整个软件哲学，也定义了 VC 的判断范式：技术领先＝时间壁垒。

但 Ben 在对话中悄悄扔下了一颗炸弹："Now that works."（现在这招管用了。）

这不是一个技术观察，而是一次范式颠覆。当 xAI 用 30 亿美元点亮一个集群就能几个月追平多年积累的 OpenAI，当 Kimi、Grok 可以"凭空冒出来就是真的"——软件行业赖以生存的"复利护城河"神话首次被资本一次性击穿。这意味着过去所有关于"先发优势"的投资逻辑正在失效，而这才是 a16z 悄悄改换赛道的真正原因，不是"AI 需要基础设施"这么表层。

一个让人不适的推论：如果金钱可以直接兑换智能，那么 VC 行业本身的价值主张——识别"稀缺的判断力"——正在被稀释。他们成立 Machine Age 基金，某种意义上是在逃向一个金钱仍然买不到答案的领域：物理约束、供应链、许可证、变压器交货周期。

二、跨领域连接：这不是"AI 泡沫"，这是"爱迪生 vs. 特斯拉"的 2.0 重演

对话里有一个几乎被一带而过的技术细节，却是整段访谈里最富历史反讽的时刻——当机架功率突破 100kW 时，交流电（AC）不再够用，数据中心开始改用直流电（DC）。而 Ben 顺口提到：这正是当年爱迪生所拥护、特斯拉击败的那种"危险的直流电"。爱迪生曾用电死大象和马来"证明"交流电危险，最终却输掉了整个电气化时代。

一个跨越 135 年的镜像出现了：电力工业的第一次基础设施浪潮由 AC 定义，第二次浪潮却在悄悄回归 DC。这不是复古，而是一个更深的规律——当负载密度极端集中时，物理定律偏爱直流。数据中心里 800V DC 的回归，意味着我们正在把电网重新分裂成"高密度节点集群"，就像互联网早期从主机集中式回到分布式，而现在又回到"AI 大教堂"式的集中。

更深层的连接：这场基础设施重构的隐藏对手不是英伟达的竞争者，而是19 世纪的水泥标准、20 世纪的电工执照制度、以及 21 世纪的地方噪音法规。整个 21 世纪的最前沿产业，正在被 19 世纪的钢筋混凝土供应瓶颈所限速——只有 2% 的美国电工持有 DC 认证。这是一场时代错位的战争。

三、最出人意料的观察：AI 正在重新发明"公司"这个概念，而它的操作系统还没写出来

Martin 提到 Grokbot 时说了一句轻描淡写却极具穿透力的话："AI 不再是你的延伸，它是一个员工——有自己的电脑，自己的浏览器。"

大多数人把这当成 UI 层的进化，但真正的震撼在别处：这是自 1602 年荷兰东印度公司发明"股份有限公司"以来，公司这个组织形式第一次遇到"非人类成员"。而 Ben 补充的那句更值得咀嚼——"我们花了很多年才学会怎么和人类员工共事，现在要重学。"

这里藏着一个几乎没人讨论的悖论：过去 400 年，管理学的所有工具（KPI、OKR、绩效考核、企业文化、组织行为学）都建立在"员工有生存需求、有社交需求、会疲劳、会走人"的前提之上。当这些前提全部消失，我们发现自己没有任何理论工具来管理一个"会烧掉大量 token、会编造事实、会突然聪明也会突然愚蠢、没有职业规划但可以 24 小时工作"的实体。

跨领域连接：这更像18 世纪工厂主第一次面对"机器"时的情境——他们不知道该按小时给机器发工资，还是按产量分红，最终发明了"折旧"这个会计概念。我们即将进入一个"AI 折旧学"和"AI 组织行为学"被发明的时代，而现在整个行业连基本词汇都还没形成。当 Ben 说"我们不是要慢慢淘汰人类"，那句话背后是没人知道新的组织均衡点在哪里——这才是 Machine Age 真正的"未开垦地带"，比任何芯片投资都更大。

而一个终极的反直觉推论：这一波 AI 最先淘汰的不是知识工作者，而是"管理学"这门学科本身。

📝 转录文本

开场：一个全新的时代需要全新的基础设施

We have a whole new technology. That's the most important technology ever. And you need a whole new infrastructure.

Normally when we talk about the infrastructure world, we're talking about the servers on the storage and the network. Here it goes all the way down to the mines of copper min. That's how widespread this thing is going to be.

It used to be when you built something, it was an engineering problem. And here it feels like it really is a resource limitation. So whether it's tokens or not, we're pouring a ton of money into systems and then those systems are producing a result. And right now we're bottlenecked on the systems ability to actually match the resources we're pouring into them.

The leading memory vendor said the demand they have today will take them 3 years of capacity to supply.

If this fund does what we think it will do, how do we see the world in 5 to 10 years?

America wins in the infrastructure and that would be awesome.

Ben, Martin, Ragu, welcome.

Thank you.

All right. Thank you.

一、引入 Machine Age Fund：史上最大的技术革命

I want to start with a Mark quote to introduce this new fund. This is the biggest technological revolution of my lifetime. This is clearly bigger than the internet. The comps on this are the microprocessor, the steam engine, and electricity, or maybe the wheel. Guys, the machine age fund. Please introduce it. Ben, start us off.

Well, um, basically what's uh happened is we have a whole new technology that's the most important technology ever. And what happens every time um there's a dramatic new way of using all of the things that we love infrastructure um you need a whole new infrastructure and never has it been more high impact as it is on this one. So not only do we need new chips, new system software, we need new ways of doing power, we need to replace copper. I mean like it's absolutely everything. So it's a very exciting time. So you know particularly for the kind of hardware aspects of of this new era um we needed a new approach.

Yeah I would agree. I mean normally when we at least in the computing when we talk about the infrastructure world we talking about the servers and the storage in the network here it goes all the way down to the mines copper mines. That's how widespread this thing is going to be. Um that's number one and number two I think what we have seen over the last 3 years is the steady increase of the capabilities of the models where the model is no longer the bottleneck and in fact using AI these models are getting better faster and faster and faster. Now the bottleneck is all what I call south of the model and so that's why we need to work on that.

You know, the only thing I'd add very quickly is like we tend to follow founders and we've been watching over the last couple of years is the number of very strong teams going after complex hardware problems has increased. I don't know the actual numbers but I was trying to estimate it over the weekend. So I think we'd get you maybe 5% of the deals from top founders would come in would be hardwood before. Now I would say north of 20% or 30% right now. So like the founder community which tends to be much smarter than the VC community has identified this as a very active area for innovation and they're responding.

I think 5% is probably generous.

Yeah, it's very low. Is very low. Yeah. 3%. Yeah.

二、宏观条件：为什么现在是硬件创业的时刻

And explain some of the macro conditions that have led to this this trans this change in terms of the surplus of founders pursuing these idea. Like what are they seeing that's that's enabled?

Well, I mean the obvious is like you know the the demand for AI is basically infinite and as a result of that every part of the supply chain is under under duress. I mean everything including like materials used to make things like like memory.

Um it's also very interesting whether there's something unique about AI. Um which because the demand is infinite and growth is infinite. Um uh what you tend to worry about is the margin of companies which is how efficient it is. Like normally you worry about growth like can I just you know can I just get people to buy this stuff. You don't have to worry about that here. The question is is can you do this in a way that's profitable? And a lot of the um efficiencies are actually strictly a physical limitation of hardware.

And so even the business model of the AI wave is really putting a lot of stress on the existing systems because they weren't built for AI. They weren't built for those workloads. And I think there's just this you know this global observation that we actually need to change the core components to get that efficiency to help drive the growth and to drive the value of the businesses.

需求真的超过供给了吗？

Yeah. And how did we know that demand is actually outpacing supply here rather than this being you know another hype cycle?

Well, I mean, yeah, there are any number of cities today. Um, firstly, it is that some of the smartest judges of demand are cutting huge purchase orders. I mean, if you look at the hyperscalers, right? Their capex spend has been exploding. Next year supposedly, it's going to reach a trillion dollars collectively across the big hyperscalers. This year, it's about 700 billion dollars, right?

And if you think about the hyperscalers position in the industry, they see demand from everywhere, right? They see obviously the frontier labs um wanting their compute, they see the AI native companies, they see the enterprise, they see the US geography, the international geography. So if anybody has visibility, it is down and they've been jacking up their capex like it's never been seen before, right? So that's a clear clear sign.

It's also a cool name. That sounds good. Futuristic.

十、创业机会：既有巨头之外的空间

Yeah. Given how much has been spent on AI infrastructure to date and how capex intensive these businesses can be are we past the point where new companies can break break in at at at sort of material levels uh you know you know in why not incumbents like Nvidia Core etc just take the line share of these markets.

They're all doing well there's no question about it right but to our discussion earlier when you're get you need funly new innovations to keep the growth both continuing or the pace of improvement continuing whether it's tokens per second per dollar or tokens per watt uh tokens per rack right um or power you take any metric if you want to have a 10x on those metrics you got to have new innovation and new innovation traditionally comes from brilliant founders thinking about solving the problem from first principles in a different way right and that's what's needed here for the next jump in innovation.

I mean this is the law of markets, right? I mean let's assume that the the existing silicon incumbents are multi-trillion dollars in market cap which is absolutely the case. Even 5% of that is a massive private company, massive private company, right? We're talking, you know, annual.

Um and you could say, well, but Nvidia could do that. They could, but why would they if they're focused on things that are in the 90% which is also driving the same amount of growth? You always ask these questions. We ask these questions during the cloud days, right? Like why wouldn't Amazon did this? You would ask these questions during the Microsoft days. Why wouldn't Microsoft do this? There's a very natural law of markets is once you get to a certain scale, there's tremendous opportunity for innovation um at at the margins.

Yeah, there's a funny uh quote from our partner Alex Rmpelle. He had this startup called Trial Pay and he was trying to sell it to or sell the it his services to to Meta and uh then Facebook and Dan Rose who was the head of corp dev at the time said Alex that's great you're it sounds like you can collect a lot of silver bricks but I'm like I have so many gold bricks I can't even pick them all up so the last thing I'm doing is looking at a silver brick and I think Nvidia is in that position.

100% yeah we were talking about as relates to the model providers that if you're, you know, in the sweet spot of of what open airropic can can do, you know, one of their main sort of interest areas, that might be a tough place to be, but anything outside of those maybe, you know, three to five areas might uh, you know, as as markets expand, they fragment, right?

历史类比：从福特到福特兰迪亚

And it happens all the time. And remember in the early days of Ford, there was the 1913, there was the Rouge River plant. Literally this, you know, this was like made cars like in went like water, coal, and rubber trees and out came cars.

By the way, he bought a whole rubber plantation in the Amazon jungle,

right? And and there's a great book called Ford Landia where so because he wanted to like own like the complete vertical thing where he created this city called Ford Landia in the Amazon jungle um which had like was all Americanized band stands and ice cream and all this kind of stuff. And it actually worked for a while until uh he made people like show up to things on time and then they were like screw this get the out of here.

So, so now if you look at the car industry, of course, there's multiple levels of supplier and there's a bunch of companies and this always happens. So, you know, as markets expand, they fragment. There's a lot of and then and then once that growth slows down, they tend to consolidate. The consolidation can either be acquisition or it can be like new challengers rise up and that that is the, you know, everlasting cycle of private markets.

Yeah. The use cases are are multiplying and there's no way like if you're the biggest company you can get to the biggest use cases but there's so many use cases and all as Martin was saying very valuable use cases that it's just very hard to get to in a great way.

Yeah even inference used to be one simple architecture right and it no longer is like it's so complex now so it's inevitable that you can optimize things in a different way.

一个反常规的商业推论：硬件优化终于影响利润

By the way here's a very interesting thing like people don't um uh often don't understand that like the margins kind of fell out of the standard way of doing the technology with software, right? Like it wasn't really a technology problem. Like once you got the business working, you tended to have pretty good margins because that's just kind of how software works.

Certainly when you shipped it but even as a service uh and that's not necessarily the case with AIS we may actually be entering an era where the optimization in the hardware is absolutely meaningful to the upside of the business in a way that we haven't seen in the past so there's a lot of opportunity here.

十一、投资细分与创业者特质

Let's get deeper in talking about the types of companies we'll be investing in um maybe we could start by either illustrating the the the subsectors or if we can talk about a few um or a couple investments that we've I know there's some that haven't been announced yet, but Robert, do you want to take us down?

Yeah, I mean the sub sectors as we've been talking all is every one of these categories, right? The obvious ones are um uh computer chips, but these days it's not enough to build a chip. You need to build a full system, right? And then therefore, what goes into the system? There's potentially memory innovation. There is potentially networking innovation. There's potentially power chips and so on and so forth. So each one of these categories are categories where you can see public company style companies emerging and those are all things that we are looking into.

Um and then once you put it all together there's a layer of software around it to automate all of these things to manage these fleets and so on and so forth. So that is another important area. So these things keep building on each other but every one of these categories is important.

这些公司有什么不一样

Talk about what's different about these kinds of companies from from the usual company. I mean one thing you can tell from the companies we announced is their first rounds have been massive. You know hundreds of millions. Is it a different kind of founder or what else is different as we think about just the practice of you know building and investing these kinds of businesses relative to our traditional software?

Well I I think the big thing is you hit on one of the big things which is a lot of money goes in um before they get to a product. Um and that's just kind of the nature of it. Now that's true on big models too, but I I would say that's a little more of a known path. Uh whereas this has got a little more risk and a little more money than uh than some of the other things that we've done.

But um and you know, look, a lot of a lot of the chip founders um are here from the past. You know, like the guys who know how to make memory, they're not young. Yeah, you know, so it's uh you know that part is different too, but it's kind of exciting, you know.

Yeah. The other thing about these founders, they have all got to be systems founders. So what I mean by that is you can't just be a researcher or a great computer scientist, right? You got to be able to architect and design the chip or the system, whatever it is. Then you got to think about how is this thing going to actually get manufactured, right? Who's going to be supplying this and a whole bunch of these downstream things which normally if you're building software you don't have to think about all of these things. So the to really the best founders um and of course Jensen is the Michael Jordan of this right they think the entire ecosystem right from the get-go before they start designing the chain right because of the nature of the bottlenecks and all these things that have to come together. So that's that's a big characteristic that is different.

There there's two environmental factors that are important too. The first one is the labs are so desperate that they will engage with startups. And so like we actually have quite a bit of signal early on because they're you labs are inking deals with companies before they actually have hardware available. And that's a big big shift than you know 5 years ago, right? Like you just didn't go and you know sell your kind of janky hardware thing to Google or whatever. So that that's a shift.

The second one is the the capital availability has loosened up a lot. I think there's general consensus that that you know it is the time that to reshape this stuff and so follow on rounds there's a lot of capital available which you know of course you want to be investing into areas where there's capital available and so the atmospherics are also just different.

为什么现在的硬件创业者往往更年长

Patrick Carlson, you know, remarked a few years ago said, "Hey, it feels like there's less younger founders today, you know, in the way that you know, Zuck, you know, in college building next Facebook or or Gates, um, you know, in the same way with Microsoft and of course, you know, the Michael Trolls of the world, there there's still, you know, some young founders building iconic companies, but it does seem, you know, to your point that there's more older founders building these these these companies or or less 20-year-olds." I'm I'm curious if you resonates and why.

Well, I think it's Ragu's point that if if you're building something that has like a very complicated supply chain, has to manufacture things um and is technically complicated that you know some experience helps uh and you know if you look at Elon or Travis Kalanick their companies when they were young were software companies. It wasn't until they got like a lot even those guys the best guys um needed some experience in building a companies building technology and so forth to kind of graduate to the much more kind of complicated or I would say elaborate domains you know there's just much more there many more moving parts in these things.

And so look when you're learning how to build a company it's hard enough if you completely understand the product. If you don't completely understand the product and have to learn it while you build the company, um that's just such a steep learning curve for a brand new entrepreneur. So, I think that what we're seeing is you see Michael on the one hand, um who is a very young guy, brilliant, but what he built was kind of a pure software AI thing.

Yeah. And then on the other end, you have like an Elon or a Travis who can who's got enough experience. I think Michael could probably do that, you know, 10 years from now, but today that would have been hard.

And it's important to remember like it's been defocused by the entire industry and academia for the last 20 years, right? It just there just hasn't been the same opportunity. Like it's been there, but like it's never been a growth area. The growth areas have been, you know software um networking things like that. And so I also think we just have a posity of people coming out of the universities or having experience at large companies that have have done this. I there just not that many.

Like you don't go intern and like build a chip. So but a lot of that's changing now. Like listen we're going to create a whole generation of of you know founders that come from these new companies that will know how to do this and you know they'll be hired in much more junior and like I would say actually one of the greatest legacies of Elon towards this is is of course he's created these great companies but the amount of entrepreneurs that have come out of SpaceX that that have are changing the entire industrial complex maybe even greater um legacy than than the companies themselves and I think we're going to see the same thing uh for for computer science and hardware.

Y as a matter of All of our investments was started by uh two founders in their 20ies. But if you go watch one of their offices, you see the experienced people as well. So it's ideal combination here.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. It doesn't necessarily have to be the founder with experience, but that founder better be able to tap into that experience with it.

Yeah. Yeah.

十二、为什么由这几位 GP 领衔

Well, and then be able to work with them and and and they have to be good and and all these kinds of things. It's complicated. Speaking of experience, this is a a big new fund we're we're launching and there's no new GPS. Um yeah, we're sort of collecting. It's because you guys have a lot of experience and the rest of the group, you know, in in this field that it's been kind of latent and uh dormant.

Yeah. Well, it's kind of funny. I think we almost had to be warned against it almost just because like our backgrounds are from is hard. And I think the reason that we needed a reminder is because all of us have spent so much in our careers existence and hardware. We're kind of drawn to that.

And so listen, we've been clearly invested um in harbor over other years, right? We're in SpaceX, we're in Andrew and all. These are very early checks. We're in astronomics, we're in Whimo, you know, so we even even early on we did a number of those investments. Um but like you know this is because it's so much in our DNA and so I don't think this is necessarily need to increase the team competencies just bonus.

十三、五到十年后的愿景

If this fund does what we think it will do, how do we see the world changing or looking like in 5 to 10 years?

Well, you know, hopefully uh America wins in the infrastructure game. Um and we have lots of like super eco-friendly efficient data centers out there and lots and lots an abundance of chips and abundance of memory and abundance of power. Uh and you know that would be awesome.

Uh, and I think we look we we, you know, it goes back to like we really think uh America is a special place and um we're important not only to everybody here but anybody in the world who wants to kind of make a contribution and do something bigger than themselves that it's kind of the best place to come with nothing and do something profound. So we'd like to keep that going and I I think that doesn't continue to go if we lose our lead in technology. Think I think we'll be in another era and it'll be another country and maybe they have a different set of values around that.

Thanks. That's a wrap.

Great for seeing me fun. Martine Beni. Thank you. Thank you.

Thank you. Thanks. Yeah.

## 一、被忽视的"心理反转"：我们正在见证软件行业最深的信仰崩塌
过去 40 年，硅谷奉行一条铁律——"神话的人月"（Mythical Man-Month）：你不可能靠砸钱和堆人追上一个领先两年的对手。这条定律塑造了从 Fred Brooks 到 Paul Graham 的整个软件哲学，也定义了 VC 的判断范式：技术领先＝时间壁垒。
但 Ben 在对话中悄悄扔下了一颗炸弹："**Now that works.**"（现在这招管用了。）
这不是一个技术观察，而是一次范式颠覆。当 xAI 用 30 亿美元点亮一个集群就能几个月追平多年积累的 OpenAI，当 Kimi、Grok 可以"凭空冒出来就是真的"——软件行业赖以生存的"复利护城河"神话首次被资本一次性击穿。这意味着**过去所有关于"先发优势"的投资逻辑正在失效**，而这才是 a16z 悄悄改换赛道的真正原因，不是"AI 需要基础设施"这么表层。

item.title: [Lex Clips] Cases where AI can write 100% of the code | DHH and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"代码烂摊子悖论"：AI并没有制造垃圾，它只是把人类一直在做的事情可视化了

DHH最锋利的一击藏在最后——当人们指责vibe coder是"垃圾生成器"，他反问："你看过普通程序员的产出吗？"这句话背后其实是一个残酷的系统性真相：软件行业几十年来一直用"人多"这个变量掩盖了"代码熵增"这个常量。AI没有让代码变差，它只是把3000个工程师用20年制造的混乱压缩到了3个月内完成，让熵增速率从慢性病变成了急性发作。

这是一种"时间显影剂"效应——就像高速摄影机让我们第一次看清水滴溅起的皇冠。行业震惊的不是AI的糟糕，而是终于看清了自己的糟糕。

二、跨领域连接：AI安全审查 vs. 冷战情报机构——"combo move智能"的稀缺性突然被商品化

DHH提到Fable模型能"串联组合技找到RCE"这一点，几乎被所有人当作技术细节滑过去了，但这里隐藏着一个地缘政治级别的系统扰动：

过去，能把"5个小漏洞串成致命链条"的人几乎只存在于三个地方——NSA、Unit 8200、以及朝鲜的Lazarus Group。这种能力被称为"vulnerability chaining intelligence"，是国家级战略资产。而现在，这种曾经等同于核武器级别稀缺性的认知能力，正在以API调用的价格被批发。

类比一下：这就像1945年之后，铀浓缩技术突然出现在了民用五金店。DHH说Fable"不安全发布"其实是软件史的一个不扩散条约时刻——但没人在讨论这个。所有讨论都还停留在"AI能写多少代码"这种表层问题。

三、令人意外的观察：Vibe coding的失败模式和"民主化设计"的历史重演

最反直觉的一点是：Basecamp 5让设计师去vibe code，结果每一个单独的PR都"在某个瞬间是合理的"，但加起来毁掉了系统架构。这不是AI的锅，也不是设计师的锅——这是一个古老的现象：

局部理性的总和 ≠ 全局理性。

这和城市规划里的"雅各布斯诅咒"完全同构——每一栋新建筑都符合规范、都美观、都提高了容积率，但整个街区变得无法居住。也和金融市场里的"合成谬误"（fallacy of composition）如出一辙——每个理性交易者的最优选择叠加成系统性崩溃。

真正的洞见在于：AI暴露了一个软件工程从未真正解决的元问题——架构一致性是一个"负熵"任务，它需要一个持续存在的"叙事者"（narrator）来维持系统的语义连贯性。以前这个角色由资深工程师隐性承担，现在它突然被抽掉了，暴露出软件的"意义"其实一直悬挂在少数人的直觉上，而不在代码本身里。

所以未来最值钱的技能可能不是写代码，而是"架构叙事的守护者"——一个能在AI的局部理性洪流中，持续为系统注入全局意图的人。这是一个全新的职业类别，还没有名字。

📝 转录文本

编程的不同领域：哪里可以让 AI 写 100% 代码？

We should mention that there's all kinds of domains that programmers operate in. There is — I actually don't know, but I think the most common domain in development is like web dev CRUD. You have a database.

Yes.

User facing interface and it does something back and forth. And it could be internal to just one person, to multiple people, to a small number of people, or to the world.

I think for that, it's — I mean, you could really get to the 100% of code written by AI. And really, almost, if you're a good programmer and you have a good intuition about what's happening behind the scenes, you can legitimately not look at the code. At least that's been my experience.

I don't know how much a prior experience with programming you need to have to kind of know that things are working correctly behind the scenes — like intuitively, by observing the ripple effects, of symptoms of the system. But I think for that domain, it's close to 100%.

And then there's domains like you're also operating in, which is writing Linux distribution. There, maybe there's more, because you're obsessed with speed and all that kind of stuff. There maybe you need to look at the code a little bit more.

Then there's maybe safety critical systems, all the way down to operating a nuclear power plant, or a self-driving car. Maybe you need to look at the code more carefully.

AI 与安全漏洞：串联"组合技"的稀缺智能

Yes, but that said, AI is insanely capable at both finding —

Yeah.

— and fixing security vulnerabilities. This was the whole blow up about Fable. This model was so capable of finding holes that an attacker could exploit that was simply not safe to release.

So the irony here is that when you look at that field, it seems like we've reached levels of intelligence that virtually no human can match. Because many of these security holes are about stringing combo moves together. You find one little vulnerability here that by itself might not be the worst thing in the world, but then you combine it with four others, and suddenly you have RCE — remote command execution.

Humans who are able to do that are very rare. Usually work inside state-sponsored organizations or other clandestine operations. They're not just out and about finding things. So they've gotten so good at that.

HEY Quattro：一个 100% 由 AI 构建的产品

The Linux distribution is why I've gotten 100% AI built. Because I've been working on HEY for the last 3 months — this version that just dropped a few days ago called Quattro. And almost right from the beginning I'm working on that version, the agent acceleration neared 100%. And in the last 2 months it has been 100%.

I have not written — Really? — any of the code that shipped in Quattro by hand. I've reviewed the shape of all of it. I've reviewed the individual lines of anything that's critical in the model layer of the system. And I've not looked at a bunch of the UI code. I have not looked at a bunch of the auxiliary code. And I've not written any of the new functionality entirely by hand.

成熟代码库的困境：Basecamp 与 HEY 为何更难加速？

But then the web part — actually evolving Basecamp and HEY, are professional products that have lots of users and are relatively large code bases — have proven surprisingly tricky to fully accelerate with agents.

We just released Basecamp 5 not too long ago. That was the first product at 37signals that was really agent accelerated, because we were in this final sprint phase from around February. By then, agents were already good.

And we had this early surge of "it's solved." We could just have the designers do the programming. They know what features they want. They know what shape they want it to take. Let's just let them vibe.

And we let them vibe.

Yeah.

And we ended up with a lot of PRs that individually perhaps could have been justified for a hot moment — taken all together, destroyed the architecture of the system. And we actually had to clean up — manually mop it up by hand, by human hand — to get back to an architecture that felt cohesive and coherent.

So we still have a bit of that. That was February, by the way. Things are quite different now.

Vibe Coding 的前提：你必须是个程序员吗？

Oh, hold on a second. What's the lesson from that? Is one of the lessons from that that you have to be a programmer at this stage to be able to vibe code?

To be able to vibe code on existing substantial code bases — even if they're CRUD — if you want to retain the elements of architecture that got that system to where it was.

对"垃圾代码"指控的反击

Now, that's also a point where I've stressed many times that when people accuse vibe coders of being slob generators, I go right back at them and say: "Have you looked at the average programmer's output?"

That is some other slob, too. If you've looked at behind the scenes of many great companies and what their code bases look like after there's been 3,000 humans through them — they're awful. Absolutely awful.

Mhm.

观看原视频 →
