item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

失败作为一种商业模式：凯尔特人的"负向护城河"

大多数俱乐部把失败视为成本，凯尔特人却把它变成了资产负债表的润滑剂。他们的运营逻辑令人惊讶地类似于保险公司的精算模型——预设每年欧冠出局的"损失概率"，然后通过压低支出、囤积现金来抵消这种失败带来的收入缺口。但这里有一个致命的悖论：保险公司卖的是"你不出事我赚钱"，而凯尔特人卖的是"我们出事你还得买"。90 million镑现金堆在银行，主看台亟待重建，而 Dermot Desmond 却像一个把股东红利锁在保险箱里的信托管理人——问题在于，他管理的不是资本，而是60,000人的文化身份。

这里有一个跨领域的连接值得思考：凯尔特人的困境与日本"僵尸企业"的现象惊人相似——不是因为亏损而僵化，而是因为过度稳健而丧失了冒险的肌肉。当一个组织的KPI从"赢得欧冠"退化为"不破产"，它就已经在心理上离场了。

英国板球的"男孩终究是男孩"叙事：一种被制度化的幼稚

真正令人意外的观察不是球员喝酒，而是整个板球生态系统对"稚气未脱"的集体默许。Charlie点出了一个关键结构性问题：16-17岁就获得保障合约的团队运动员，其个人绩效与收入的反馈回路被人为切断了。这与高尔夫形成了极其鲜明的跨领域对比——高尔夫选手是"个体经营者"，一次宿醉直接体现在奖金支票上；而板球选手是"契约雇员"，宿醉的成本由团队和粉丝共同承担。

这里有一个更深层的洞察：英国板球把"表现问题"重新包装成了"公关问题"，这是所有失败机构的经典自欺——把因果关系倒转，从而免除结构性改革的责任。这与凯尔特人董事会把"失败"包装成"审慎"是同一种病理学。

FedEx Cup vs LIV：一场关于"稀缺性经济学"的公开课

最反直觉的观察是：LIV通过取消淘汰机制、保证出场费来"降低摩擦"，反而摧毁了自己产品的价值。这违背了体育产业最古老的定律——观众买的不是舒适，而是不确定性。FedEx Cup的天才之处在于把"精英meritocracy"和"叙事张力"焊接在一起：70→50→30的漏斗设计，本质上是把整个赛季压缩成一个三幕剧结构。

而这里的跨领域连接才是真正的"啊哈时刻"：FedEx Cup的奖金进入球员养老金这个细节，暴露了一个远比表面更深的博弈——PGA Tour正在用德国式的"共同决策制"（Mitbestimmung）来对抗LIV的沙特式"金主赞助制"。前者赢在制度韧性，后者输在缺乏共谋。这解释了为什么英超足球在与球员工会的关系上如此脆弱：因为PFA还停留在"要更多钱"的原始工会阶段，而PGA Tour的球员已经进化成了准股东。

隐藏的系统性真相：足球俱乐部市场正在经历一场"流动性坍塌"

Rob提出的"42/72俱乐部待售"数据背后，是一个远比表面严峻的结构性问题：当年度亏损接近资产估值时，破产比出售更经济。这不是足球问题，这是任何长期依赖"更大的傻瓜理论"的资产类别都会遭遇的市场失灵——想想2008年的次贷、2022年的加密货币，或艺术品市场周期性的崩盘。10-100 million镑这个中间地带的买家真空，本质上是"新贵已经买不起，超富看不上"的经典中产陷阱。IFR即将面对的挑战，不是监管问题，而是流动性做市商问题——他们需要的可能不是更严格的所有者测试，而是像美联储那样的"最后购买人"机制。

第一部分：凯尔特人的欧战溃败

一场无以复加的崩盘

Things which will have annoyed some people. Um — Celtic exiting the Champions League qualifying stages last night. I'm not sure I know of a greater footballing collapse than this, Charlie. I mean, I've seen matches — I've even been at matches — between two highly competitive teams where one team goes 3–0 up, and famous Champions League final of course, and then the other one roars back in some way.

But last night, Celtic actually collapsed. And it's a slightly different thing when you're watching it.

So, let's just, for those who don't follow it closely or haven't seen the result from last night — it was a two-legged game against LASK of Austria, the Austrian League being ranked somewhere below the Championship in European football terms. Okay, so it's sort of bottom-end Championship, top-end League One in quality. It's that sort of thing.

Celtic won the home leg at Celtic Park at Parkhead 3–0. Happy days. Job done. We're finally going to qualify for the knockout stages — or the group stages rather — of a Champions League. Great. Fantastic. We're back on top.

Go to the away leg. Go 1–nil up away from home. 4–nil up on aggregate. Even that was not enough as they then proceeded to concede five goals in the following 70 odd minutes to lose 5–4 on aggregate.

It's a football disaster.

一门以失败为基础的生意

It's a business disaster as well. Right. And that's why you look at — I mean, look, are we just commenting on a collapse in a random game? No, that's not our style. Are we commenting on the collapse of a performance in a really really important part of a season when they have built a business model, as we've discussed before, that they have claimed protects them from missing out on European football?

Oh, it does. You know that — "That's why we don't spend the money, guys. We can't overexpose ourselves."

What they've really done now is they've gone back-to-back years going out in Champions League qualifying to Kairat — Kairat Kazakhstan.

Goes back a lot longer than that. So this goes back quite a long time. This goes back to pre-Covid. During the last seven years they've lost in these qualifying stages to AEK Athens, to Cluj, to Ferencváros, to Midtjylland, and to Almaty. Okay. And now LASK. So that's six defeats over a seven- or eight-year period to clubs who — with the greatest of respect, and absolutely respecting all different clubs of all different kinds; my own clubs and the clubs I've worked at have not been huge huge huge clubs, and I'm very respectful of all different types of clubs — but this is Celtic. This is Celtic. This is one of the biggest franchises in the world of football losing every single year to European minnows.

内置失败的商业模式

Now, you mentioned that this was a financial disaster for them. It just unfortunately isn't — because they've built an entire business model out of failure, right?

So, in other words, they set out basically saying: we're going to fail. And how can we be profitable despite failing?

So they basically bake in their own failure as part of their business model to make sure that they make a profit, to put money aside for rainy day in case they don't make it to Europe.

No, no, no — because that's already baked in. They're profitable even without going to Europe, right? So this money has just been piling during these years, these seven or eight years that they've been failing in Europe. They've been piling up cash in the bank. They're now sat on about 90 million pounds of cash in the bank with a main stand at Parkhead that desperately needs knocking down and turning into a massive cash machine, which would then give them the revenues to then go and be seriously competitive in Europe.

But the board refuses to spend that money, right? It just leaves it in the bank account and every year the same thing happens.

转会窗口的时间错配

What happens every single year is they go and sell three or four players in the relatively early stages of the transfer window. They then sit on that money to wait for bargains towards the back end of the transfer window.

What's the problem with that within a European calendar, Charlie?

The European qualifying games happen before the end of the transfer window, right? So every single year they start European qualifying with a squad that is short — on the basis of "well, we don't want to overpay to bring players in before we play our European games." Right? So they're already accepting that they are going to be weak in Europe. They've got a business model that's predicated off then failing in Europe.

董事会与球迷的错位

And meanwhile, the fans are providing all of the money — because the board is a quoted company. It's a stock-market-quoted company. So the board — it's so dysfunctional as to be almost unfathomable, right?

The board is led effectively by a non-executive director. So last year when they had big ructions over changes of managers and all this type of stuff, there was a statement put out on behalf of the club by the club's non-executive director who owns about 30-odd% of the shareholding, Dermot Desmond.

What's a non-executive director doing making statements in the public domain? He bought his shares and built up a shareholding in the club as a listed-company investor, and yet effectively he's now running the club and putting out statements on behalf of the club and overseeing a strategy — if you can dignify it with that word — which basically says: "We're going to take in all of our fans' money because we've got such an enormous fan base. We know they're going to carry on spending money with us no matter what. We're going to chuck it in the bank account here and we're just going to sit back and watch our club — one of the biggest clubs in the world — beat St Mirren and claim that that's successful."

流浪者衰落带来的意外庇护

Now, the one thing that has saved them during this terrible period under Dermot Desmond has been, of course, that Rangers went into a meltdown. If you remember, they went through a period. They overspent. They got themselves way in over their head. They went bankrupt. Had to go all the way down to the bottom of the Scottish pyramid and fight their way back up again. And it's probably only just about now when Rangers is in a roughly stable financial position.

So effectively, because Celtic have been winning the title more or less every year — although last year they shouldn't have done; they should have been beaten by Hearts last year, which would have been an epic upset, but they still just scraped across the line with a hell of a dodgy refereeing decision in the second-last game, a penalty which I would have been very upset if it been given against my club if I was Hearts — a handball on the edge of the box. But leaving that to one side:

Because they're winning the title, the board claims that that's success. And the fan base says, "No, no, no, no. You misunderstand the nature of why 60,000 of us turn up. We don't turn up to support a club because we beat St Mirren. We turn up to support a club that represents our entire culture, our entire identity, which has a proud history of operating at the top table, indeed being former Champions League winners themselves."

罕见地站在球迷一边

So there's a total mismatch between the fan base and the directors. And for once, I'm on the side of the fan base. And I'm on the side of the fan base because they're the ones putting all the money in.

Normally it's the owners putting the money in and the fans shouting at them — telling the owners "you should be putting more in," right? And I go, "Well, hang on a second. If you want more money to be spent on your club, how about if you start paying more in ticket prices?" At Celtic, it's the other way around. It's the fans who put money into the club and the directors who then sit back and say, "Well, you know what? On balance, actually, we're not going to spend your money on what you want us to spend it on. We're just going to stick it in the bank."

场上溃败的责任归属

Where does that feature from the behind-the-scenes perspective — looking at, as you've just said, probably one of the biggest chokes? Where you could have had a manager who had done X number of things throughout a game; you could have had an ownership who'd operated incredibly well — as you said, when you're 4–nil up in a game to qualify for a Champions League and, you know, cruising — there's an element of that which is just players on the pitch taking your responsibility. Is it all a product?

Of course. But who do those players, where do those players come from? How much have those players played? What is the recruitment team in place that selects those players? Does Celtic have a technical director? No. Who is the Celtic head coach? Martin O'Neill — bless him. A good manager 20 years ago, but in his mid-70s now and having had health problems, etc.

It's almost like the Celtic board don't actually know any managers other than Martin O'Neill. Every time that they're in trouble, they go, "Oh, what should we do? Should we give Martin a call?"

结构性僵化与出路

The whole situation is so sclerotic and mad. Now, I know the Celtic fans have gone into sort of this little campaign saying "not a penny more" in terms of extra-mural spending. They don't want to give up going to games, but they don't want to be spending on lots of other things to prop up this bonkers, failed non-strategy.

But you can't help but think at some point something has to give here. This club needs to be bought out. It needs to be bought out — or it needs to use the fact that it is a big financial beast to become a proper quoted company with a proper independent board to actually apply the fans' money in a strategic and progressive way.

I just don't know how the lack of self-awareness and the lack of ability to sort of just look in the mirror and ask questions of myself — that must beset Dermot Desmond and the crew around him — is that surely you are, surely you should be able to see as an intelligent man that what you are doing is not being seen as successful by your entire customer base. You cannot enjoy the fact that whenever you come to Celtic Park, you're being made not to feel welcome.

Is this a 15-, 20-year thing really, you know, at a time when clubs of Celtic size are generally speaking being perceived as being quite valuable in terms of asset class? He could walk out of here with a very healthy profit in terms of what he originally paid for those shares in the first place. So what's the purpose of hanging on?

That's what no one knows. It's not about money. Desmond's a billionaire and he would make a profit out of getting out at this point anyway. It's not because he's got some alternative plan — because the only plan that he and his board have got is to suck in all the money, stick it in the bank account and reappoint Martin O'Neill.

Right? So, I just don't understand what's going on in their mind. I can see what's going on in the fan base's mind. I think it's totally reasonable. Anyhow, there we are. It is what it is.

第二部分：英格兰板球队的纪律问题

德比的深夜

Moving on. Um, Charlie, I got a question for you. Have you had a couple of beers recently?

Well, actually, you and I had a couple of beers on Sunday, late Sunday afternoon. Oh, we did.

Got a second question for you. Did we get arrested?

Oh, sorry. Were we put in handcuffs? The Cornish constabulary was very understanding of me as I stumbled my way down the stairs from the upper deck of the waterfront bar and restaurant on Polzeath Beach.

So of course what Charlie Junior is referring to is yet another centrally contracted England cricketer being found in a disgraced, compromised position following a night out drinking in a nightclub in Derby.

One thing I'm quite impressed by — I will give this to Brydon Carse and Ben Stokes — finding a nightclub in Derby.

I wouldn't know.

Particularly one that you want to go to.

Really? I mean, I do remember there was a couple of years ago, we went up there with Charlton and we won an important game, epic game, and I did say afterwards to a couple of the guys, I said — because we were staying in Derby — "So, should we try and go find somewhere to go out afterwards?" And one of the Derby directors said, "Couldn't advise it, lads, you know, etc."

So, look, well done Brydon Carse and Ben Stokes for having found a place in Derby to go out and get absolutely smashed late into the night.

PR 问题掩盖了真正的问题

But it's another bit of publicity they don't need at all, is it? And we've talked obviously at length about it. I don't think we need to go over our thoughts on why this is just such poor practice from a top elite end sports team.

But when you look at it in the context of England going into its first test match post the appointment of Steven Fleming, of Joe Root becoming captain again, winning it very very comfortably against a Pakistan side that was nowhere near the standards that England were at — to have to deal with this again. The one step forward — I mean, 15 steps backwards.

Joe Root's interview — and I would like to know your thoughts on this because he spoke pretty frankly about it. He gave an interview and he said: "If I'm being brutally honest, I'm really hacked off, really disappointed after last week's performance. We're sitting here talking about something that's got nothing to do with it — but it does have something to do with it."

And Joe Root is the person who said, "I don't want to have a curfew. I don't want to put people on strict rules. People should be allowed to do whatever they want to do. They need to be able to behave like adults," etc., etc.

So, when you are the leader or part of the leadership, you have to take some responsibility. You are clearly not getting your message across in the right way. I'd be fascinated to know if Joe Root had spoken individually to all 30 or — other than him — 29, yeah, centrally contracted players. I bet you the answer is no.

Right. So this strikes at the heart of what I think the problem is, Charlie, which is that English cricket perceives all of this as a PR problem. Well, it is a PR problem, right? Just like Celtic losing to LASK is a PR problem. But the PR problem bit of it is less fundamental and less important than the actual core bit of it, which is: professional elite sportsmen who need to be operating at the peak of their performance — potentially, in Carse's case, he's one tweak of a hamstring away from one of the other bowlers from actually having to run out and open the bowling at Lord's four days later, something like that.

It's like the performance element of this is what continually irks me.

"两杯啤酒"的稻草人谬误

I'll tell you the other thing that irks me: English cricket — and I will put it really broadly, including the cricketers themselves, the coaches, the people at the MCC or the ECB, the cricket media, ex-players who are in the cricket media — they create this fake straw man, Charlie, which is: "Well, of course, no one minds, you know, no one, you know, anyone who's against a couple of pints, a couple of pints" (hence your quip early on about us on Sunday night, you know) — "No one's suggesting that people shouldn't have a couple of pints. It's just a question of be sensible, don't get caught," right? Is the gist of what they're constantly saying.

But let's be honest — these aren't a couple of pints. And yet it gets washed away, and anyone who is critical of it gets cast as being this puritanical figure who won't even allow a cricketer to have a beer or two after a well, you know, hard-earned win — a well-earned beer or two.

If it were a beer or two, we would never hear about it. We would never hear about these things if it was a beer or two.

Do you think that Harry Brook gets chinned by a bouncer in New Zealand after two beers? Do we think that Ben Duckett wanders around New Zealand asking where his hotel is after two beers? Do we think that Brydon Carse gets handcuffed outside a nightclub in Derby after two beers?

This is not two beers. This is a drinking binge. Not to say that one doesn't do it from time to time, but this is clearly something that's happening on a very very regular basis and is being smiled upon by the whole cricketing establishment as a "boys will be boys" type thing. And then subsequently there's a "Oh, well, I mean, you shouldn't be so stupid as to get caught." Okay, but how about not doing it in the first place?

Well, how about not getting arrested? I mean, even if you're going to go — I mean, you know, genuinely I joke, but you know, how many times do you go out and get in trouble with the police? It seems ridiculous.

宵禁与合约体育的成人化难题

And Charlie, I wanted to ask a question on the curfew piece because that was something that we brought up. You actually spoke very well about it when we talked, because you said, you know, really the symptomatic element of this was that they're just children that have never really grown up. They still operate in a way that —

True of professional sports people in general. But I just want to — that is true of a lot of professional sports people. I'm going to except golfers from this, who tend to mature over time and have to look after themselves and their own performance is — they have to work out, "if I go and get absolutely smashed and don't play very well, I don't earn as much money."

The problem about team sports and contracted team sports is that from the age of about 16, 17 these guys are being given quite a lot of money on a guaranteed basis to be part of a team, where your own individual performance, yeah, might dip a little bit, but does that change your contract? No. So as long as you turn up enough over the course of a season —

Now, the very very top players hold themselves to a very high account and there will always be those people. You know, I remember hearing from a friend of mine who was a journalist who was on the Ashes tour last winter, who said, "Do you know who the two batsmen netting on the MCG on Christmas Day were? Steve Smith and Joe Root."

Shock. QED. The two best batsmen in the world are the ones out practicing.

So, there are certain elite sports people even in team environments — where you're on guaranteed contracts — who are able to hold themselves to a very high account. But in general, I wouldn't trust I wouldn't trust them an inch.

足球俱乐部的宵禁实践

I can't remember — did you have curfews when you were running football clubs?

Oh, yeah. Yeah. Oh, yeah. I mean, not imposed by me. Yeah. I have to say. I mean, the m— the so — football clubs every single week —

Let's say you got an away game on a Saturday. They will travel on at the very Friday morning, sometimes even Thursday, but Friday morning, right? And on the Friday evening. But sometimes also the Tuesday night they'll be staying in a hotel away, and sometimes they'll be staying even in the night after being away.

So quite often, given the amount of away matches there are because of the cups and all this type of stuff, you know, two to three nights a week professional footballers are staying in hotels in a team environment away from home.

If the question you're asking me is: do football managers place considerable restrictions on what footballers do under these circumstances? Bloody right they do. Absolutely they do. 100%. Yeah.

I mean, the idea that "oh yeah, don't worry lads, go out and have a few beers" — not in a million years.

And that is the thing which most worries me about this. I read an article the other day when someone said — it was an English cricket person, I can't remember who it was, it wasn't a player, it was a commentator or a former player — said, "Of course, you know, I was quite surprised actually when I was over in India to find that actually when they win matches they don't go out and get smashed afterwards."

Why are you surprised? I don't — this is totally bizarre. You know, "Yeah, so it was interesting watching Sachin. He seemed to be quite happy with a cup of tea and a bottle of sparkling water afterwards."

Oh, no Sherlock. Right? They have got themselves into this bubble where they honestly think that getting absolutely smashed all the time is absolutely fine and has no impact on your performance and has no impact on injuries. "Oh, just make sure not to get caught, lads."

It's just wrong. It's just wrong. I'm sorry. It's wrong.

骨灰杯赛程与北方赛场的缺失

The performance side reminded me — with the fact that after a really good result at Headingley, one of the great grounds in the north of England — there are going to be no Ashes tests in the north. Old Trafford and Headingley most notably left out of the five venues that will be played at in 2027.

I've seen a lot of people come out and start talking about this, questioning that decision again because it doesn't seem to make a huge amount of sense — and whether it is from an England performance perspective, a business perspective, or whether it's just from ensuring that the parts of the country which have cricket at their heart, i.e. like a Yorkshire, being omitted from the opportunity to host a test match for a great series.

Yeah, I'd be wary of basing the choice of test grounds around where England happened to win. We went for a long period when we kept on winning at Edgbaston and then, you know, everyone went "Oh wow, it's England's fortress" — and then suddenly we couldn't win a game at Edgbaston. I think these things are much more random than one might think.

But I do agree that having a proper spread of test grounds throughout the country is really important. You know, if we want to make sure and safeguard the future of test cricket as opposed to short-form cricket, we have to recognize that Yorkshire is a hotbed of cricket in this country. It's a place where cricket is still played in state schools and it's obviously produces a big chunk of the England team at any one time.

If all that the young people in that county are being exposed to at the top level is short-form cricket, you're not exactly doing your best to safeguard your audience of tomorrow from a test perspective. So I think that's just from a marketing perspective not a very smart thing to do.

There is a bit of a challenge, which is that they pretty much guarantee every five-match series that the Oval and Lord's have two, one each. Right. So that only leaves three to share around. And there are four to five other test grounds. So there are going to be test grounds missing out on a regular basis. Even in five-match series, let alone in three-match series.

You would have thought one of Old Trafford or Headingley —

100%, Charlie. Absolutely. Funny enough, I actually think it's a bit odd — the focus on holding international matches at Southampton. You know, it's not difficult for somebody from Southampton to get up to London. That's quite an easy trip. I would much rather they focused on trying to bring Taunton up to speed because the West Country is a massive cricket hotbed. Somerset County Cricket Club itself gets big crowds and Taunton's a pretty good ground, and they have held international matches there before.

I'd rather they thought about making sure they had the West Country looked after and the North looked after — just so those two ends of the country, people, young people in particular, can get two test matches and see it live. I think it's really important. Yeah, I don't think anyone would have an issue with rotating at some stage between Headingley, Old Trafford, Trent Bridge, Edgbaston. You know, no one's going to say that all of those grounds are going to have something every single series, but again, to have a complete omission —

Yeah. Okay. So this has been a deal that should have been done a couple of years ago. It's meant to be done every 5 years. Hasn't been for seven years. So we're two years beyond when the redistribution deal should have been agreed.

When that gets agreed — with either the imposition of it by the independent football regulator, or the independent football regulator manages to encourage both sides to come to a deal which works for both of them before he has to step into the play into the playroom and do it himself — that is the moment at which the football league clubs have to get their house in order.

Because as we've seen from — I see the situation right now in the football league as being identical to what Formula 1 was before Liberty came in — which is an amazing product with a great audience but uninvestable. And everything always needs to be investable, right? Because if it's not, if it's uninvestable, then basically from that moment everything does have to run at break-even. And that's why I say about unintended consequences to the PFA is that: you guys should be happy that there are football club owners who are willing to lose money. Don't feel that you need to push it as far as you're currently pushing it, because you could end up in a situation where the whole bubble bursts and every club ends up going, "you know what, we can't lose money because we — there's no way of ever getting any money back."

对业主的一课：花费克制反而增值

The final message would be to some of the owners in the football league, particularly the Championship, who vote against spending restraint in general, is: you are guilty of a fundamental misunderstanding about sporting asset value, which is you think that if you're able to spend more than some of the other clubs in your division, that gives you a better chance of success and that then your club will become worth more even if the rest of them go to rat ship.

Okay. The lesson of Formula 1 and every other sport is the biggest single increase in sporting value, sporting asset value, that you get is when you get spending restraint. But that's a bigger increase that you'll get even from going to the Premier League one or two seasons.

Right. So — reinforces better practices, efficiencies, makes you review your business. How —

Makes you investable. Makes you investable.

买家分层：10-100M 的真空地带

Yeah. And just on your point of having enough buyers, you know, you mentioned the "bigger idiot theory" last week. If you're looking at what we've talked about here, you can look at all the clubs across the divisions and let's say you could bucket them, and you could bucket the different types of investors that would find each of those clubs attractive — should find each those clubs attractive.

Let's just say, you know, up if you're hitting up to 10 million pounds, you could have an individual businessman who's done very well and is keen to go and buy something and add a little bit of the kind of social side to the business side. You go over 10 million and you start getting either a couple of groups of those people or some slightly smaller financial houses keen to go and dip their toes in it. Let's call that the 10 to 50. Then you get the 50 to 100 which is only just a slight upgrade on that, but it's people doing the same type of thing with a bit more money. And then over a 100 is when you start becoming attractive to a private equity type individual. You start becoming attractive to maybe the billionaires that you were referencing.

But the big problem is the hardest bracket really is that 10 to 100 million. That's the hardest bit — because you're not just talking about the buy price of these clubs as you've said. You're talking about the cost of running them operationally, and that over a 5-10 year period is what will put the most pressure on this industry. Not necessarily what they grab the club for. That they can finance early on.

And the challenge with that — straight away you're suddenly going, "oh, but that means we just said the Championship and League One teams. Most of those fall within the 10 to 100 million price range."

Absolutely right. That's the concern.

「1 亿净资产也不够」的数学

100% Charlie. So the typical type of person who would be able to get involved in this kind of stuff, either on their own or with one other person, would be somebody who created their own business, had then sold their business for £100 million, let's just say, just to use a round number. Post-tax, £100 million. And whether it be in the US or here, whatever. And the purchase price they can say, "well that's an investment, it's a risky investment, so if I'm paying 20 million, I've still 80 million," right? So that 80 million is enough for me because there's not so many other different things. Perhaps I want to have a boat or something like this, but I've got a nice house. I'm okay.

The problem is the person with the total net worth of 100 million will most likely have an annual passive income, or maybe even active income, of about 5 million a year. After tax, 3 million a year, 3.5 million a year. So, even if that person were to devote their entire post-tax income to funding the football club, which would be a bit awkward at home — "Sorry honey, I'm afraid we're not able to eat right now because our entire disposable income is going on paying the football club."

So what that basically gets to is that even somebody with £100 million is no longer actually an appropriate owner of a football league club. So then you move up into the 200, 300, 400 million category. There aren't that many of them. This is the problem. And then you take: okay, there are X amount of them; only half of them are interested in football; only half of those guys got an appetite for actually subjecting themselves to the public glare of owning a football club; only half of that lot have got the gambler mentality of "if I do this, it could end up being great" and whatever it might be.

You end up with quite a small number of people, right? And that is where we are right now. That is what I'm referring to when I'm saying there is too many sellers, not enough buyers. And the fundamental problem is the annual loss rate.

Yeah. Brilliant.

第六部分：PGA Tour 与 FedEx Cup

一个「感觉良好」的赛季

Should we have a quick look at the PGA Tour?

Talking about organizations that not just are investable but have been heavily invested recently. The US PGA Tour is reaching the climax of what must — must feel good to be a PGA Tour executive right now.

Charlie, champion year, isn't it?

Oh, champion year. God, especially when you're — key, your golfers are coming out in their media, in their media chats. And as you said, you know, for the Čeferin piece, isn't it lovely when someone actually sits down and answers a question? And whether it's the executives doing it or the athletes like Rory McIlroy, or if it's Patrick or others just sticking the knife just further into those that —

Joyous exchange between McIlroy and Westwood in the last couple weeks. Did you see that?

I did. I loved it.

McIlroy basically came out and said, "I thought LIV — I always thought LIV was a shower of — and I've been proved to be right." And Westwood — in that sort of, you can imagine that 20 years ago, 25 years ago, he was the senior guy in the Ryder Cup team room and Rory was the junior guy. Yeah. Right. And he came out this — yeah, "Well, Rory just often gets these things wrong." But sorry, Lee. No, he got it right and you got it wrong. You know, the fact that he's rubbing salt on the wound now doesn't mean he wasn't right all along and he didn't call it right.

PGA Tour 的漂亮反击

Anyhow, the US PGA Tour — we've been through it before. They basically from a very poor position that they started the whole LIV war in, they then played an absolute blinder. They propped up the European tour here. They took in external financing here. They created an equity percentage of the commercial arm of what they do here for the big players to incentivize them to stick around. They increased prize money and they tightened up their FedEx Cup playoff system at the end of the season, which is now — I think — epic.

I think the FedEx Cup is brilliant. I don't follow the US PGA religiously week by week, but I do follow the FedEx Cup — because when you think about the format of the FedEx Cup, which Charlie will lay out in a moment, it's the exact opposite of what LIV was doing.

Right? So what LIV was doing is they were doing everything possible to make it as uncompetitive as possible, right? So if you're on the LIV tour, you are automatically on the LIV Tour unless you perform really, really badly, but basically you're on for the time of your contract. We're not going to bother having a cut. So in other words, in the US PGA tour and indeed the European tour and all other professional tournaments, halfway through the tournament, the bottom number of players — it's not quite half, but almost half — bottom number of players have to just leave and don't get any prize money at all. Have to bugger off back home having made a loss on the weekend.

LIV said, "Well, we're going to get rid of the cut, thus removing a whole layer of jeopardy. Um, we're going to basically pay massive appearance money contracts to be here, etc."

The FedEx Cup is the opposite of all that. It's the most brutally meritocratic sporting thing that you can ever ever see.

FedEx Cup 的漏斗结构

Do you want to lay it out, Charlie?

Yeah. So the reason we're talking about it actually is because the final tournament, the Tour Championship, actually is on right now. So this coming out on a Friday, it started on Thursday.

And really throughout the whole season — so the PGA tour season — you have all of the individual tournaments, but behind it you have a point system. And the point system, you're accumulating points based on how you're performing in various events throughout that season. And come the end of the season — pretty much where we are right now — you have three events.

And the three events are: first one, top 70 players. So first, if you haven't — you know, 140 odd players on the PGA tour — the bottom half don't make it to the FedEx Cup. These three events — so the top 70 players play in that first event. The second event, which we just had, the BMW Championship, which Wyndham Clark won. That then cuts the field down. That that's then 50 players that event. After the BMW Championship, we then go into the Tour Championship, which is what we've got on now, which is 30. The final 30 players.

从「让分」到「公平对决」

Now, previously what had happened on the tour is when it got down to this final event, whoever was one to 30 in those rankings — if you were number one, you would start on minus 10. If you were number two, you were eight under.

Minus 10 in the golf scoring system, which means that that is like starting off like you're 2–nil up in football.

Yeah. Now, if to make it fair, you really need to be starting Scottie Scheffler on plus 10, right? And putting everything else together. The challenge with it is that — well, the thought behind it is clear. You play very well throughout a whole season. When it gets to this flagship event, which has huge prize money attached to it — about 10 million for this specific event, and then there's a tour of merit type thing which is about $22 million, I think, on top of that for the winner — they get rewarded for their performance throughout the season by starting in an incredibly favorable position.

However, while that makes a lot of sense, it was a challenge from a viewership perspective. Because yes, the most likely candidate to be number one is probably the best player. If you give them the head start, it doesn't create a great product for the fans. That final little bit of the players who were already towards the top of the FedEx rankings —

You have the top 30 players coming in to an event. And this is — you said it — is the most meritocratic piece. It is the top 30 players throughout a whole season. No one can have a complaint that if you're not there, you should be there. Everyone knows what you got to do. Why not start it and have it as a flat-out shootout from word go?

粉丝调查驱动的变革

Now the PGA tour, from all of its learnings of the last few years, one of them has been a real focus on what the fans want. And what they've done to change this has been driven by the fans.

All of you who may skip through surveys and everything, right — won't skip through a survey if your sports organization that you follow and love gives you the opportunity to have a say to change how a tournament operates. So the fans — 50,000 people, 50,000 fans of the PGA Tour — got on one of these surveys and basically highlighted the scoring system in the Tour Championship as an issue for them.

And so the PGA tour listened to that. There would have been consultation with the players. If you listen to someone like Scottie Scheffler, he's actually kind of said, "Look, you know, I could win every tournament from now to the end of the season and get two shots at the final. Like it doesn't make it's not the end of the world." So the players weren't basically saying, "We have to have that advantage." And therefore, it was quite an easy change for them to make.

I think the difference that it has made to the product though I think will be huge, because you really then do come back to this incredibly exciting shootout of the best players against each other. They have also, interestingly, building into the whole live fan fair piece that everyone was very excited about — you know, they are going really hard at the concessions, the food stuff on site, the entertainment that's going to be around it. They're making this kind of Tour Championship final a proper thing.

The money obviously is a huge part of it and the PGA Tour has really upped its prize money. I mean, got to 200 odd million into the prize part. But at the heart of it still is a really great product. And this is a fantastic exciting way to round off a season.

顶尖 10 人的名单

Here are the players in the top 10, right? This is these are the people who will be playing off for FedEx Cup: Scottie Scheffler, Rory McIlroy, Collin Morikawa, Tommy Fleetwood, Matt Fitzpatrick, Wyndham Clark, Cameron Young, Ludvig Åberg, Sungjae Im, Si Woo Kim — these are just the best players in the world, right?

So this is a full-on major, but only for the top 30. Yeah. That's how — it's nice to have that sometimes a total outsider can win it, like happened in the Open, and sometimes in this case it's going to be one of the big stars who's going to win it because the only people who qualify it are the very biggest stars who have been winning a lot on the tour in the first place.

If you look at who's won it previously — I think Rory's won it three times, Tommy Fleetwood was the defending champion, Tiger won it twice — and that's just in the last 18 years it's actually been going, right. So it absolutely has been the apex of the game from a pure meritocracy and pure performance basis.

在传统中创新，把奖金放进养老金

So I just think it's an interesting example of a really thoughtful structuring of something where — innovation, you can innovate within tradition, right? So you can keep the absolute tenets — we're a four-round competition. It's 72 holes. It's all about who stroke play event and all this. But there's stuff that we can do that makes it more interesting and that gives it more of a narrative arc.

Another interesting thing I found about this is from the FedEx bonuses. A big chunk of them get paid into players' pensions.

Yeah, I didn't know that. You told me that.

Yeah. Again, it's something which has been done in discussion with the players.

Why do you find that interesting?

Do you remember I said to you about how I felt that really effective trade unions work with their employers to work out what is the best balance, the most sustainable best balance for all parties — balancing lots of different things.

So this clearly has been a result of negotiations with the players over a number of years where they say, "you know what, actually one thing we could do here, because there are some golfers and always have been who do blow their career earnings whilst they are at the peak of their powers and end up, you know, having to — dare I say it — sell stuff from Hooters outside the US Masters every year, which I know is great fun, but it's still a bit odd that a two-time major champion basically is hawking concessions outside the Masters."

Apparently, it is so fun. Apparently, it's great, but I'm just saying it's a bit sad he has to do it.

Charlie, we'd be there. Of course, we'd be there. Of course, we'd be contributing to John Daly's old age.

与球员的成熟合作

But I do think it's just a really interesting example of how mature current relations are between the US PGA tour and the leading players on the US PGA tour. You just mentioned there about Scottie Scheffler's very mature reaction to being told that he wasn't going to get a several-shot head start, etc.

And then you look back on how they actually beat LIV was through cooperation with the leading players. That cooperation happens because you're already on good relations with them. And the players get huge benefits from that.

Yeah. Right. Because once you start to get that influence — do you remember what I said about the PFA, which is I think the PFA should be very focused on the calendar. I think there are real risks to footballers' physical well-being and their career longevity from the current way in which the calendar's progressing.

If you're at the top table and if you have been shown to be cooperative on stuff which really matters to the organizations and the employers, you absolutely have the authority then to say, "guys, there's some stuff we do need to talk about here." But if you're the type of player organization, the type of trade union who's just got "give us more money, we want more money, more money," then effectively you're basically just pushing yourself down the food chain and you go, "okay, you're just one of those guys. Okay, well here have a bit more cash and off."

Right? So I think that that is a really good example — the US PGA tour of how the organizations and players can rise together. And I love it. I'm so, you know, happy with the way in which the PGA Tour has safeguarded golf. You know, if we talk about the way in which UEFA has been safeguarding football, the PGA Tour has been safeguarding golf from what was frankly in my view a really risky way of doing it.

一个警示：如果 LIV 消失了呢？

No, I will caveat it. With — now if LIV doesn't continue at all in any capacity, what continues on the PGA side, what gets dropped if it gets its monopoly back? Do we keep that balance?

I think prize money has to come down. And I've seen, you know, I think I quoted before a couple of players — senior players — saying, "look, it's not sustainable to keep prize money at current levels."

Paul McGinley said that, right? So they know that the reason why prize money is so high at the moment is because of the LIV threat. They know this and they're intelligent enough to understand it and they're intelligent enough to know that the US PGA tour can't keep on taking external finance because that external finance is going to eat away at the equity which they themselves have earned in their own commercial arms.

They're very aligned in that way. So I think it's a really good ecosystem and I would encourage anybody who's got an interest in golf to pay some attention to Tour Championship this week. It's going to be a cracker.

收尾

Yeah. Do you know what else is a cracker? Being back in the studio with you Charles.

Oh Charles, thank you very much.

It's been fun. I think as you said earlier on, we should go for a couple of beers now.

I've got meetings. I'm working.

For those of us who are interested, you'll be seeing Charlie outside a police station on the King's Road in about 10 hours from now after a couple of beers.

Be arrested. I'll just be handcuffed. Big difference.

Thank you guys. We'll see you next week.

Thanks a lot.

item.description:
## 失败作为一种商业模式：凯尔特人的"负向护城河"
大多数俱乐部把失败视为成本，凯尔特人却把它变成了**资产负债表的润滑剂**。他们的运营逻辑令人惊讶地类似于**保险公司的精算模型**——预设每年欧冠出局的"损失概率"，然后通过压低支出、囤积现金来抵消这种失败带来的收入缺口。但这里有一个致命的悖论：**保险公司卖的是"你不出事我赚钱"，而凯尔特人卖的是"我们出事你还得买"**。90 million镑现金堆在银行，主看台亟待重建，而 Dermot Desmond 却像一个把股东红利锁在保险箱里的信托管理人——问题在于，他管理的不是资本，而是**60,000人的文化身份**。
这里有一个跨领域的连接值得思考：凯尔特人的困境与日本"僵尸企业"的现象惊人相似——不是因为亏损而僵化，而是因为**过度稳健而丧失了冒险的肌肉**。当一个组织的KPI从"赢得欧冠"退化为"不破产"，它就已经在心理上离场了。
## 英国板球的"男孩终究是男孩"叙事：一种被制度化的幼稚
真正令人意外的观察不是球员喝酒，而是**整个板球生态系统对"稚气未脱"的集体默许**。Charlie点出了一个关键结构性问题：*

item.title: [Lex Clips] Secret to 10x productivity with AI agents: Why most companies fail | DHH and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、真正被 AI 取代的不是程序员，而是"中间协调层"

DHH 这段话最反常识的洞察是：AI 革命的真正牺牲品，不是媒体天天渲染的"码农"，而是产品经理、VP、CTO、审批链这一整套中层结构。程序员反而变得更重要——因为唯有他能直接和 agent 对话，把 10x/100x/1000x 的杠杆拉满。

一旦你在人和 agent 之间插入一个"human bandwidth"，杠杆就瞬间坍缩回 1x。这意味着过去二十年里，硅谷精心搭建的整套 Scrum/JIRA/sprint/design review 机制，本质上是对"程序员注意力稀缺"的补偿性组织架构——就像人身体里的阑尾，是对早已不存在的饮食结构的历史遗迹。当稀缺性消失，整套补偿机制就变成了纯负债。所以大公司做不到 10x，不是因为它们不够聪明，而是因为它们的免疫系统会主动排斥直接人机交互——那会让一大批高薪岗位的存在理由蒸发。

二、"每个人自己的 5%"：软件产品这个类目正在死去

DHH 顺手抛出了一个几乎没人展开的经济学炸弹：Office 每个人只用 5%，但每个人用的是不同的 5%。过去四十年整个 SaaS 商业模式的底层逻辑，就是把 10 亿人的 5% 打包成一个产品，让所有人为其他 95% 付费——这是软件的规模经济。

Agent 时代把这个模型彻底反过来了：从"打包分销"回到"自织自穿"。这不是渐进式创新，这是软件从"产品"退化成"手工艺品"。有意思的跨领域联想是：这正是古登堡印刷术之前和之后的镜像倒转——中世纪每本书都是手抄孤本（个人化），古登堡之后变成大规模分发（标准化），而 AI agent 让软件从"印刷时代"退回到"手抄时代"，但没有失去印刷的速度。DHH 20 分钟写出 Typora 替代品，就是软件领域的私人手抄本复兴。

三、"不耐烦"作为一种新的经济信号

这段对话里一句被轻描淡写的话其实是全场最狠的："impatience is the first step of doing it yourself." 在前 agent 时代，用户的挫败感是终端信号——你只能忍受、抱怨、迁移到另一个也很烂的产品。挫败感是一个死胡同。

在 agent 时代，挫败感变成了创业信号。DHH 讨厌 Typora 的臃肿——过去这只能变成一条 Reddit 抱怨帖，现在直接变成一个 C++ QT 应用。这里藏着一个更黑暗的洞察：未来最好的软件不会由"用户需求调研"驱动，而会由"个人怨恨"驱动。Grievance-driven development（怨恨驱动开发）会取代 user-centered design。

跨领域连接：这和博客对报纸编辑部的瓦解是同构的。1995 年一个人对某篇报道不满，只能写信到编辑部；2005 年他直接开博客反驳。中间那层"编辑审稿链"消失了，因为出版的边际成本归零。今天软件正在经历同样的时刻——"发布"和"发怒"之间的距离正在归零。而当这个距离归零，DHH 说的"polyglot programmer"就不再是精英标签，而是普通人的默认状态：语言精通被商品化，品味和视野变成稀缺资源。这是编程史上第一次，"想清楚要什么"比"能实现什么"更贵。

📝 转录文本

Lex 的提问：为什么成熟软件的开发没有加速？

Lex: Can you tell me the intuition you have? I seem to just stepping back and observing the different apps that we all rely on — I don't know, Adobe Photoshop, all this kind of stuff. There seems to be — the progress on development there has not accelerated. So why is it? What lessons can you draw from Basecamp, like well-established huge user base? Why aren't we seeing like super rapid increase in new updates, features, all this kind of stuff in these well-established apps?

DHH 的回答 (一)：瓶颈从来不是实现，而是人的带宽

DHH: Multiple reasons. I'll start with the first one that's the most critical.

As soon as you're having human teams work together on something, the bottleneck is rarely implementation. It's human bandwidth and communication. When you have a product manager and a couple of designers and a VP above them and a CTO above them, and everyone wants to be part of the shaping process because we're all justifying why we're here — that's where all the productivity goes to die.

The revelation I've had working on Amachi the last 3 months is that to get that magical 10x, 100x, in a few rare cases a 1,000x productivity boost, you have to interact with the agents directly. And you cannot intermediate that bandwidth with another human because it's simply too slow.

And on the one hand that's a bit of a bummer. I mean, I like humans and it's great to work together. But it also means we need to temper our expectations with what these agents can do if it's humans driving it and you have three layers of approval and all the other machinery of a large corporation — the implementation part is only a small segment of it.

(二) 组织真正缺的不是实现能力，而是想法、视野和品味

The other thing I'd say is that most organizations don't know what they want. They don't know how to make it better. They're not bottlenecked on implementation — they're bottlenecked on ideas. They're bottlenecked on vision. They're bottlenecked on taste. And if you don't have those elements in excess of your implementational capacity, it doesn't help.

So you can make a lot of shitty ideas come true — then what? Are you going to ship that? That sounds like, I don't know, something coming out of Microsoft. That's not what we're trying to replicate here. That process is not actually — because we already had this.

If you step back for a moment and think of the towering organizations we have who have had tens of thousands of programmers at their disposal — I mean, I'm picking on Microsoft here. I love Microsoft some of the time. But I'll pick on them in this case because they have had endless resources, endless programming capacity for decades, right? This is what's showing us that just being able to write a lot of code does not produce great compelling software.

(三) 对"AI 还不够快"的反击

Now, the other thing is — we've had this capacity for about 6 months. That's not very long in human life cycle capacity of internalizing what's going on.

And I think it's actually funny that the critique of AI is, "Why isn't it going faster?" What are you talking about? We've not had any other form of progress that has moved as fast as AI. And you're impatient because in the last 3 months we haven't rewritten the whole world and made it a utopia of software goodness.

Lex：那 Linux 桌面呢？谁来重写 Premiere 和 Photoshop？

Lex: You're basically saying everybody should be switching to Linux now. One of the arguments is like — we can rewrite all the software that's not available in Linux, in Linux. Linux has been the love of my life for many years, but one of the reasons I'm still attached to Windows and now Mac is because of video editing, Premiere.

DHH: We're going to fix that, but —

Lex: So the question is, who's going to build Premiere and Photoshop for Linux? And it feels like one person can now —

DHH: 100% one person can.

Lex: And so — and I'm allowed to be impatient. In fact, me or anyone else — impatience is the first step of doing it yourself, right?

DHH: Correct.

Lex: And there's a community of tens of thousands of people that use Adobe Premiere or DaVinci, all these non-linear video editors, that know the frustrations. Everybody shares them. You can look at Reddit, you can look at the forums. Everybody knows it.

I don't know what it is — maybe the management, maybe the meetings, all the things you've always discussed is the bureaucracy that's in development of features — but it feels like if you just let some of the developers loose with a bunch of agents, you can fix all that. But again, based on everything you're saying, maybe the way to do that is to start over from scratch, maybe through open source, or somebody launches a new company. Within large companies now, it's hard to really accelerate into the agentic era by letting developers just build.

DHH：这是经典的"创新者窘境"

DHH: This is the classic innovator's dilemma. These companies have gotten so good, so established at the old way, and therefore their entire structure — management layers, processes — are tuned for a time that no longer exists. But you can't pivot that. These are supertankers. It just doesn't happen.

This is why we're finally getting this upset in the technology industry. For a while, I was very upset about the duopoly between Apple and Google on mobile, because it felt like mobile was the most important computing platform that we had, and I could not see a path to unseat either Google or Apple sitting on top of that, controlling everything, taking their toll booth money.

But the game changed. This is no longer the most important platform. Mobile phones are important, but there's also a lot of other form factors coming — whether it's glasses or earpieces or whatever else have you. It's all in play now.

计算平台四十年来第一次真正松动

But the computing platforms themselves are in play for the first time in probably 40 years, if you look at the desktop.

Linux has been around since '91. It's not taken off or taken over on the desktop. It's taken over everything else. All the devices you have on your desk, your fridge, your toaster — everything runs Linux except for your computer. Now, funnily enough, your Android is actually Linux, but wrapped so sufficiently that you can't really recognize it.

But now there's an opening — and the opening is exactly as you say it. If there's a piece of software you depended on that bound you to Windows, it is completely within reach for you personally to start rewriting it. And maybe you won't get to 100% coverage, but — this is the old joke about Microsoft Office: I only use 5%. Yeah, well, we all use a different 5%.

Well, what if we all just built our own 5%? What if I just took the functionality that I need and just did that? That is a completely different challenge, and one agents are incredibly capable of doing right now today. And I've done it a lot of times over.

亲身案例：一个 Ruby 程序员如何变成 polyglot

So, one of the amazing things I found with the latest Agent to Gauge is I have become a polyglot programmer. Something I was absolutely not before. I was a Ruby programmer first and foremost, and then I dabbled a little bit in Bash when I had to.

And in the last 2 months I've written C++. I've written three applications that have shipped in a Mach Quattro.

20 分钟重写 Typora 的故事

I wrote a writing app. I was using this app called Typora, which is a very nice app, which in itself is based on another app called iA Writer, which was my real love on the Mac for a clean, simple markdown writing environment. That's where I write all my essays.

And then I moved to Linux and I couldn't get iA Writer, so I moved over to this other tool called Typora. It was a piece of — where — and it had a lot of features I just didn't need.

And about 6 weeks, 7 weeks ago I thought, "Do you know what? I only need 5% of Typora, which is already a basic app." I literally told the agent to get going — that I wanted it written in C++ and QT, because that would fit well with the aesthetic of what I was building with Quattro. And in, I think, about 20 minutes it had the first version.

I started using it, and it wasn't quite right. Within 2 days I'd given up Typora, and I wrote — and have written — all of my essays since that moment in iA Writer.

item.description:
## 一、真正被 AI 取代的不是程序员，而是"中间协调层"
DHH 这段话最反常识的洞察是：AI 革命的真正牺牲品，不是媒体天天渲染的"码农"，而是**产品经理、VP、CTO、审批链**这一整套中层结构。程序员反而变得**更**重要——因为唯有他能直接和 agent 对话，把 10x/100x/1000x 的杠杆拉满。
一旦你在人和 agent 之间插入一个"human bandwidth"，杠杆就瞬间坍缩回 1x。这意味着过去二十年里，硅谷精心搭建的整套 Scrum/JIRA/sprint/design review 机制，本质上是**对"程序员注意力稀缺"的补偿性组织架构**——就像人身体里的阑尾，是对早已不存在的饮食结构的历史遗迹。当稀缺性消失，整套补偿机制就变成了纯负债。所以大公司做不到 10x，不是因为它们不够聪明，而是因为它们的**免疫系统**会主动排斥直接人机交互——那会让一大批高薪岗位的存在理由蒸发。
## 二、"每个人自己的 5%"：软件产品这个类目正在死去
DHH 顺手抛出了一个几乎没人展开的经济学炸弹：Office 每个人只用 5%，但每个人用的是**不

item.title: [Lex Clips] The biggest threat to Apple | DHH and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"5% 悖论"背后的软件工业革命反转

DHH 顺手抛出的那个"我只用 Office 的 5%，只是每人用的都不是同一个 5%"的老段子，其实藏着一个足以让整个 SaaS 时代动摇的观察：过去 40 年，软件之所以必须"通用化"，是因为分销和开发成本极高，只能靠"最大公约数"回本；而 Agent 让这个经济学假设彻底反转——每个人只写自己那 5% 的成本，第一次低于购买通用软件的成本。

这不是"AI 让我写代码更快"，而是软件从规模化工业品回到手工定制品的相变。就像 3D 打印没有杀死宜家，但让"我需要一个刚好卡在这个墙角、正好这个高度的柜子"从奢侈品变成日常。真正被威胁的不是苹果这个公司，而是"通用软件"这个品类本身存在的合理性。

二、Linux 的"隐形登基":最大威胁从不是同类竞争者

一个几乎没人愿意点破的反常识事实——Linux 早就赢了，只是赢的方式让所有人都没认出来。你的路由器、冰箱、烤面包机、Android、汽车中控、数据中心，全是 Linux。它输掉的只有你桌上那台电脑，而这恰恰是最没意义的那场战役。

这里有一个跨领域的强烈共振：这和电力革命的路径几乎一模一样。爱迪生和特斯拉打得你死我活时，没人意识到最终的胜利者不是"某个电力公司"，而是"电"本身变成了看不见的基础设施，藏在每一面墙里。Linux 对 Apple 的真正威胁，不是有一天你会装 Ubuntu，而是"操作系统"这个概念本身正在像电力一样蒸发成后台。当 Agent 成为你和机器之间的新界面，Windows/macOS/Linux 之争会像"你家用交流电还是直流电"一样无人关心。

三、DHH 自己就是他描述的那艘"超级油轮"——而他成功掉头了

最出人意料的一层，是这段独白的元叙事：DHH 是 Ruby on Rails 的作者，是"用一门语言解决所有 Web 问题"这一整套哲学的教父。而他在这段话里得意地宣布：过去两个月他写了 C++、写了 Qt、成了 polyglot。

翻译一下潜台词——他刚刚亲手告别了自己二十年的身份认同，而且语气轻松得像在换一双鞋。这才是这段视频里最值得警觉的信号：当连"框架布道者"这种最深度锁定于某个技术栈的身份都能在 20 分钟内溶解，那么苹果生态里所有靠"Xcode/Swift/App Store 三件套"筑起职业护城河的开发者、公司、投资逻辑，都在同一片流沙上。

跨领域再连一次：这几乎是新教改革的技术版。路德的关键突破不是"神学更好"，而是印刷术让每个人都能自己读圣经，中间的神职阶层瞬间失去了不可替代性。Agent 就是软件世界的印刷机，而 App Store、认证开发者、平台税，就是那批即将失去解释权的神职阶层。DHH 一边写着自己的 Markdown 编辑器一边说话的样子，就是 1517 年那个把《九十五条论纲》钉在教堂门上的人——表面上在聊工具，实质上在宣告一个中介阶层的黄昏。

📝 转录文本

超级油轮困境：为什么大公司无法转身

This is the classic innovator's dilemma. These companies have gotten so good, so established at the old way, and therefore their entire structure — management layers, processes — are tuned for a time that no longer exists. But you can't pivot that. These are supertankers. It just doesn't happen.

This is why we're finally getting this upset in the technology industry.

移动双寡头的松动

For a while, I was very upset about the duopoly between Apple and Google on mobile, because it felt like mobile was the most important computing platform that we had, and I could not see a path to unseat either Google or Apple sitting on top of that, controlling everything, taking their toll booth money.

But the game has changed. This is no longer the most important platform. Mobile phones are important, but there's also a lot of other form factors coming — whether it's glasses, or it's ear pieces, or whatever else have you. It's all in play now.

But the computing platforms themselves are in play for the first time in probably 40 years.

Linux 的悖论：赢下了一切，除了桌面

If you look at the desktop, Linux has been around since '91. It's not taken off or taken over on the desktop. It's taken over everything else — all the devices you have on your desk, your fridge, your toaster, everything runs Linux, except for your computer.

Now, funnily enough, your Android is actually Linux, but wrapped so sufficiently that you can't really recognize it.

5% 的突破口：Agent 时代的软件重写经济学

But now there's an opening, and the opening is exactly as you say it. If there's a piece of software you depended on that bound you to Windows, it is completely within reach for you personally to start rewriting it. And maybe you won't get to 100% coverage, but this is the old joke about Microsoft Office: "I only use 5%." Yeah, well, we all use a different 5%.

Well, what if we all just built our own 5%? What — [snorts and clears throat] — if I just took the functionality that I need and just did that?

That is a completely different challenge, and one agents are incredibly capable of doing right now, today. And I've done it a lot of times over.

亲身经历：从 Ruby 独尊到多语种程序员

So, one of the amazing things I've found with the latest agent age is I have become a polyglot programmer — something I was absolutely not before. I was a Ruby programmer first and foremost, and then I dabbled a little bit in Bash when I had to.

And in the last 2 months, I've written C++. I've written three applications that have shipped in a Mach Quattro.

案例：20 分钟重写 Typora

I wrote a writing app. I was using this app called Typora, which is a very nice app, which in itself is based on another app called iA Writer, which was my real love on the Mac for a clean, simple markdown writing environment. That's where I write all my essays.

And then I moved to Linux and I couldn't get iA Writer. So I moved over to this other tool called Typora. It was a piece of shareware, and it had a lot of features I just didn't need.

And about 6 weeks, 7 weeks ago, I thought, "Do you know what? I only need 5% of Typora" — which is already a basic app.

I literally told the agent to get going: that I wanted it written in C++ and Qt, because that would fit well with the aesthetic of what I was building with Quattro. And in, I think, about 20 minutes, it had the first version. I started using it, and it wasn't quite right. Within 2 days, I'd given up Typora, and I wrote — and have written all of my essays since that moment — in iA Writer.

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] Why Isn’t China Further Behind in AI? - Dylan Patel
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被误读的"算力差距"：真正的瓶颈其实是"研究带宽"

大部分人把中美 AI 竞争理解成一场"电力/芯片军备竞赛"，但 Dylan 在无意间抛出了一个反直觉的拆解：在 Anthropic 手里，5 GW 的算力真正被用在"那一次预训练"上的只有不到 200 MW，占比不到 4%。剩下的 60% 训练算力里，50% 是"研究"——试架构、调数据配比、跑消融实验，10% 才是"开发"（真正的训练执行），另外 40% 是推理。

这意味着：中国头部实验室用 100–200 MW 就能"看起来不落后太多"，并不是因为他们有神秘的效率红利，而是因为当前范式下，前沿的瓶颈不是"能把训练做多大"，而是"能同时跑多少个想法"。中国以 1/25 的电力做出接近的模型，本质上是在打一场"研究带宽"的仗，而不是"训练规模"的仗——这是一个只有拆到二级预算才能看到的隐藏结构。

真正令人不寒而栗的推论在后面：一旦 automated coder / automated researcher 上线，研究和训练的比例会开始反转——研究可以被自动化打薄，训练规模反而重新成为瓶颈。也就是说，中国现在"用小算力打出大模型"的窗口，恰恰会在自动化研究员诞生的那一刻突然关闭。这不是渐进式落后，而是范式转换那一天的悬崖跌落。

二、跨领域连接：中美创新体制是两种"进化策略"

Dylan 顺口说了一句极关键的话：美国金融体系愿意"YOLO"押注初创；中国金融体系一旦选定行业，补贴力度超过全球其他国家半导体补贴的总和。

这其实是生物学里两种截然不同的进化策略： - 美国 = r-策略（大量后代，高变异，高死亡）：一次同时孵化 50 个 AI 实验室、100 个 fabless 芯片公司，跑得快的通吃。 - 中国 = K-策略（少量后代，重投入，高存活）：一旦锁定"半导体"这个生态位，就把整个资源池灌到几个国家队里，压低失败率、拉长存活时间。

推论：如果 takeoff 很快（自动化研究员两年内出现），r-策略压倒性获胜——中国还没来得及"选中赛道"就被拉开。但如果 takeoff 慢一点，K-策略反而更占优——因为 r-策略最怕的就是"资源持续消耗但环境不剧变"。所以出口管制的真正意义不是"封锁"，而是赌一场时钟战：赌自动化研究员会在中国国产芯片 hockey stick（他预测在 2028 年）之前出现。这是一场关于时间差的豪赌，不是关于绝对能力的差距。

三、意外观察：政治正在做一件"角色反转"的事

访谈里有一句极其容易被略过的话："the only thing they're going to do is accelerate it"——中国唯一会做的事就是加速 AI，而美国政客却开始尝试为 AI 踩刹车。

这在冷战叙事框架里是完全反过来的：过去我们习惯认为"威权体制会因为怕失控而减速，自由社会因为分散决策而加速"，但在 AI 这件事上，中国正在扮演历史上"美国"的角色（无脑加速），美国反而在扮演过去"苏联"式的自我审查角色。

再叠加一个隐藏的资本流向：Dylan 的"质量加权 gigawatt"概念——中国 50 GW 国产芯片 ≈ 美国 20 GW 英伟达芯片——本质上是在为算力世界发明一种类似 PPP（购买力平价）的换算单位。这是一个非常重要的思维工具：未来讨论 AI 军备竞赛，我们需要的不是"多少 GW"，而是"多少质量加权 GW"，就像讨论 GDP 需要 PPP 一样。当研究者、政策制定者、投资人还在用裸 GW 争论时，实际的战略地图早已经在另一套坐标系里展开了。

一个可能让你意外的收尾：Dylan 作为公开的自由意志主义者，居然承认出口管制"真的起作用了"——这本身就是一个信号。当一个意识形态上反对干预的人，被数据逼到承认干预有效时，说明这套结构性差距已经大到无法用理论优雅地否认了。

📝 转录文本

全球算力版图：从 2022 到今天

Q: If you think there's 200 gigawatts globally in 2028, how much is in China by that point? And how does Chinese compute continue increasing through this whole trend? Because if the RSI stuff kicks off in the West before China has a large amount of compute, maybe we're living in a different world than when it doesn't.

Dylan: Yeah, so China today — so if we sort of level set back to 2022, the US was adding about 45 to 50% of the world's compute. China was adding about 30 to 35% of the world's compute, and the rest being taken up by the rest of the world.

Since 2022, we've had big regulations against China, and a dramatic increase in America. So today, 70% of watts are being deployed in America. And, you know, China is really a very small number. It's sub-10% of watts being deployed for data center AI compute in China.

And as we step forward, they're still at a very small number. Their domestic production is quite small. Their purchasing from Nvidia is still quite small. And a lot of that ends up in other places as well, right? You know, Malaysia or what have you. So ultimately, China domestically still continues to have sub-10% of incremental new compute.

So in 2028, might start to inflect up, I think. But it's pretty easy to say China will have like 30 gigawatts of AI compute or less.

Q: By 2028?

Dylan: Yeah, in 2028.

走私、晶圆厂与 2028 拐点

Q: Okay. And then how fast does their hockey stick go up?

Dylan: I do think in 2028, they have a big uplift in what compute they're able to deploy. 2026, they're still mostly relying on a lot of the smuggled chips — you know, a lot of the chips that TSMC made for companies that they thought weren't Huawei, but ended up being Huawei, or a lot of HBM that Samsung is shipping.

But in '27, fabs start to go up. In '28 especially, fabs start to go up from SMIC and CXMT and such, where domestic production is actually reaching many millions of units a year. And now they're incrementally adding, you know, 5–10 gigawatts in just 2028 of domestically produced chips.

Those chips are definitely worse than the chips that Nvidia will have in '28, or Google will have in '28, or OpenAI will have in 2028.

质量加权：30 GW 的真实含金量

Q: So even the gigawatt number overstates things, you're saying. Like it's 30 gigawatts but it's really much worse chips. But then — how, yeah, how does it… If you think the world is going to add 100 gigawatts the following year? Or something — you know, I know you said you can't really say that far out. How much is China able to add the subsequent year? Basically, I want to know: did they just hockey stick at the point at which they are able to start shipping large amounts of compute, or is it still going to be less than US plus allies?

Dylan: There's a lot left to — you know, whether or not the US passes the MATCH Act, whether or not ex-tools continue to get export controlled, how fast China can build their new equipment that they're starting to be able to domestically produce.

But ultimately, you know, China is definitely going to hockey stick. If there's anything China's really good at, it's scaling manufacturing really, really quickly. And I imagine China will start to be able to extract more and more purchasing of even foreign chips into domestic China, or at least close the gap in what the US is allowing Nvidia to sell them or what have you.

Q: But do you think China could do adding 50 gigawatts by 2029? Marginal incremental gigawatts in 2029.

Dylan: I think that's completely reasonable. And part of that could also be purchased from foreign.

Q: Yeah.

Dylan: But yeah, I think it's completely reasonable that China in 2029 can do 50 gigs. But if most of those are the domestic chips, there is some factor there where that 50 gigawatts is really worth as much as 20 gigawatts in America — or from American chips.

Q: Right, right. So you're actually projecting a world where maybe the leading lab in 2028 has more compute than China will have in like all of China will have in '29 or even '30 — if you weight gigawatts by their quality. Implying that there's nothing to done to slow down the US labs, but clearly the government is starting — politicians are starting to do that. Whereas China is not going to slow down AI. In fact, the only thing they're going to do is accelerate it.

出口管制：一个自由意志主义者的重新评估

Q: So honestly, when Aaron and I were chatting and asked about export controls — I am a libertarian person, and I wasn't genuinely sure what I thought about this issue. I was steelmanning what is the opposite view that he has, and — because I think it's important to hash out ideas. But I'm like, yeah, maybe there's a world where if we just cooperated with China, it would be better for us, especially since they control so much of the supply chain and the other things that will be needed for robotics and other things.

But I didn't realize the compute situation was as as you're saying. Like actually the export controls do seem to have really — if they ship the amount that you're saying, that's a huge difference. By the time we have automated coder and even getting into automated researcher, China is like way far behind on the compute stock. And so if that ends up being the case, that would have worked. I think that's actually a notable success.

Dylan: I would say the only caveat there is: some of it is export controls, but some of it is also just financial systems, right? American financial systems are more willing to YOLO into startups than Chinese financial systems. But once Chinese financial systems choose an industry to focus on, they'll subsidize it a hell of a lot more.

Q: Yeah.

Dylan: And so the Chinese semiconductor industry has significantly more subsidies than the rest of the world's semiconductor industries combined — which points to, like, if takeoff is not as fast as sort of you're implying, but actually takes longer, then ultimately China will catch up drastically on the semiconductor side, which then is compute at some point.

中国实验室的"效率悖论"

The other aspect of this that I think is noteworthy is: Chinese companies today are not that far behind in AI models, at least perceivably by the public, relative to the amount of compute they have, right? The leading Chinese labs have 100–200 MW total of compute at most. ByteDance — Seed being the one outlier where they have significantly more than that. But, you know, Kimi is not running a gigawatt or anywhere close to it.

Q: Yeah.

Dylan: Whereas Anthropic is nearly 5 GW by the end of the year, right? Or more — sorry.

拆解算力预算：研究 vs 开发 vs 推理

And so the question is sort of: well, does it matter? And I think right now it doesn't matter that much, this difference in compute. Because when we break down the compute ratio or budget of a lab historically, it's been, you know, let's say 60 or so — so far it's been like 60% training, 40% inference.

But that training gets broken down further. And that's actually like: 50% of the compute is research, like 10% of the compute is development, and then 40% is inference.

And what I mean by research and development is: you know, researchers are generating ideas, testing new architectures, testing new data mixes, testing new hyperparameters, whatever it is they're doing — new attention techniques, blah blah blah. But ultimately, when they do the training run, when Anthropic trains Mythos, it's sub-200 MW, right? The pre-train of the whole —

Q: Thing.

Dylan: The pre-train. Yeah. It's sub-200 MW for call it 2 months. And then the RL is even less.

Q: Do you think the RL was less than the compute than the pre-train?

Dylan: At least in terms of single-side inference. I mean, single side of the pre-train, yeah.

Q: But total compute was probably higher, right?

Dylan: Total comp — but it's like sequential, right?

Q: Yeah.

Dylan: So at most, the most they ever used at one point in time was maybe 200 MW. And then in reality, they had multiple gigawatts, so most of their compute was going to the research, not the development of a model.

为什么无法把 2 GW 全部用于训练

And there's reasons for this, right? You can't — it's hard to coordinate all these clusters. It's hard to collocate all of them. It's hard to do multi-site training. It's hard to do RL — you know, generating even more rollouts during RL does not necessarily make it better. There's all sorts of reasons why you may not be able to leverage, you know, all 2 gigawatts that you have for training onto training, right? Actually, I can only leverage 200 megawatts.

As we get closer and as we get further and further down implementate automated coding, automated researcher, I actually expect the percentage of the compute budget that goes to research versus training to start to become a lot more fuzzy, or even higher for training. Also things like continual learning, right? All of these things start to mean that more and more is actually going to training the model.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

观看原视频 →
