item.title: [All-In Podcast] Eric Weinstein: The State of American Science, Breakthrough Coverups, and the Danger of Physics
item.dc:creator: All-In Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、令人意外的观察：物理学的"停滞"可能是人类的保命符

Weinstein在采访中扔出一个几乎无人敢想的悖论——过去50年物理学的停滞，可能是人类物种得以存续的关键。他用"boom/vroom/zoom"（武器/能源/推进）三元结构解释：如果1983年后SU4×SU2×SU2的路径没有被弦论"劫持"，我们可能已经拥有的不是核弹，而是能瓦解山脉的夸克-轻子转换武器、能穿透地球的中微子武器、以及只需高中生水平就能制作的"暗化学"。

这里藏着一个反直觉的系统性洞见：学术垄断有时充当了物种的免疫系统。一小群人（他点名Witten、Susskind、Gross）在1983-84年把整个领域推向"数学上美但物理上无害"的AdS/CFT，客观上创造了一个"可以邀请中国研究生参与而不泄露任何真正危险信息"的安全区。他称之为"给物理学做了绝育手术"——但被绝育的物理学，同时也是被驯化的物理学。

这与生物学中的"进化陷阱"（evolutionary trap）惊人相似：一个物种因某种适应机制（此处是学术共识）暂时脱离危险环境，但这种适应本身削弱了其继续演化的能力。

二、跨领域连接：科学同行评审 = 1940年代的"参考委员会" = 曼哈顿计划的隐形延续

这是全场最锋利的洞见，值得放在系统性框架里咀嚼：

Weinstein追溯了"peer review"这个词在Google Ngram上1965年前几乎不存在这一事实，然后把它接到一个鲜为人知的历史节点——1940年的Reference Committee。当时Briggs在国家研究委员会内设立一个秘密审稿机构，专门"退稿"任何关于链式反应的论文，让曼哈顿计划外的物理学家以为自己的方向"不够成熟"。

跨领域连接：这与金融业的"信息壁垒"（Chinese Wall）、情报圈的"隔间化"（compartmentalization）、Jeffrey Epstein作为"多重伪装职业身份"的运作模式——本质是同一套结构：用一个看似合法的评估机制（同行评审/合规部门/税务顾问）来掩盖信息的定向流动。

更惊人的是他把Renaissance Technologies的Medallion Fund放进这个模式：一个坐落于Stony Brook旁、雇佣纯理论物理学家而非交易员、雇员离职后资金仍留在基金内、拒绝外部资本的机构——它的"对冲基金"身份，可能扮演着与Epstein的"对冲基金"身份、Los Alamos的"男校"身份相同的封面角色。

无论你是否相信这个具体推论，方法论本身极具启发：当一个机构的官方叙事在市场逻辑上说不通，就要追问它的真实功能是什么。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：AI训练语料的"垃圾桶偏差"，将成为下一个知识范式的引爆点

Weinstein随口抛出了一个可能在未来3-5年内验证的预测——"垃圾桶语料库"（Trash Can Corpus）：

目前所有主流LLM的训练都优先加权Nature、Science、Cell、Annals of Mathematics等"共识期刊"，这意味着AI正在被训练成学术Cartel的复读机。但当有国家（他直指中国）训练一个专门读取被主流嘲笑、被拒稿、被贬为"边缘"的文本的模型，并让它假设"弦论是一个刻意的转移视线"——AI可能率先突破物理学停滞。

跨领域连接：这与创业投资中的"共识反向阿尔法"结构完全同构——最好的回报来自当时看似荒谬的下注（Airbnb早期、比特币早期、SpaceX早期）。Weinstein实际上在提出一个"AI版的Peter Thiel问题"：What important truth do very few people agree with you on? 但把它变成了训练目标函数。

更深一层的系统性观察：知识的生产结构与资本的生产结构，正在通过AI这个中介被彻底重构。当"什么被人类专家嘲笑过"变成一个可查询的数据集特征，异端思想的经济价值将首次被算法化定价。这可能是自古登堡印刷术以来，思想传播机制最根本的一次重构——不是让信息更快传播，而是让被压制的信息第一次获得系统性发言权。

一个额外的"啊哈时刻"

注意Weinstein反复用的一个词——"nail house"（钉子户）。他说自己是"民主党里的钉子户"。这个隐喻里藏着他整个人生的元结构：在一个所有人都被规划路径的系统里，做那个拒绝出售的孤立单元，让整个开发项目不得不围绕你重新设计。

从他的物理学（拒绝弦论共识）、他的政治立场（拒绝离开民主党）、到他对科学家生存的建议（"第三套房子"）——这是同一个策略在不同尺度的重复。这可能是他所有"洞察"背后真正的操作系统：识别那些看似孤立、实则处于系统关键位置的锚点，然后拒绝移动。

📝 转录文本

开场：一位数学物理学家的DC之行

主持人： We have become a nation when it comes to science.

Weinstein： You were called a fringe scientist.

主持人： I keep saying fringe.

Weinstein： Yeah. I totally disagree with the narrative of the field. I want to blow a giant pole in the civil rights act. The stagnation in physics may have led to the survival of the human species. When we make this jump, the world will become unrecognizable. I'm going all in.

（广告插播：Creative Planning — creativeplanning.com/allin）

主持人介绍： Eric Weinstein, mathematician, physicist, economist, PhD in mathematical physics from Harvard, National Science Foundation postdoc, O&R fellow at Harvard, published a proposed mathematical framework and speculative unified field theory called geometric unity in 2021, formerly with Thiel Capital, podcast host and guest. Welcome to the all-in interview.

Weinstein： It's great to be here. Now, where are the besties?

主持人： They declined the opportunity because this is an extended science corner.

Weinstein： Can't believe that Jason has turned tail and ran.

主持人： No, you and I. I mean, just for the audience, you and I both happen to be in DC right now. So, we're in a rented studio doing this interview. But good timing — what brings you to DC?

Weinstein： Uh, opportunity. I'm really excited. I've been meeting with the Department of War and took the opportunity to stay a couple extra days. Been talking to Director Kratsios over at OSTP and the White House science adviser — fantastic meeting. Been talking to Jay Bhattacharya, who's an old friend, over at NIH. About to talk to Jim O'Neill, who's hopefully coming into NSF. And really just taking a look at the first major proposal to reform American science since Vannevar Bush at the end of World War II. So this couldn't be more exciting.

主持人： Did Kratsios tell you that I just interviewed him on this topic?

Weinstein： No.

主持人： Okay. Well, I did.

Weinstein： Okay.

主持人： You guys are old colleagues, right?

Weinstein： Yeah. Yeah. Michael's great. So that came up — he said, "You know, here I am in this new role."

主持人： Yeah, I guess I was sort of worried that this report — obviously he's filling huge shoes — I was worried that it was going to be a disaster and I was stunned how good it was. I mean, it wasn't perfect, but never is.

Weinstein： And then I told you that.

主持人： Mhm.

Weinstein： And you said that well, you and I had been talking, and that you had been conveying a lot of these issues to him, and I feel like he's really grown into this role, trying to become a student of the American science project. And I couldn't be happier at hearing him say things like "We know that we don't know everything. We're just at the beginning. We're just getting started." So it looks like a great blueprint.

美国科学是否停滞？

主持人： Government-driven science has played a fundamental role in the success of the republic — at least over the last hundred years, last 50-75. Prior to that there's an argument to be made. In Science and a New Golden Age that Kratsios published, and that others have been making — I've heard you make it — that science has really stalled in America. Can you make that case for us now?

Weinstein： Well, it's a question of which science has stalled. One of the great things about what Michael's saying is that science is a big place and it's not being done in one way. So what I really think is the biggest — if you wanted to sort of fly over and give an idea of what's at risk — it's the absolutely courageous science that we can afford to do as a rich, ruggedly individualistic nation that no one else can afford to do.

More or less, when I see us doing incremental research and doing things that are incredibly careful with low variance and calling it excellence, I get depressed. Because my feeling is that what we should be taking on is the bets no one else can afford to take on.

It's also the case that our chief geopolitical rival, China, has a problem with freedom. And quite honestly, freedom is a weapon. It is a serious advantage that we can afford to look at ourselves and say we don't do everything perfectly and we want to know the truth.

I want to know whether Fauci killed 10 million people. I should be able to investigate that as a virologist, as an epidemiologist. I should be able to get answers and go through the process of justice. When we have a situation in which our scientists are hamstrung because the conclusion is known ahead of time, we limit our own ability to use cowboy science to drive the rest of the world. And quite honestly, we're giving away our biggest advantage — which is the middle finger, the American ability to say "screw you" to a supervisor who tells you what is true and what isn't true.

A young person should be able to say, "Hey, I think my field is going in entirely the wrong direction and I'm willing to bet my career on it. Don't interfere."

COVID、共识与"科学无产阶级"

主持人： This was always the biggest question for me — where were all the skeptics? Where were all the scientists that are supposed to question the dogma during the lockdowns, during COVID, during that pandemic? I talked to Kratsios about this: if everyone in the room agrees on something, it's probably wrong. There has to be some degree of skepticism, particularly because the fundamental basis of science is to ask questions, interrogate, generate evidence, generate data and then draw some conclusion and ask your next question. But it's almost like the asking questions stopped.

Where did that come from? It sounds like you're saying it's because folks were hamstrung socially. Was it economic? What is it that happened — that not just in this pandemic but broadly, we're seeing this happen in these scientific domains where everyone aligns around one thesis, one dogma? And if you don't, you're not going to get funding, not going to have friends, not going to get colleagues to work with you, you're going to get chastised.

Weinstein： This is the question. And let me just answer it: we created the scientific proletariat. We created a world in which professors cannot afford to go against a consensus.

Now, the problem is consensus, because if everybody agrees on something, you shouldn't need a consensus. There's no arithmetic consensus. Do we have an arithmetic consensus that 2 + 3 equals 5? No, it just is. When I hear the word "consensus," I get very, very nervous — because a consensus is usually an artificial agreement achieved through pressure. The Washington consensus is some sort of thing where we're all going to go in a particular direction and if you don't go in that direction, you don't have a job.

So when you ask, "Well, what happens?" — my question is that Jay Bhattacharya is a perfect example of what should happen. You have a guy who has a PhD in economics and an MD, and he went against it with the Great Barrington Declaration. Now he's the head of NIH. I knew Jay when he was called a "fringe epidemiologist" by this loser Francis Collins and his sidekick, who was probably our bioweapons czar, Anthony Fauci.

If I say Anthony Fauci was probably our bioweapons czar, that's going to strike all these people, particularly on the institutional left, as "Well, that's conspiracy theory talk." So my question is: we signed a couple of agreements in the '70s — the Geneva Convention and Bioweapons Treaty. We have a cryptic system. Somehow we chose in that case a mysterious Ukrainian-British zoologist to receive huge amounts of money through a hippie-dippy charity called the EcoHealth Alliance — money from DTRA, the Defense Threat Reduction Agency. The whole thing doesn't make any sense.

So if you start doing things through covert operations, the problem is that scientists can see right through covert operations. If you have great tools — you know, if you say, "I wasn't at the scene of the crime," I said, "Oh, well, but we have a hair follicle and I can pretty much tell you you were at the scene of the crime." That's how powerful science is.

So now you have this different problem, which is that you've got all of these B-minus policy people in Washington — particularly in the covert community, not the intelligence community, but the covert community inside the intelligence community — who don't want kick-ass independent scientists, because they're telling stories and narratives that are easily exploded. So right now, we don't just have a problem with good science, we have a problem with good journalism.

主持人： Right. They also have to fall in line with the pride narrative.

Weinstein： Exactly. So there are times when — you know, when the US went to war, Roosevelt was in a wheelchair with these leg braces and there was a general agreement that we won't report on the state of the president's health. Well, we had the same thing with Biden. Biden was undergoing some form of dementia. Did anyone think to ask a leading geriatric neurologist, "Look, examine his gait, examine his speech patterns, and tell us where he is likely in his cognitive trajectory"?

So if you're trying to tell a lie that's important structurally, you really don't want scientists exploding it. When we did — and I'm not arguing with that — we shouldn't have been honest about what we were doing at a New Mexico boys' school from 1940 to 1945 because science was creating the most powerful weapon ever seen on planet Earth.

主持人： For those not aware, that's the Manhattan Project.

Weinstein： Absolutely.

So what I'm trying to say is that right now, you're not taking those people who stood up and making them the president of a university or the chairman of a department. You're not giving them a chair. I just gave a talk on this at Jordan Peterson's ARC conference. You haven't reinserted the tiny number of people who stood up. You haven't rewarded them.

My question is: where's my third home for standing up? Where's the ability to put my kids — I want to put three kids through school. I want to participate in the security and the prosperity that we provide to everyone else. This is the key issue. You've created the American scientific proletariat.

That's one of the reasons why you have such strange political affiliations, where you don't have balance in the professoriate. You've got this incredibly dangerous situation where we are not participating in freedom.

And I will say in particular — theoretical physics is the only profession to have lost free speech, because of something called restricted data, where I am not allowed to put pen to paper to write down a physics equation if in any way it affects nuclear weapons. Well, try doing really good physics in a way that doesn't affect hadrons and nucleons. Impossible. So you have this threat that somehow — I'm not even protected by the First Amendment.

异端思维的代价：个人经历与激励结构

主持人： I want to go back to your point about incentives. When you say "I want to have a third home," you're saying — I'll do the Eric Weinstein translation here — as a professor, I have to fall in line in order to gain tenure, in order to get a grant, in order to get the chairmanship role or whatever fellowship I'm looking for. If I don't fall in line, if I'm fringe, if I say things that are nonconformist — is that the right kind of way to —

Weinstein： Heterodox?

主持人： Heterodox. If I choose to just go against the orthodoxy — I believe that it was insane to take the idea of the Wuhan Institute of Virology off the table when it came to the origin of COVID.

Weinstein： Right.

主持人： Okay. Insane. It was clear then. And when you said that, you were called a fringe scientist, chastised, labeled an outcast — therefore you lost access, lost jobs, lost income. There was much that was left out of the equation for you because you asked questions that were heterodox.

Weinstein： I came up with a set of equations in differential geometry in 1987 and I was really treated incredibly badly. Those equations took over my field in 1994, and there was never an attempt to go back and say, "Wait a minute, we just brutalized somebody who got things right and very early."

By the same token, it's just a very simple process: you're not allowed to want better for your life. You're supposed to be humble. "True scientists don't care about money. True scientists don't care about security. The reward is the work." Blah blah blah. It's all of this absolute drivel. The fact is that we are providing your security.

And I say "third homes" to be deliberately provocative. I used to say "second homes" and I'm done with that. You're dealing with a level of prosperity in a world in which the Gini coefficients are blowing out. It's almost entirely due to the technology that is derivative of science, and the scientists are not participating. So what you're doing is creating a collectivist mindset because we can't get paid. We can't win. If we get things right, we're out.

转折点：1965-1975 与MIT反战运动

主持人： When did this change happen? Because did we not value and prize heterodoxy, hereticism, outlandish ideas? The origin of science, the origin of great innovation — which arguably America is still the global leader in today — arises from what initially seems heretical, far-fetched, unrealistic. But all it takes is one out of ten of those things to be true, and ultimately the envelope is pushed forward and we find ourselves in a new frontier.

Science should follow the same formula as entrepreneurship — technological or industrial kind of entrepreneurship, roughly. But where did things change and why? Is this just the natural course — you know, Ted Kaczynski, the Unabomber, wrote this manifesto where he talked about "oversocialization." Is that ultimately what happened here? 主持人： Quantum gravity universe, right. And we're in a different universe where we have — what does that physics look like today? If we progress physics — help an audience that's a generalist audience understand a little bit about what it means if physics didn't stall out.

And before I do that, let me just ask this question. Some would argue that physics has played an important role — maybe it's not fundamental, and that might be your answer — in advancing things like semiconductor manufacturing technology, advanced lithography, material science. We've made tremendous progress in our capacity to drive compute, and that's led to this moment today where we have these tools that we call AI. And all of the underlying advancements in chemistry, material science, physics got us to this moment. And that we have made progress and it has been applied. That would be one argument. So maybe tell me why that kind of misses the point, and then we can talk about what the world would look like today if we didn't go off track in '83-'84.

Weinstein： Great question. Let me try to engage that and then feel free to redirect me if I'm not answering the question.

In the theory we have — which I'm going to call the frontier model, which combines general relativity and the standard model of particle theory — we know certain things that we can't use. We found out that there were three valence quarks inside of every proton and every neutron. Nobody has ever pulled a valence quark out of a proton or a neutron in isolation — something called "infrared slavery." And screw the woke for not saying we can't say the word "slavery." Infrared slavery. Deal with it, boys.

You have a situation in which there is no industrial application. We've known about it since 1968. So sometimes you don't get to use something for an extraordinarily long period of time.

But what happens if — maybe we're never going to pull a quark out of a proton. Maybe it's impossible. What if there are other things we might be able to do had physics actually advanced?

For example, in the mid-1970s two gentlemen called Abdus Salam and — I forget Pati's first name — put forward the Pati-Salam model. I believe that the Pati-Salam model will be found to be the correct first-order grand unification above where we are. Problem is that it has something called SU(4) rather than SU(3). The SU(3) is what generates the force that keeps all those protons from running away from each other inside of a nucleus — because obviously like charges want to repel. That's why we were able to take out two Japanese cities in 1945 — we got control of the strong force and that allowed us to use the electromagnetic force to generate completely destructive power, but it didn't destroy protons and neutrons.

What happens when you have SU(4) is that you see that the electron and the neutrino are the fourth color that we associate with the up quark and down quark, which make up protons and neutrons. You could have a weapon that rotates up quarks and down quarks into the lighter leptons that disintegrate matter. You could have dark chemistry. "Dark" is not the right concept — it's really decoupled matter. Dark matter is decoupled matter. Neutrinos are essentially dark matter. They're barely detectable.

主持人： They don't interact.

Weinstein： Well, they do, but very, very weakly. Only through the gravitational and weak forces, which are the two incredibly weak ones. And gravity's so weak, it's not — worth enough neutrinos concentrated, you can —

Well, here's another possibility. If you rotate a neutrino into some charged particle, you can send it through the earth.

主持人： Just explain what you mean by "rotate." These neutrinos are subatomic particles. They don't really interact well. What does it mean to rotate them?

Weinstein： Well, let's take — I think a large amount of the energy produced in the sun is neutrinos that come out. You and I are being irradiated by neutrinos, by billions of neutrinos. The only reason that we're not dead is — imagine —

主持人： They don't interact with our atoms.

Weinstein： Well, they barely interact. Once in a blue moon they do. At night the sun is streaming this through the earth. When it gets to us, it goes — it keeps going. You can shoot it through, I forget, a light year of lead and you very rarely interact.

What happens with the "rotation" — is in this sort of internal sense. So it's kind of a metaphor of rotation in this abstract place, which leads to a neutron. If I put a neutron on the table and we just sit there and watch, with a half-life of something like 17 minutes, I forget, it'll turn into a proton. This is called beta decay, because people saw an electron scream out of the neutron and that's why a neutral particle became positive — because the "negative-ness" went off in the electron.

主持人： Just to be clear for the audience, a neutron can turn into a proton and release an electron at the same time.

Weinstein： Yeah. But that turned out to be the wrong model — because there were three quarks inside of it, and one of the down quarks — so a neutron is down-down-up. A down quark let off something called a W-minus, which is a force particle, not a matter particle. And then that thing decayed into an electron and something else.

The only reason we determined that there was something else going on — it's a little bit like accounting. If you have a really good accounting system and you notice that the envelope from the till is a little light, you say, "Okay, according to conservation principles, somebody has been messing with the money till." And that turned out to be the neutrino.

So a neutrino and an electron have the same relationship as an up and a down quark, and you can transmute them using these W particles.

The danger of this is that when you have more force particles than we know currently, things that are to all intents and purposes stable now might not be stable in that new regime. So you could disintegrate a mountain potentially, if SU(5) is present. SU(4) is more stable than SU(5). I don't think SU(5) is relevant.

If you think about physics, think about boom, vroom, and zoom as an easy way to keep track of why this is our most terrifying and most amazing subject. Boom is weaponry. Vroom is energy. Zoom is propulsion, computation, and all the cool stuff that we get to do.

You've been denied — let's say the standard model got finalized more or less 53 years ago. For 53 years, you've been denied new boom, vroom, and zoom. And potentially the stagnation in physics may have led to the survival of the human species, because the boom is so terrifying. I can't tell you whether that's true or not, but it means that you don't have any vroom and zoom from the new stuff that could have occurred.

更大的Boom：为何科学的杠杆令人恐惧

主持人： So we have to be honest. I want the zoom in particular. We could probably make the case that no one on earth got there, and everyone has aligned around the distraction, the disinterest and the pursuit, because of that absolute risk. Because if someone did actually make advancements and they could access the bigger boom — it would be game over already. There's no such thing as more absolute power that would give an individual or a group the ability to leverage that in some way to their infinite will.

Weinstein： I don't agree with this at all.

主持人： Great, okay.

Weinstein： I spent two years indoors, being hounded to be vaccinated, because of four amino acids being spliced into spike protein of coronavirus. My guess is that that's pretty easy, right? Think about it: you need 12 nucleotides to code for four amino acids at the exact right place in spike protein — and that's enough to shut down Earth. This is high-leverage science.

Before we decide that what we want is "let's get back to kicking ass and taking names," let us at least pause and say most people are ignorant of how much power is present with a little bit of scientific knowledge.

There's a marvelous scene in Breaking Bad where the protagonist, named Heisenberg, takes what appears to be crystal meth and throws it in the office of a psychopath named Tuco. Tuco says, "Well, what the hell was that that caused that massive explosion?" I forget whether it was lead azide or mercury fulminate or one of these extremely volatile compounds.

Do you have any idea how easy it is to make black powder? I ask modern audiences — nobody knows that it's 75% saltpeter, 10% sulfur, and 15% charcoal. The Anarchist Cookbook has gone out of discussion.

The power of science, the leverage of science, is so profound that we should at least ask the question: what if you had nuclear weapons that didn't require centrifuges? What if there are easy things to do that high school students could do?

You remember this guy who scavenged the americium in smoke detectors to build a working reactor — I think it was Brooklyn. Nobody thought "collect 218 smoke detectors and you can have a working nuclear reactor."

If you want to think about Walter White as a paradigm, you have to go back to something called United States vs. The Progressive, the Progressive magazine, in which the Teller-Ulam design for thermonuclear weapon was put forward by a publication, and the government said, "No, no, this is restricted data. We need prior injunction. This is the most dangerous piece of geometry."

This is Stan Ulam's work. The whole idea is: if you're going to use a fission device — chemical shell compresses subcritical fissile material to create a detonator out of an atomic bomb — how do you get that to compress a rod or something into a fusion device? The only thing that can reach that tertiary stage fast enough is light. You have to figure out the geometry, because the detonator is going to rip apart the entire assembly if it doesn't get —

Now, that secret got published, and the only reason the government didn't go after Howard — what is it — Morland, is that we stupidly declassified all sorts of pieces and shards of this, and he went to the Los Alamos library and he pieced it together.

If you don't know the story of John Aristotle Phillips, the substandard physicist who in his Princeton PhD thesis — as the Princeton mascot — said, "Look, I'm not very good, Freeman Dyson. I want to use the fact that I'm not very good to do something amazing. Tell me whether or not you will let me come up with a plan for an atomic bomb." And Freeman Dyson said, "I will give you no help, but I'll tell you whether it will work."

So the substandard physicist put together this and submitted his junior thesis, and I forget whether it's page 24 — but that thesis is not in the library, and the government removed the page that has the plan.

The fact is that this stuff is readily present, and we've never seen an atomic weapon used since 1945 — mostly if we don't use this power. But if it turns out that it's easy to do, then — and by the way, if the US fails with Iran, you're going to see a proliferation of countries acquiring nukes. Because we trusted the US. You've got this — you are the world's policemen. Petrodollars aren't petrodollars. They're violence dollars. The US was supposed to have the violence needed to secure the oil, and the oil backs the money.

We're watching the disintegration of that regime in real time as the US goes through its Suez moment. Whether you think Donald Trump should have gone in to Iran or not — and I happen to think that he was courageous and did something that we should have done in 1981 or '82 — we have to win. We have to win, because if you have a world that decides that there is no world's policeman, everybody's going to want their own nuke. And you can go back to the Tom Lehrer song called "Who's Next?" and you'll find that you're going to have a world in which you can't figure out the game theory because it's no longer dyadic. It's multipolar.

超越核武：多时间对手与太阳系逃生室

主持人： Imagine a world beyond nukes. What does that world look like? What else is there beyond the boundaries of what at this point is almost an 80-year-old technology? And again, I go back to the '83 story — we're making advancements. Did we stop making advancements? And is someone else — is China going to make these advancements? And what does that look like? Is that what UAPs — unidentified aerial phenomena — are? Because you've recently made comments that you were a deep skeptic on UAPs, but now you have a view that maybe there's something there.

Weinstein： Oh, there's definitely something there there.

主持人： Okay.

Weinstein： That something there there, by the way, may be China. It may be us. It may be a fake story — but there's definitely something there.

主持人： Based on the videos and the first-person accounts?

Weinstein： It's not the videos. I've never cared about the videos. I've talked to too many smart, sober people, too many similar stories. There are definitely special access programs that are all about this. The only thing that works to keep secrets is compartmentalization. We are so compartmentalized that almost no one can piece the story together. It may be that the stove-piping is such that we can't figure out what we know because we can't talk to each other.

If you want to know what's possible, I could freak you out and it would be super cool and super frightening.

One thing is: I'm worried about multi-temporal adversaries.

主持人： Time-traveling?

Weinstein： Times, travel, times.

Everybody says "time travel" because they think that time can only be one-dimensional. Imagine, for example, that you put a giant gun on a rail car. The rail car can only move in one dimension. Now, somebody puts a giant gun on something like a tank and you go to the Bonneville Salt Flats — now you can move in two dimensions. Now you put it on an A-10 Warthog and you can move in three.

Those are all spatial dimensions. Why do you think there's an arrow of time? It's because you believe time can only be one-dimensional. I don't think time is one-dimensional. And if you meet an adversary who has access to multi-time, it's like you're trying to compete with them with an A-10 Warthog and you've got your only gun on a track — except with time rather than with space. If I could sneak up behind you in time knowing your intent...

I mean, this is terrifying stuff to me. And it's also — I would love to have this over our adversaries, but I don't want to meet anybody who knows how to do this kind of stuff, not on a level playing field.

Let me say another one. The solar system is an escape room. Elon was focused on Mars. I said that Mars is a red herring — it's a McGuffin. Tonight he's focused on the moon. He is our only adult, as far as I can tell, crazy and mad as he is, and he uses that to motivate engineers because Mars is barely doable.

These are the only rocks that are potentially habitable. It's not enough diversity if we have this much power. In these few spheres with which we could put atmosphere — assume that you could put atmospheres on the Mars and on the moon and you could get back and forth between them with chemical rockets — you'd have three places to screw up. We need tens of thousands, if not millions of places before we figure out how to civilize ourselves.

So we have to get out of here. It's too expensive to leave the solar system. My claim is that in an Einsteinian world, you're never going to. If Einstein is left to be in force, the speed of light is too brutal. You go to Alpha Centauri, four light years away, you come back, you do it at nearly the speed of light — everything is eight years advanced by the time you get back home. Nobody wants to do that. And that's just the first star.

My claim is that we have been too long in Einstein's prison.

Desi、暗能量与几何统一

General relativity really begins in 1913. It's really due to Grossmann and Einstein, not just Einstein alone. I don't know why we say that. It's not really Einstein-Hilbert. It's really Einstein-Grossmann. More or less since 1915-1917, the equations haven't moved.

They're going to break because of what's happening in southern Arizona. Kitt Peak has this object called DESI, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument. And I believe that it is going to show that the cosmological constant times the metric — which is how we encode dark energy into the equation — is going to break, because it's not constant.

The only reason that you have lambda times the metric, which is this term, is the product rule. If you take a derivative called divergence, you have to take the derivative of lambda times the metric left alone, plus lambda times the derivative of the metric. The derivative of the metric has to vanish. That term is the only possible term that can go there because of something called Lovelock's theorem. If you're within general relativity, trying to do this geometrically —

My claim is that that's going to break. We're going to get to five sigma if we aren't there already. I haven't kept up with the news. And then we're going to realize that the dark energy — the most important —

主持人： Generally makes up 60-70-80% of our universe.

Weinstein： We have the wrong formula for it. We have no contemplation of what it is.

Well, I'm focused on saying I have a candidate formula, and I think everybody who has one should come forward. We should hold a conference and say who wins, who's got the best idea. We can't just have Ed Witten patting himself on the back saying, "Well, string theory is the only game in town." 42 years later — come on. This is preposterous.

Getting back to policy: give me some money and get rid of these people. I don't want them reviewing anything that I'm doing. Give me somebody competent to talk to.

主持人： So sorry, let me just go back. The dark energy measurement, which we're going to end up having a very high accurate estimation, tells us that the general theory of relativity and the equations associated with it are wrong because of the relationship that we see between matter and rotation and movement. And so there's something off about that.

Weinstein： We know that general relativity is not the last. We know general relativity is wrong. It is a view. It is a derivative. It is the map and not the territory. It is a great, great model. Whoever comes next has to recover it.

But there is no initial singularity due to the Big Bang. Nor is there a singularity in the center of a black hole called the Schwarzschild singularity. That's where our ignorance shows. We have two singularities we can't get rid of inside the theory. So you have to go outside of it. But the thing is, it's so perfect that nobody can figure out — you know, sort of in the first four seconds of a physics talk, you say "let X13 be a spacetime manifold" — well, okay, it's over. That's the sarcophagus, and you're already in an Einsteinian frame of thought.

We know that it's wrong, and nobody can figure out how to make it wrong. And that is what keeps us stuck here.

There's a marvelous demonstration around 2003 at a TED talk of this guy showing a surface — he's got some sort of display and he does this and suddenly everything enlarges and then he does this and everything gets smaller. This is the beginning of a multi-touch gesture called pinch-to-zoom that we all use.

My claim is that we don't realize that pinch-to-zoom is probably built into the thing that we're confusing for spacetime. So we don't know to do this. And when you do that, you change the distances. So you don't need to break the speed of light.

This is — again, you're asking somebody who can't come in to the physics establishment. I am in the physics establishment. We're in some sort of crazy world in which people who have radical ideas can't do the radical ideas inside of the institutions.

Like, a radical idea is that male and female are mostly determined by the SRY complex on the Y chromosome. If I say that, I can't be in a meeting because I'm a bigot. I can't be in a physics department because I think Ed Witten drove the field off of a cliff. Nobody else is saying it. Clearly the one person who's saying that has to be wrong.

Now, this is the whole thing: I have the first paper, I think, on the danger posed by mortgage-backed securities. I think I was the only person to loudly say you don't know whether Biden's going to make it to November. And I think I said loudly, I think this is four years of dimension.

When people say something different, do you force them back into this consensus? Well, that's what nations do. And we have become a nation when it comes to science.

中国、AI与"垃圾桶语料"

主持人： Talk about China. From what you know, is China thinking differently about physics? Is China trying to recast the paths? Is China trying to invite innovative ideation amongst their scientific community, or are others — I mean, it seems like the West is probably clumped together. Is China different? Is anywhere different?

Weinstein： Yeah, let's talk about that. First of all, France is historically the world's greatest mathematical country. China, where we're always taught to be so scared of the Chinese in math — couldn't buy a base hit until very recently.

Now, what they're doing is that they're looking at us with our absolutely ridiculous collectivist fictions, and they're sidling up to our best people and saying, "Are you sure you wouldn't want to be free? You sure you wouldn't want to get paid? Come over to China. Taste the freedom. Get paid. Have fun."

And our people are going there.

主持人： American scientists are going to China.

Weinstein： American scientists, Russian scientists, all sorts of scientists are going to China for some prestige, some money, and some freedom. And we are going to train them up and they are going to be frighteningly good — up until the point that that freedom involves Tibet, Tiananmen Square, and Taiwan.

主持人： Are they going to rethink some of these thoughts on the path we're taking in physics? Are they going to be fundamental in how they rethink things?

Weinstein： Let me tell you what I really believe on that. The AIs are going to change soon.

Right now the AIs are trained on a corpus that privileges things like Cell, Nature, and Science as the prestige journals of biology, or in mathematics it would be the Inventiones and the Annals and the Journal of the American Math Society. These are where the narratives of the fields are held.

The trash can is also a corpus. Take all of the ideas that have been pooh-poohed and laughed at, and call that the trash can corpus, the TC corpus. The AIs are going to start reading all of the things that our quote "leading physicists" have laughed at. Look out.

China is going to have a private model, and they're going to say, "Assume for the moment that the most failed theory in the history of modern physics — string theory and something called M-theory and quantum gravity — assume for the moment that it's a red herring meant to distract us. It's not our leading theory. It hasn't been our leading theory for 42 years. The dog can't hunt. What was it meant to stop us from seeing?"

主持人： And the AI will get there.

Weinstein： The AI will get there. Everyone who has an AI that can do this — again, I'm saying completely radical things, because quite honestly, that's what we're supposed to be doing. We're supposed to have John von Neumanns and Richard Feynmans and Paul Diracs and all of these characters, and we don't have any of them.

So I'm trying to say what this sounds like: "You're all wrong and I'm right." And don't tell me that I'm arrogant or that I'm conceited, or that real scientists are humble, or "if you understand something you can explain it to a five-year-old." That's all nonsense.

What I'm trying to say is: string theory has not been our leading theory for 42 years. It has never been the only game in town. And just the way Jeffrey Epstein was never a hedge fund manager, we're not allowed to say this.

I don't know why. I want to know: is there somebody over at CIA and the Science and Technology Directorate who would like to have that conversation? Is there anybody over at the Department of Energy who would be interested in not having this conversation right now? You and I are having a conversation with our friends the Chinese and the North Koreans and the Russians. Why are we doing this? Are you so confident that I'm wrong, given this obviously huge amount of knowledge that most people have never heard?

主持人： Well, I think the question is: can you really cage the AI? At the end of the day —

Weinstein： Say more.

主持人： So if the rate of progress with AI is such that — and the ubiquity of access, and the corpus, to your point, of knowledge and non-knowledge is apparent to everyone — the AI can be directed from anywhere. And it's probably a conversation about what does humanity look like. And I think that's a conversation with humanity, not with nation-states per se.

Weinstein： Well, I think what I'm trying to get at is — my model of the AI is: it is insane to have pushed out the AI as a commercial product. It's just funny. Let me imagine the scene from Silence—

主持人： It's just matrices and linear algebra.

Weinstein： Yeah, it's just inner products.

There's a scene in Silence of the Lambs where Hannibal Lecter is wheeled out on a gurney in a straitjacket with a crazy mask, and there's all these people around because he's so dangerous, but he's very, very intelligent.

That's what I think Anthropic is doing. Here's your new employee, Hannibal Lecter. He's a consultant. You've hired Hannibal Lecter from a temporary agency. And the harness that is supposed to keep you from hurting yourself is all the people around him, the mask and the straitjacket. And we've decided that this military research project is something you need in your home.

It's like telling people, "Look, the Second Amendment just says the right to keep and bear arms. We have this thing we haven't used called the Davy Crockett, a soldier-launched personal nuke. Why isn't it available at Kmart with a waiting period?"

主持人： Well, it's been distilled at this point. I don't know if that's a relevant point anymore, because models have been distilled or the model development has been commoditized, and it's been open-weight released and it's out there now. So models are here.

Weinstein： Yep.

主持人： And to your point, maybe those models get pointed at the path of discovering novel physics and look at strange texts and ideas and rethink everything.

Weinstein： It's going to be a hell of a ride.

主持人： It's going to be a hell of a ride.

UAPs、几何统一与"未接触部落"

主持人： I just want to hear your one assessment because I wonder if this is a glimmer — what do you think UAPs are today? Is that really the first window in what's happening? If there's something there, the question for you is: what do you think today UAPs are?

Weinstein： Let's answer that question, but I want to — let's do it in a debugger and we'll step through it line by line of the code as it executes.

I look at you, I'm on a podcast. My first thought is: I know what risks I'm running. If I say what I think, I can tell you which colleagues will not open their doors to me. No, I'm not kidding.

When I took a job with Peter Thiel — let's imagine that there are only about 125 people I can speak to about my work. I would say 30% of the doors closed to me just by virtue of the fact that I work with Peter Thiel. And I don't think he's the devil, and he's a close personal friend. Now you're asking me the question of how many of the remaining doors would you like to close?

Eric, it's not just a question. I know how these people think and I know how terrified they are.

Let's answer it anyway.

If general relativity is really the last word, I think that these UAP/UFO things are nation-states' experimental weapons systems. I think that there's been some breakthrough particularly in the 1970s. No, sorry, in the '60s. There's a 1971 Australian intelligence document where Australia — which was the testing ground for nukes of the United Kingdom — started seeing all these UAPs near their nuclear tests, just the way we see them near ours.

And the Australians revealed that many of our best people, and many of our top institutions, were doing anti-gravity — technically gravity shielding — research. And the cover story was the "golden age of general relativity" where suddenly general relativity was hot from the early '50s to the late '60s, early '70s. The claim from the 1971 document is: no, no, the only reason everybody went towards gravity is that there was interest in gravity shielding, anti-gravity, etc.

I don't believe general relativity is the last word. I believe pinch-to-zoom exists. There's another multi-touch gesture called shear-to-tilt, and that means that we can leave our solar system.

Okay, that's great news because it means we can survive. The implication is: if we can leave, everyone else can come. And given the size of the universe, the odds that we are the most advanced life form is laughable. There's no point in worrying about them.

So if we can leave, I think they're here. And I think we can leave. And I think the scenario to worry about is North Sentinel Island. Everybody who lives on North Sentinel Island is considered a citizen of India, and they don't know the word "India." They're an uncontacted people who don't know that they're part of something larger that watches them, that does not allow people to land. But if they started sending out radio signals, and then they started letting off nukes on that tiny little island, India would not have this paternalistic attitude towards its primitive tribe.

So my concern is that when we let off a nuke in 1945 — or when Italy became very good at quantum theory with Fermi and the Via Panisperna boys, and there was this Magenta incident under Mussolini — somehow UAPs are very tied to nukes. And I believe that a nuke is the sign that you become advanced enough that the next thing you figure out how to do is to leave and traverse through propulsion.

We don't realize that yet because we've never seen that happen. But my claim is that almost every civilization, before it gets to using the profound propulsion game — which is these multi-touch gestures — first lets off a nuke. And that we alerted whatever "India" is in this analogy — we're almost ready to come out, and we're so pathetically un-evolved that we are a danger to any other civilization if there's so much power in the next theory.

I believe geometric unity is the next theory. Now, that will cause a certain percentage of your audience to say, "Oh, it's just self-promotion." As opposed to: no, no, no, that's what you're supposed to do. If you have a theory, you talk about — yes.

I think that there are all sorts of things that you can do. I think there's multi-temporal movement. I think that there's dark chemistry. I think that there's dark light. I think that there are two other families of chiral matter left to discover at a luminous level. Spin-three-halves matter exists. I believe that SU(4) × SU(2) × SU(2) is the next grand unified theory that we'll find.

There is so much more to do that when we make this jump, the world will become unrecognizable. And I believe that there are other life forms in the universe and that they can come and they can visit. And I don't think that that's preposterous. I think that we are an uncontacted people.

结语：All In

主持人： On that note, I think we have more to talk about in the future. This has been a truly unique, fascinating — and I think for a lot of people in our audience, this is not a typical conversation. But I just want to highlight the importance of hearing what you have to say. Because I think it's very important that even if something seems not apparent, particularly when things seem unlikely, or when things seem outlandish or heretical or whatever term you might want to put onto things, it's valuable to take that in. It's definitely a lot to think about — the paths ahead — and I'd love to talk more.

Weinstein： I'd love to do that. I'd love to do it with your friends. And I also just want to say thanks for having me.

It's time for America to lead, because there's no other nation I trust like I trust our people to take care of this planet. We should make common cause with our rivals as fast as we can, because the danger of getting to the next level of leverage in a contested situation is overwhelming. It's very important we went into the Persian Gulf, and it's very important that the scientific community recognizes that, despite their feelings about Donald Trump.

We've got four or five individuals with the science portfolio who are much, much better than the PhDs think. And before you turn up your nose at this, consider doing what I did — which is to come for a few days to Washington DC and utter the dangerous words: "How can I help?"

I'm going all in.

## 一、令人意外的观察：物理学的"停滞"可能是人类的保命符
Weinstein在采访中扔出一个几乎无人敢想的悖论——**过去50年物理学的停滞，可能是人类物种得以存续的关键**。他用"boom/vroom/zoom"（武器/能源/推进）三元结构解释：如果1983年后SU4×SU2×SU2的路径没有被弦论"劫持"，我们可能已经拥有的不是核弹，而是**能瓦解山脉的夸克-轻子转换武器**、能穿透地球的中微子武器、以及只需高中生水平就能制作的"暗化学"。
这里藏着一个反直觉的系统性洞见：**学术垄断有时充当了物种的免疫系统**。一小群人（他点名Witten、Susskind、Gross）在1983-84年把整个领域推向"数学上美但物理上无害"的AdS/CFT，客观上创造了一个"可以邀请中国研究生参与而不泄露任何真正危险信息"的安全区。他称之为"给物理学做了绝育手术"——但被绝育的物理学，同时也是被驯化的物理学。
这与生物学中的**"进化陷阱"**（evolutionary trap）惊人相似：一个物种因某种适应机制（此处是学术共识）暂时脱离危险环境，但这种适应本身削弱了其继续演化的能力

item.title: [Lex Clips] Will AI replace programmers? | DHH and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个反直觉的观察：DHH 其实在偷偷宣扬"反规划主义"

表面上看，这是一段关于"程序员如何面对 AI 冲击"的常规安慰。但如果你仔细听，DHH 说了一句在硅谷语境里近乎异端的话："Don't try to anticipate anything." 一个白手起家、创立 37signals、发明 Rails 的连续创业者，居然在告诉年轻人"不要规划未来"。这与整个科技行业奉行的 OKR、路线图、五年计划文化是正面冲突的。

真正的洞见在于：当变化速率超过认知带宽时，"规划"从一种美德变成了一种精神消耗。DHH 用了一个几乎精神病学的词 —— "AI psychosis" —— 来形容那种试图预测两个模型代际之后世界的行为。这暗合了佛教的"活在当下"和斯多葛学派的"控制二分法"（focus on what you can control）。也就是说，AI 时代最反常识的生存策略，可能不是"更聪明地规划"，而是主动放弃长程规划这项人类引以为傲的能力。

跨领域连接：Jevons 悖论 × ATM × 织布机 —— 但真正的类比是"抗生素"

DHH 举了 ATM 和 19 世纪英国 Luddite 织工的经典例子。但我想指出一个他没说、但更精准的类比：抗生素之于医生。

抗生素诞生时，很多人预测"感染科医生要失业了"。结果恰恰相反 —— 因为治愈变便宜，人们开始做以前不敢做的手术（器官移植、开胸、化疗），反而创造了以前不存在的医疗需求。今天 AI 之于程序员就是这个位置：不是消灭程序员，而是把"写程序"这件事的价格降到足够低，让过去因为太贵而没人做的软件（比如一个只有你一个人用的、专门管理你家冰箱库存的 App）第一次变得经济可行。

这就引出一个让人意外的推论：未来软件的总量会爆炸，但每个软件的用户数会崩塌。程序员不会消失，但会从"造产品"变成"造私人订制物件的工匠"。这正是 Rails 早期"一个人也能做一个 Basecamp"哲学的极端版本。

隐藏的系统真相：痛苦的时间不对称性

对话中埋了一个心理学炸弹 —— DHH 顺口说的一句话："Pain in the moment is difficult. Pain in the rearview mirror is accomplishment."

这不只是鸡汤。这是系统层面的时间不对称性：调试 8 小时的痛苦、编译报错的沮丧、凌晨 3 点的段错误 —— 这些构成了老程序员身份认同的核心。AI 消除的不仅是"低效"，它其实在消除一整代人的"创伤共同体"。

想想这个跨领域连接：老兵、老医生、老程序员 —— 三个职业的社群黏合剂都是"共同承受过的痛苦"。当 AI 让下一代程序员再也不用体验 segfault、再也看不懂堆栈跟踪、再也不需要通宵，一个更深的问题浮现：程序员群体的"部落身份"靠什么维系？

DHH 谈到 Omakub 社区、开源 camaraderie 时，其实无意间给出了答案 —— 未来程序员的凝聚力不再来自"共同吃过的苦"，而必须主动构建（共同的项目、共同的价值观、共同的美学）。这是一个从"苦难型部落"向"意图型部落"的迁移。对于习惯了前者的老一代，这种迁移本身可能才是最深的存在焦虑，而不是"失业"。

啊哈时刻：程序员这次面对的不是"技能过时"，而是"部落解体"。真正需要重建的不是技术栈，是归属感的来源。

📝 转录文本

关于程序员群体的普遍焦虑

Lex： Can we talk about the general anxiety that programmers feel going through the same transformation — that maybe [they] gone to university, uh, majored in computer science, dreamed of being programmers and building stuff, high salary, and now everything is changing, and there's deep anxiety about "what do I do with my life?" Can you empathize with that, and what the hell are they supposed to do?

DHH： Huge thing. Because just because I have this disposition, I'm keenly aware that that's not evenly distributed — that not everyone sits with this disposition and this optimism for the future.

But I do think I want to separate things a little bit. I think you're going to have a hard time coping with the new reality if the only thing you loved about programming was the mechanical bits of putting the right logical construct together to produce something other people told you to produce. Because that mechanical process is under threat.

If you are, as you just mentioned, excited about building things, I don't think you're under threat at all. In fact, I think there's a great argument for us needing far more builders than what we have now.

就业数据与 Jevons 悖论

And if you look at the employment stats, it's fuzzy. It's not clear what's going to happen at all. Some stats actually show an increase in openings, because the advent of AI is so dramatically lowering the price of programs that people want a lot more programs. This is the classic Jevons paradox — that says when the price of something goes down, there's going to be more demand for it.

And this is the example of the ATMs, too. When the ATM originally came, a lot of bank tellers were very afraid for their job because suddenly there was a machine that could dispense money from people's account. Well, what the ATMs did was lower the price of a branch, and suddenly banks could afford to open a lot more branches, and we ended up with more bank tellers than we did before.

历史转折点：农业机械化与 Luddite

Now, none of this is guaranteed. There are also moments where things do change. The vast majority of people worked in the fields up until the late 1800s. And then suddenly we got mechanized harvesting tools, and we did not need human labor with a hoe and an ox out there — we had mechanical tools to do that for us.

In that moment, are there people who were threatened that their job and their livelihood was at stake? Yes. Was that a reasonable thing to feel threatened about? Yes.

The Luddites smashing the weaving machines in England had the same thing. I think maybe that's a better parallel than people working in the fields, because weavers were actually highly skilled professionals doing a job that they liked on rather favorable conditions — not slaving outside in the sun all day.

But where we live now, would we still like for clothing to be this heavily constrained resource? Like, what if this T-shirt was $400? I mean, okay, then I'd have to — well, my wardrobe probably looks like I have two.

生产力提升的真实含义

But I think the general progress of mankind depends on productivity improvements. And what are productivity improvements? This is very important, because in the abstract, I think everyone says, "Yay, productivity. That's good."

What did you think this was all just vibes?

No — productivity means fewer people to do the same number, or the same job. Now, the amount of job you want done may increase, and therefore you get people. But it also may not. There may be pockets where — [sighs] — a company just needs a certain set of fixed tasks done, and suddenly they can do them with a 10th the number of people.

This, by the way, could — is tragic and difficult in the moment for the individual being laid off. It's also amazing for the economy at large. Suddenly you freed up these resources who can now go do more productive things. This is how the whole economy evolves and improves, and how we get growth. And growth is good.

为增长辩护

I think this is the other thing to make a strong defense for: that growth in general is a good thing. We do not want to wind the clock back to 1920 or 1950. We should be excited about the fact that we've discovered new technology that allows us to do vastly more.

And while some of the tasks that may be taken over by AI were tasks that humans were excited to do — and they're just no longer economically viable — a lot of the tasks were just drudgery.

This is certainly true of my programming. There were a lot of moments of programming I thought were amazing. These were the moments that produced that state of flow we talked about last time. And they were ecstatic.

How often did they happen out of the course of a year? If you took your average programmer, how much time out of 2,000 hours at the job that that person spend in a flow state? 100? 200? 25? I think all those answers could be plausible for someone. And taking that drudgery, handing it over to machines — that is the history of civilization.

Lex： Yeah, I mean, the hours spent debugging… so the programming has so many painful, painful hours in it. And now they're gone.

DHH： For them, I mean, for the most part, it's just fun.

关于痛苦的时间不对称性

A lot of it is gone in a lot of domains, and the rest of it may be gone very soon. So that's where some of the romanticism also comes in — because pain in the moment is difficult. It's hard. It's annoying.

Pain in the rearview mirror is accomplishment, proud, learning, steps forward, all the things, right? So we encompass all of this as part of the human experience — that we hate pain in the moment, but we cherish it when it's 5 minutes past and we don't remember the hardship. We just remember the progress.

给年轻开发者的建议

Lex： So certainly at the societal level, at the macroeconomic level, growth is exciting. But the individual level, there's going to be a lot of anxiety, potentially a lot of suffering. So, by way of advice, if you're like a young DHH, young developer, programmer now — what would you advise they do?

DHH： Don't try to anticipate anything. You will literally go crazy, because even the smartest brains in the business cannot anticipate what two model hops from here is going to look like. It's an absolute waste of time, and you will develop an AI psychosis trying to deduce what 2 years from now is going to look like.

Focus on right now. And right now is the most incredible time to be into computers. You can make them do the most amazing things if you lean in. If you maybe for a hot moment force yourself to learn where the state of the art is, I double dog dare you not to get excited about what's possible.

公开构建与开源社区

Lex： And, uh, would you recommend building publicly?

DHH： I think it's optional, actually, to build publicly. I think it's nice to do, because then you get to be part of a community, and there's some camaraderie in open source. Not some camaraderie — there's an enormous amount of camaraderie. Open source is an incredible source of community and camaraderie.

And it's also a great way to stem some of that personal existential dread. If you're amongst other humans, you can get infected with good forms of mind viruses — exciting forms of mind viruses — the ones that tell you that it's all going to be okay, and the future looks bright. And if we build a bunch of things together, we can do things none of us ever dreamed we could do.

Omakub 与野心通胀

I was just talking to Ryan Hughes, who's been my main partner on Omakub almost since day one. And we were literally talking about, yesterday, how when we started on this journey together, our ambitions were very modest. We were just like: "Can we get this distro to not crash at 3:00 a.m. because of an Arch package that just got pushed out outside of our control? That'd be amazing. Then it'd be great."

Now we're leaning back and thinking, "How can we take over the world? How can we make Omakub go to Mars? How can we do everything we've ever dreamed of?"

And that level of ambition inflation is partly because things have gotten better with agents, but hugely also because we've surrounded ourselves with others excited about the same journey.

孤立与 COVID 的教训

And if you're just sitting in your little isolated cave worrying about the future — yeah, you're going to go a little nuts.

I think, [clears throat], if we learned anything during COVID, is that people will go nuts sitting in their little cave inside by themselves worrying about what's going to happen. That is indistinguishable from depression — ruminating endlessly about things you can't control.

I'm sorry to channel some Y Combinator lingo here, but that's just loser talk. You don't have to be a loser. You can choose to lean in and win. And "win" is very broadly defined as learning more, making more, contributing more, being part of more.

And at the end of the day, what are your choices? You don't have a choice, mate. The future's coming whether you like it or not. So you might as well choose to be excited about it.

规划几乎不可能

Lex： But — I mean, we should emphasize the fact that planning is nearly impossible with AI. I mean, most of us plan our life a little bit. When we're younger, you have hopes and dreams. There's a reason you go to college. There's a plan underlying it.

DHH： I agree with that. I'll concede that.

Lex： It is kind of nuts that it's impossible to really plan, because you really don't know if there will even be a Claude Code or Codex and Cursor 6 months from now. Maybe you'll be talking to WhatsApp. Maybe it'll be all Open Claude type. Maybe it'll just all be voice. Maybe Anthropic will take over the world and it'll be voice. Maybe there won't be operating systems anymore — you'll just, there'll be this glowing orb that you just talk to. Because if natural language is enough to accomplish all tasks in life — like, what is life about? What are the major tasks you need to accomplish in life? If you can just do that with voice, and it writes all the programs for you and all the systematized… what are the jobs needed then? Maybe it's more about the service industry. Maybe there won't be programmers like agent and engineers at all.

And so, yes, your advice is wise to focus on the moment, but that doesn't mean that it's just a crazy roller coaster ride, cuz we don't know what this December, what this January will look like.

选择信念作为对抗焦虑的方式

DHH： We don't know. And therefore, we should choose to have faith that it's going to pan out. That is my best advice towards fighting anxiety — that you have a choice, to a large degree, of how to lean.

Do you want to lean into P(Doom)? P(Doom) is going to happen whether you lean into it or not. You don't have control.

观看原视频 →

item.title: [All-In Podcast] The Scientific Precariat, China's Brain Drain, String Theory's Collapse & UAPs w/ Eric Weinstein
item.dc:creator: All-In Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：物理学的"停滞"可能是人类幸存的原因

Weinstein 抛出一个令人脊背发凉的假设——1983年后理论物理的集体停摆，或许并非偶然的智力枯竭，而是文明层面的"免疫反应"。他把物理学的产出重新编码为三个字："Boom（武器）、Vroom（能源）、Zoom（推进/计算）"。过去50年我们只在 Zoom 一栏获得了红利（半导体、AI），而 Boom 与 Vroom 的完全冻结——恰恰让人类熬过了核时代。

这里藏着一个惊人的跨领域连接：弦论的失败与冷战后的核不扩散体系，可能是同一个"文明恒温器"的两个表现。当一个物种掌握 SU(3)×U(1) 就能毁灭两座城市时，让最聪明的大脑集体沉迷于"AdS/CFT"这种"连苍蝇都伤不到"的数学游戏，可能是一种被隐性选择出来的社会防御机制。Renaissance Technologies 的猜想（在长岛悄悄做真物理的秘密曼哈顿计划）无论真假，其背后的"分区隔离 + 表面故事"结构，与 Epstein 的"多策略外汇基金"、与 Los Alamos 的"神秘城市"是同构的社会拓扑——每当人类掌握过大杠杆，社会会自动长出加密层。

二、隐藏的系统性真相：科学界的"精准阶层"（Scientific Precariat）

Weinstein 用了一个极具颠覆性的经济学词汇——precariat（不稳定无产阶级）——来描述今天的科学家。这不是抱怨薪水低，而是揭示一个更深的结构性事实：当科学家买不起第三套房时，他不是缺钱，他是失去了"说不"的定价权。

这里的跨领域洞察在于：同侪评议（peer review）本质上不是学术制度，而是1965年医疗保险法案（Medicare Act）催生的财务合规工具——政府开始成为最大付款方后，医生们发明"我们自己审自己"来抵御政府监管，随后这套逻辑被科学界全盘接管。也就是说，今天钳制物理学家自由发言的"同侪评议"，其基因源头是医生对付保险审计的一场官僚政变。这解释了一个悖论：为什么科学越"专业化"，反而越像会计——因为它的评审机制本来就是从会计逻辑里长出来的。

三、意料之外的启示：AI 即将"从垃圾桶里读物理"

最后一个"啊哈时刻"——Weinstein 预言 AI 训练即将发生一次相变：从"Cell、Nature、Science 的正典语料"转向"被主流嘲笑过的所有想法组成的垃圾桶语料（Trash Can Corpus）"。

这个断言的震撼在于它把两个看似无关的领域连了起来：科学史的"异端目录" + 大模型的下一轮训练数据 = 一次绕过学术权威的降维打击。中国若率先训练一个"假设弦论是障眼法"的私有模型，将获得一种荒诞而致命的优势——用被西方学术圈踢出去的垃圾，反向重建物理学。这本质上是知识生态里的一次"套利"：过去50年被主流"做空"的所有想法，正在变成一个巨大的负β头寸，而 AI 是唯一有能力一次性平掉这个头寸的工具。

再往深处走一层：这也解释了为什么 Weinstein 反复强调"多时间维度"（multi-temporal adversaries）——如果 AI 能在语料时间轴上前后穿梭，把1970年被埋葬的 Pati-Salam 模型和2026年的实验数据缝合起来，它就已经在扮演一个"时间维度更高的对手"。物理学的下一次革命，可能不是某个天才在黑板前完成的，而是某个模型在夜里"回读"了整整一代人的学术尸体。

📝 转录文本

开场：一个反常的物理学家

"We have become a nation when it comes to science." "You were called a fringe scientist." "I keep saying fringe. — Yeah. — I totally disagree with the narrative of the field." "I want to blow a giant hole in the Civil Rights Act." "The stagnation in physics may have led to the survival of the human species." "When we make this jump, the world will become unrecognizable." "I'm going all in."

[Sponsor break — Creative Planning]

As your wealth grows, have you noticed how much more complex things get? Between investments, tax strategy, and estate planning, managing it all is a full-time job you didn't ask for. Creative Planning can help. Their coordinated team of investment managers, CPAs, and affiliated estate attorneys can do much of the heavy lifting so you don't have to. Creative Planning, where wealth works together. Go to creativeplanning.com/allin.

嘉宾介绍与开场对话

Eric Weinstein, mathematician, physicist, economist, PhD in mathematical physics from Harvard, National Science Foundation postdoc, O&R fellow at Harvard, published a proposed mathematical framework and speculative unified field theory called Geometric Unity in 2021, formerly with Thiel Capital, podcast host and guest. Welcome to the All-In interview.

It's great to be here. Now, where are the besties?

They declined the opportunity because this is an extended science corner that —

Can't believe that Jason has turned tail and ran.

No, you and I. I mean, just for the audience, you and I both happen to be in DC right now. So we're in a rented studio doing this interview. But good timing — what brings you to DC?

Opportunity. I'm really excited. I'm meeting with the Department of War, and took the opportunity to stay a couple extra days. Been talking to Director Kratsios over at OSTP and the White House science adviser — fantastic meeting. Been talking to Jay Bhattacharya, who's an old friend, over at NIH. About to talk to Jim O'Neill, who's hopefully coming into NSF. And really just taking a look at the first major proposal to reform American science since Vannevar Bush at the end of World War II. So this couldn't be more exciting.

Did Kratsios tell you that I just interviewed him on this topic?

No.

Okay. Well, I did.

Okay. You guys are old colleagues, right?

Yeah. Michael's great. So he — that came up. He said, "You know, here I am in this new role."

Yeah, I guess I was sort of worried that this report — obviously he's filling huge shoes — was going to be a disaster, and I was stunned how good it was. I mean, it wasn't perfect, but never is.

And then I told you that.

Mm-hm. And you said that we had been talking and that you had been conveying a lot of these issues to him. I feel like he's really grown into this role, trying to become a student of the American science project, and I couldn't be happier at hearing him say things like, "We know that we don't know everything. We're just at the beginning. We're just getting started." So it looks like a great blueprint.

政府资助科学的角色与美国科学的停滞

Government-driven science has played a fundamental role in the success of the republic — at least over the last hundred years, last 50, 75. Prior to that, there's an argument to be made — in Science and a New Golden Age that Kratsios published, and that others have been making, I've heard you make it — that science has really stalled in America. Can you make that case for us now?

Well, it's a question of which science has stalled. One of the great things about what Michael's saying is that science is a big place, and it's not being done in one way. What I really think is the biggest — if you wanted to sort of fly over and give an idea of what's at risk — it's the absolutely courageous science that we can afford to do as a rich, ruggedly individualistic nation that no one else can afford to do.

More or less, when I see us doing incremental research and doing things that are incredibly careful with low variance, and calling it excellence, I get depressed. Because my feeling is that what we should be taking on is the bets no one else can afford to take on.

It's also the case that our chief geopolitical rival, China, has a problem with freedom. And quite honestly, freedom is a weapon. It is a serious advantage that we can afford to look at ourselves and say, "We don't do everything perfectly, and we want to know the truth." I want to know whether Fauci killed 10 million people. I should be able to investigate that as a virologist, as an epidemiologist. I should be able to get answers and go through the process of justice.

Now, what they're doing is that they're looking at us, with our absolutely ridiculous collectivist fictions, and they're sidling up to our best people, and they're saying, "Are you sure you wouldn't want to be free? You sure you wouldn't want to get paid? Come over to China. Taste the freedom. Get paid. Have fun." Right? And our people are going there.

American scientists are going to China.

American scientists, Russian scientists, all sorts of scientists are going to China for some prestige, some money, and some freedom. And we are going to train them up, and they are going to be frighteningly good, up until the point that that freedom involves Tibet, Tiananmen Square, and Taiwan.

AI 与"垃圾桶语料"：下一场物理革命

Are they going to rethink some of these thoughts on the path we're taking in physics? Are they going to be fundamental in how they rethink things?

Let me tell you what I really believe on that. The AIs are going to change soon. Right now the AIs are trained on a corpus that privileges things like Cell, Nature, and Science as the prestige journals of biology; or in mathematics it would be the Inventiones and the Annals and the Journal of the American Math Society. These are where the narratives of the fields are held.

Okay. The trash can is also a corpus. Take all of the ideas that have been poo-pooed and laughed at, and call that the trash can corpus — the TC corpus. The AIs are going to start reading all of the things that our so-called leading physicists have laughed at. Look out.

That's where the discovery and the reinvention is going to happen.

China is going to have a private model, and they're going to say, "Assume that the completely failed — the most failed theory in the history of modern physics — string theory, and something called M-theory and quantum gravity — assume for the moment that it's a red herring meant to distract us. It's not our leading theory. It hasn't been our leading theory for 42 years. It can't — the dog can't hunt. What was it meant to stop us from seeing?"

And the AI will get there.

The AI will get there.

And when the AI gets there —

Everyone who has an AI that can do this. Again, I'm saying completely radical things because, quite honestly, that's what we're supposed to be doing. We're supposed to have John von Neumanns and Richard Feynmans and Paul Diracs and all of these characters, and we don't have any of them.

So I'm trying to say what this sounds like: you're all wrong and I'm right. And don't tell me that I'm arrogant or that I'm conceited, or that real scientists are humble, or "if you understand something you can explain it to a 5-year-old" — that's all nonsense.

What I'm trying to say is string theory has not been our leading theory for 42 years. It has never been the only game in town. And just the way Jeffrey Epstein was never a hedge fund manager, we're not allowed to say this. I don't know why. I want to know: is there somebody over at CIA and the Science and Technology Directorate who would like to have that conversation? Is there anybody over at the Department of Energy who would be interested in not having this conversation right now?

You and I are having a conversation with our friends, the Chinese and the North Koreans and the Russians. Why are we doing this? Are you so confident that I'm wrong, given this obviously huge amount of knowledge that most people have never heard?

Well, I think the question is — can you really distinguish, and can you really cage the AI? I mean, at the end of the day —

Say more.

So if the rate of progress with AI is such that — and the ubiquity of access, and the corpus, to your point, of knowledge and non-knowledge — is apparent to everyone, the AI can be directed from anywhere. And it's probably a conversation about what does humanity look like — and I think that's a conversation with humanity, not with nation states per se.

Well, I think what I'm trying to get at is — my model of the AI is: it is insane to have pushed out the AI as a commercial product. It's just funny. Let me imagine the scene from Silence —

It's just matrices and linear algebra. I mean —

Yeah, it's just inner products.

Mm-hm.

There's a scene in Silence of the Lambs where Hannibal Lecter is wheeled out on a gurney in a straight jacket with a crazy mask, and there's all these people around because he's so dangerous, but he's very, very intelligent. That's what I think Anthropic is doing. "Here's your new employee, Hannibal Lecter. He's a consultant. You've hired Hannibal Lecter from a temporary agency." And the harness that is supposed to keep you from hurting yourself is all the people around him — the mask and the straight jacket.

And we've decided that this military research project is something you need in your home. It's like telling people, "Look, the Second Amendment just says the right to keep and bear arms. We have this thing we haven't used called the Davy Crockett — a soldier-launched personal nuke. Why isn't it available at Kmart with a waiting period?"

Yeah. Well, it's been distilled at this point. I don't know if that's a relevant point anymore, because models have been distilled, or the model development's been commoditized, and it's been open-weight released, and it's out there now. So models are there, models are here.

Yep.

And to your point, maybe those models get pointed at the path of discovering novel physics, and look at strange texts and ideas, and rethink everything.

It's going to be a hell of a ride.

It's going to be a hell of a ride. Yeah.

UAP、外星文明与"未接触部落"

I just want to hear your one assessment, because I wonder if this is a glimmer — what do you think UAPs are today? Is that really the first window in what's happening? If there's something there, the question for you is: what do you think today UAPs are?

Let's answer that question. But I want to — let's do it in a debugger, and we'll step through it line by line of the code as it executes. I look at you, I'm on a podcast. My first thought is: I know what risks I'm running. If I say what I think, I can tell you which colleagues will not open their doors to me. No, I'm not kidding.

When I took a job with Peter Thiel — let's imagine that there are only about 125 people I can speak to about my work. I would say 30% of the doors closed to me just by virtue of the fact that I work with Peter Thiel. And I don't think he's the devil — and he's a close personal friend. Now you're asking me the question of "how many of the remaining doors would you like to close?" Eric, it's not just a question. I know how these people think, and I know how terrified they are.

Let's answer it anyway. If general relativity is really the last word, I think that these UAP UFO things are nation-states' experimental weapons systems. I think that there's been some breakthrough particularly in the 1970s — no, sorry, in the '60s. There's a 1971 Australian intelligence document where Australia, which was the testing ground for nukes of the United Kingdom, started seeing all these UAPs near their nuclear tests, just the way we see them near ours. And the Australians revealed that many of our best people and many of our top institutions were doing anti-gravity — technically, gravity shielding research. And the cover story was "the golden age of general relativity," where suddenly general relativity was hot, from the early '50s to the late '60s, early '70s. The claim from that 1971 document is: no, no, the only reason everybody went towards gravity is that there was interest in gravity shielding, anti-gravity, etc.

I don't believe general relativity is the last word. I believe pinch to zoom exists. There's another multi-touch gesture called shear to tilt, and that means that we can leave our solar system. Okay, that's great news, because it means we can survive. The implication is: if we can leave, everyone else can come. And given the size of the universe, the odds that we are the most advanced life form is laughable. There's no point in worrying about them.

So if we can leave, I think they're here — and I think we can leave.

And I think the thing — the scenario to worry about — is North Sentinel Island. Everybody who lives on North Sentinel Island is considered a citizen of India, and they don't know the word "India." They're an uncontacted people who don't know that they're part of something larger, that watches them, that does not allow people to land. But if they started sending out radio signals and then they started letting off nukes on that tiny little island, India would not have this paternalistic attitude towards its primitive tribe.

So my concern is that when we let off a nuke in 1945 — or when Italy became very good at quantum theory with Fermi and, I forget, the atomic boys, and there was this Magenta incident under Mussolini — somehow UAPs are very tied to nukes. And I believe that a nuke is the sign that you become advanced enough that the next thing you figure out how to do is to leave and traverse through propulsion. We don't realize that yet because we've never seen that happen. But my claim is that almost every civilization, before it gets to using the profound propulsion game — which is these multi-touch gestures — first lets off a nuke.

And that we alerted whatever "India" is in this analogy. We're almost ready to come out, and we're so pathetically unevolved that we are a danger to any other civilization if there's so much power in the next theory. Which — I believe geometric unity is the next theory. Now, that will cause a certain percentage of your audience to say, "Oh, it's just self-promotion." As opposed to "no, no, no — that's what you're supposed to do. If you have a theory, you talk about —"

Yes. I think that there are all sorts of things that you can do. I think there's multi-temporal movement. I think that there's dark chemistry. I think that there's dark light. I think that there are two other families of chiral matter left to discover at a luminous level. Spin-three-halves matter exists. I believe that SU(4) × SU(2) × SU(2) is the next grand unified theory that we'll find. There is so much more to do that when we make this jump, the world will become unrecognizable.

And I believe that there are other life forms in the universe, and that they can come and they can visit. And I don't think that that's preposterous. I think that we are an uncontacted people.

结语：美国必须领先

On that note, I think we have more to talk about in the future. This has been a truly unique, fascinating — and I think for a lot of people in our audience, this is not a typical conversation. But I just want to highlight the importance of hearing what you have to say. Because I think it's very important that even if something seems not apparent, particularly when things seem unlikely or when things seem outlandish or heretical or whatever term you might want to put onto things, it's valuable to take that in. It's definitely a lot to kind of think about the paths ahead, and I'd love to talk more.

I'd love to do that. I'd love to do it with your friends. And I also just want to say thanks for having me. It's time for America to lead, because there's no other nation I trust like I trust our people to take care of this planet. We should make common cause with our rivals as fast as we can, because the danger of getting to the next level of leverage in a contested situation is overwhelming. It's very important — we went into the Persian Gulf, and it's very important that the scientific community recognizes that, despite their feelings about Donald Trump, we've got four or five individuals with the science portfolio who are much, much better than the PhDs think.

And before you turn up your nose at this, consider doing what I did — which is to come for a few days to Washington DC, and utter the dangerous words: "How can I help?"

I'm going all in.
