## 一个反直觉的观察：这不是"QE"，而是"债务的期限套利"——美国正在把自己变成一家投行
大多数评论把 Bessant 的长债回购简单等同于 QE，但 John Butler 点破了一个更让人不安的真相：**这是用短债融资来回购长债**——不是印钞扩表，而是"缩短负债久期"。这个动作在结构上和 2008 年之前雷曼、贝尔斯登所做的**期限错配套利**惊人地一致：借短、买长、赚利差、维持流动性幻觉。
换句话说，美国财政部正在把自己**资产负债表投行化**。这个洞察真正让人后背发凉的地方在于：投行倒下的方式从来不是资不抵债，而是**短端融资突然拒绝滚动**。当整个联邦债务的加权期限被系统性缩短，美国就把自己暴露在了"日频再融资风险"之下——这是雷曼式的脆弱性，只不过发生在主权层面。
## 跨领域连接：Rollover（1981 电影）× 中国黄金 × 期权定价理论
Butler 提到那部 1981 年的 Hollywood 电影《Rollover》——但他没有明说的深层类比是**期权定价**。
他关于中国 10 年期国债收益率为何异常低的解释，本质上是一个隐含期权价值论证：*

item.title: [Business of Sport] Vik Banerjee on The First Season of New Ownership, Big Sponsors, & What Comes Next
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一场被伪装成"体育联赛"的风险投资实验

表面上，Vik 谈的是板球联赛"The Hundred"的第一个新赛季。但如果把耳朵贴近他的措辞，你会听到一个更陌生的声音——这其实是一场用"体育 IP"作为标的物的种子轮融资仪式。

100 多个买家竞投 8 支队伍、"venue + investor"的相亲式配对会议、最后一轮拍卖定价、5 亿英镑分配给英格兰板球生态——这些不是传统体育联盟的语言，而是 YC Demo Day 的语言。ECB 不像在办联赛，更像在做一个 "体育资产孵化器"：中央先用 5 年建立最小可行产品（MVP），达到"因成功而触及天花板"的临界点，再把 8 个"子公司"拆出去独立融资，让每支队伍在下一阶段各自跑增长。

这里有一个让人意外的观察：Vik 反复强调"我们没有印度球员，但除此之外都有了"——听起来是限制，其实是结构性护城河。IPL 靠垄断印度男球员保住了金字塔尖；The Hundred 恰恰因为"抢不到 IPL 球员"，才被迫把资源、叙事、球员体验、女子板球溢价全部拉高到最大值。限制反过来成了产品定义。这和 Netflix 早年因带宽不足被迫做剧集算法推荐、后来变成核心壁垒，是同一种逆向进化。

女子板球被"藏"在双打包里的隐形革命

大多数体育联盟推动性别平权靠的是宣言、赞助商 KPI、政治正确的仪式性投入。The Hundred 做了一件在结构上无法被回退的事：把男女比赛物理绑定成一张票、一天一场的"双头赛"。

Vik 顺口一句话暴露了这个设计的真正杀伤力——"如果我们改成 T20，每场多 20 球，一天下来就多出接近两小时；带孩子的家庭 9 点就得走，女子比赛的时段就会被牺牲。"

翻译一下：100 球制不是为了让比赛更"现代"，而是为了在时间预算里给女子比赛留出不能被商业逻辑侵蚀的位置。这是一种典型的"制约设计"（Constraint-Based Design）——把伦理选择编码进物理规则，让后来的商人即使想牺牲女子板球也做不到，因为那会打碎整个产品架构。

跨领域看，这和建筑师 Christopher Alexander 的"模式语言"如出一辙：真正的公平不是靠道德说服，而是靠让不公平在结构上"跑不通"。也很像瑞典把育儿假强制切分给父亲——不是鼓励，是让"不休"变得比"休"更麻烦。

100 球 vs T20：一场关于"感知复杂度"的心理战

所有质疑者都在问同一个问题："这跟 T20 差 5 个球，为什么不直接改成 T20？"

Vik 的答案表面是市场调研（"英国观众的三大障碍是时间、复杂度、感知"），但更深的答案藏在他没明说的地方——"100 球"是一个心理定价锚。

T20 = "又一种版本的板球"，观众会自动调用旧脑回路：规则、术语、要坐 3.5 小时。 100 球 = "一种新东西"，观众被迫放下预设。

这是行为经济学里 "类别重命名" 的经典操作：Uber 不是"出租车 App"，Airbnb 不是"民宿"，Peloton 不是"卖健身车"。当一个产品能被塞进旧类别，它就永远逃不出旧类别的价格上限和期待上限。

The Hundred 的核心创新其实不在球场上，而在感知层——它需要在观众心里被归类为"新事物"，才能吸引那 40% 从不看板球的家庭。5 个球的差异不是竞技规则，是一道认知防火墙。

有意思的是，Vik 自己也承认："对我 6 岁的儿子来说，这就是 T20 少一个球。"——他知道这件事在竞技层面无关紧要。真正重要的是它对不看板球的人来说"看起来不一样"。整个联赛的成立，建立在一个精心设计的"外行错觉"之上。这不是欺骗，这是产品设计的最高级形式。

作为普通观众的体验与外界评价

Host: Well, look, I — you know, I sent you a message and said I'd love to do this because for anyone that does tune in — really they — I'm a fan, right? I've been to a few games. Thank you.

Vik: Thank you.

Host: And I love it as an experience. I think it's been really good. I think it's been really fresh and the atmospheres that I've been in as a standard like punter sitting in the seats, you know, it's been really cool and something that I think cricket has desperately needed in this country for a long time.

There is also the other side of it where newspaper headlines and people — you know, the people that know their cricket — will come and all the time comment or say to me, "Oh, well, you know, I don't like it. This isn't for me. Attendances are down." All of this. You're always going to get that in sport and you got to be open to it. But I thought this was a really perfect time to actually have a look at this from the development perspective because when we did have the chat, it was — you were positioning something which had had a few years of really good, should we say, establishment, but that was the major time you were taking this from centrally owned and controlled and operated to — does this really have value to people outside of it? And that could have backfired massively on you. People could have said no, sorry, don't see the value, don't find the assets attractive.

So from this year, what really changed? Give people an understanding of why this was kind of like iteration one almost all over again.

从"中央运营"到"八队独立"的结构性转变

Vik: So yeah, it was a strange brand — so for the first five years the 100 had been run entirely centrally. And what that means is the initial team names and brands were all controlled centrally. For a fan buying a ticket to any of the games, was all sold and issued centrally. For all of the kind of player contracting we did at the ECB, for hiring the security guards — everything from start to end was all done centrally from one office at Lords.

And that was great and, as to your — use your word — establishment, it established the tournament and it did great things and it had done some wonderful things in its five years that it had done and a lot of credit to a lot of people for that. But we just felt that, almost because of its success, it had hit a ceiling of what could be done with a small number of people based out of St. John's Wood. How do you take what it had done and build on it and go to the next level?

So that's where the investors came in. That's where the kind of the operational change with the teams came in.

Host: And that was in the plan from day one.

Vik: That was always the plan. That was always the vision when we went to market: okay, if we can't do it, then who can? Who are the very best people in the world at fan engagement, at digital and data, at commercial growth, at cricket? And so on and so forth. And if you can get them round a metaphorical board table all looking at the hundred going, "Well, here's how I can help. Here's how I can improve. Here's an idea." Then some magic is bound to happen. I don't know what that is, and some of it we've seen, some of it will come in years to come, but something will happen.

And so that was always the plan when we went out to seek the investment. We've absolutely got that in my opinion. We've got incredibly proud and humbled of the investors that we've got. Four from the IPL, four from other sports. We've got NFL. We've got the Premier League. We've got NASCAR. We've got the tech giants. We've got all sorts of different experiences and knowledge now in that melting pot.

What then happened this year in terms of the amount of change is massive. So you go from that all being run centrally to effectively now the league being run similarly to the NFL or other leagues of our nature, where the teams themselves are responsible for their ticket sales. They're responsible for their branding. They're responsible for their commercial sponsorship. We at the center effectively do a few things. We govern the league. So a lot of the regulations and that governance side sits with us. We work with broadcasters and help the broadcasters display our tournament in the best possible light. And then we have our own commercial deals that we work with.

And then what happens effectively is the central revenues get distributed 80/20. So each team gets what turn out to be 10%. We keep 20% which then gets redistributed into the sport.

8 支队 = 16 个新关系的运营挑战

Host: Okay. And therefore the challenges — if you're going into this season to overcome — were from an operational perspective having eight individual businesses really running and making sure that all of those different parts of those businesses could function to ensure that the business maintained its — what power, I guess.

Vik: It was huge. I mean I don't know of any others that's gone through — the level of change that we've gone through is unprecedented. Because it's not just eight, it's kind of 16. Because this time last year, October — actually last year, some into December — the teams were signing their own deals. So you've got the venue like an Oval or Surrey signing a deal with Reliance — two very successful organizations in their own right. They were coming together to create a partnership. That partnership was them figuring each other out and, at the same time as doing that, they were — that we were — figuring out a relationship with them as a team, as my London.

And so to go from that and then go, okay, now by the way, you've got to find sponsors. You've now got to sell tickets to your home games. You've got to create a brand and start to build an affinity and a fandom in your own kind of location and do that eight times over. So effectively 16 times over — was huge.

And hopefully not really massive for a fan, if that makes sense. I would hope that a fan would be able to buy a ticket with their family, come and watch and just enjoy the experience. But behind the scenes there is a huge amount of change that's gone on there.

上座率：数字、亮点与不足

Host: Okay. So, attendance — something that was brought up immediately.

Vik: Yeah.

Host: I will say, some people talking about it from a positive perspective — I was at the oval for that opening game.

Vik: Yeah.

Host: With you — and I saw it in all its glory, to the extent where over 20,000 people for the men's game, over 10,000 for the women's, I think. The concourses were alive. It was great, right? It was a really good atmosphere. Then you see other matches which didn't have as good attendance. The total stats — you had over half a million I think throughout the —

Vik: About 550,000 total, yeah.

Host: But not as many as you did last year.

Vik: Correct.

Host: Stick beat for people, right? How have you looked at attendance internally from that success perspective and where you really wanted to be?

Vik: Yeah, look, given the change that we talked about, I'm very happy with where we are. To get 550,000 tickets sold I think is a real positive. It's a real positive for cricket to get that number. Importantly as well, the demographics were there — to your point — I challenge anyone to walk around any of the concourses and not have a smile on their face because there are kids everywhere having a great time. So — I think we had 40%, just over, of our attendees were families with kids and that's brilliant. That's brilliant for the sport.

So given that, I really happy with the attendances. Yes, look, we hold our hands up — we're not perfect. We haven't achieved a sellout at every game. That's obviously the aim. And there were games and lessons learned where we want to improve next year. But I think having had this year, I think next year will be even bigger still and even more positive. We'll keep going with our demographics. We're still all about growth. We're still all about families. And so it'll be bigger and better next year.

Host: Do you think that the fact it didn't follow a major test series does play a part? I saw that referenced by a number of people.

Vik: Um, without getting too technical — there's effectively — the 100 shifts year-on-year, so some years it is after a major five-match men's test series (so the men's Ashes or an India series) and then the hundreds a bit later in August. In other years, like it was this year, we have a New Zealand series and a Pakistan series and we slot in the middle. The ticket sales historically have always been much higher after the Ashes or after an India series. Couple of reasons. It's a bit later so you have more time to sell those tickets. But cricket rises and cricket sells other cricket. You think next year with the Ashes coming up and the opportunity hopefully that England have to do well off the back of that, we will sell tickets and that will really help. So for an even year when we're slightly earlier, I believe we were thereabouts as the highest year ever of ticket sales — which again comes back to my point that we're really happy with where we are, but places to improve next year.

拓宽板球观众群：家庭、女性、儿童

Host: Yeah. Colin Graves when he came on talked about a core reason for the hundred being to not just recycle the — let's say — 1 million people that engage with cricket in this country, which is what we'd seen historically for many years. I.e. if there was a new short form tournament, it would still be the same people that would be engaging with maybe the test format or the 4-day game. The aim of the 100 from day one was to do something different to that and bring people that didn't have that history, that association with cricket, into the ground.

Now, you mentioned those stats — I did have a look at it, and from my side, it's massively influential in developing what Colin said about that — because if 22% of tickets were to junior fans under 16, 40% of families, 28% for women, they're not coming necessarily to lots of other forms of cricket.

Vik: Our purpose is simple. We have to throw cricket's doors open to as many people as possible. And that can be — look, if you're a — you know, so I play for Gloucester. There are people there that follow the county championship. They're very welcome. Absolutely. But equally welcome and accessible needs to be for those that are maybe a sports fan but have never tried cricket before or find cricket a bit daunting. We've got to bring children in because they're the lifeblood in generations to come. They're those that are going to be playing it. They're going to be watching it. They're going to be buying tickets. So bringing them into the sport is huge. So that is our aim. That is what we've set out — almost a simple purpose right from the very start. And that DNA runs through everything we try and do as a tour.

沟通挑战与真诚性

Host: How do you reflect on your communication? Do you think you speak about it in the best way possible when you talk about the things and the ways you can develop? And I'm not pinning this on any form of communication that I think hasn't been good — you know, how you communicate with an audience, how you try and capture them, how you try and deal with the negativity that's around something, how you quell the fears of emotion in sport — which, you know, we said before we came on is obviously the driver of so much about the best things of sport, but it can also be a big problem. You being able to communicate to this potential audience in the right way is going to be a huge part of you filling those stadiums that aren't necessarily full, of making those people feel included in something that is new and — let's be honest, right — maybe threatening or challenging to the sport that they love.

Vik: Yeah. Look, I think you can always improve how you do things. I think what we have tried to be very clear on is a core set of principles — what we're about and what we're trying to do. And I think then if you put at the heart of that some high quality cricket. So the product — what you see on the field — is unbelievable, and that is impressive, you know, in the final Ciphert smashing it to all parts of the ground. My dad was there and my son was there. My dad's watched cricket for his whole entire life. He was really impressed with that, as was my 8-year-old who just enjoyed balls flying everywhere and fireworks going off.

And so if that product stays really positive and high quality, then our role is to be authentic in how we talk about the sport and who we're trying to talk to. I think this year one of the things that we've learned is that with eight or nine teams and us, we can do that better in terms of how we coordinate amongst ourselves. But I would like to think that hopefully you have an authenticity in what we're trying to do. We are always going to receive some criticism. We take that on board. We do listen to it. We look at it and see if there are things that we can improve off the back of it, because we don't want to exclude anyone. That's the opposite of what we're trying to do. We want everyone, as I say, regardless of your affinity already to the sport, to feel like actually the hundred is something I really enjoy and want to come and see.

破纪录的上座率 & 伦敦 vs 全国

Host: Record attendances this year. You had a few. Right. They were — you had, am I right in saying three? I think. Yeah.

Vik: Three in — you had one in Wales which was a record for them. But you also had three record attendances — total number, as in most people through the gate. Is that — Yes. For a women's game at Lords, and the third one I believe was the Oval, but I may have got that wrong.

Host: Yeah. Do you have a London versus the rest of the country challenge? The experiences I've had — and this is all I can base it on — have all been in London. So I'm very conscious of that, and me saying this is great. But it does also strike me that it is perfectly tailored for London.

Vik: I think there are differences and I think that's what we have to be alive to, and part of the reason for doing the JV, if you like, and having the county involved in each of the teams, is that you are then able to have that deep-rooted connection and knowledge of the local area. And I think what I've learned through this last year is that is a hugely important — and I won't call it a challenge. I just think there is a difference with the fan base in Birmingham as there is in Cardiff as there is in South London. I don't think one is good or bad or more attuned or less attuned. But those that have done well this year — and you mentioned Welsh Fire — they've done brilliantly this year. Their fandom numbers, their digital numbers, their attendances — like you say, they sold out on a Saturday, they had great crowds in on a Monday night. It was unbelievable. But what they did fantastically was lean into the fact that they are the Welsh Fire and lean into that aspect of the local audience, the local fan base, and that was driven through the Glan team that know that area.

So I think that's important, and that will increasingly be important going forward — that as a tournament we have teams that are rooted in the local geography, and a competition we are rooted in the England and Wales kind of foundation of one of our tenants.

品牌重塑 vs 保留身份

Host: So what were the discussions, if you were privy to them, on the branding elements? Because you had four teams that rebranded, let's say, and four that maintained their original identity. When there's the rebrand, you've been working for 5 years to establish something from scratch, which is incredibly hard in sport. Now you're, as you said, kind of going again — any associations that may have been established now have to develop or change again. How did you deal with those challenges?

Vik: I think the teams have done a great job. You can completely understand why teams would want to do that, especially when you have a global portfolio and brands that you can therefore use to your advantage to bring fans in from around the world. But those that did rebrand were aware that they had work to do and have done brilliantly. From the Manchester and Leeds teams that were giving away shirts, from my London that had the shirt exchange — so if you had an Oval Invincible shirt, you could swap that in — I thought they've done a great job, in one year.

It was fascinating to see the amount of Manchester Super Giant shirts or the Sunrisers Leeds shirts not at the cricket grounds. So you'd be wandering around Leeds, you would run around Manchester. Interestingly as well, you'd see them at away games — which I think that's the first time, and it's anecdotal, but the first time I've really noticed that you would go to the Oval and see yellow for Trent Rockets, or you'd go to Birmingham and see the orange of Sunrisers and so on and so forth.

So I think they've all taken it upon themselves in different ways, aware of the challenge to establish that brand over the coming years. It will take time. It's not an overnight thing, but we've had a really good start.

面对头条与"深度球迷"的漫长养成

Host: What do you think about the headlines? Because I've seen a few and it — I was quite interested to see what people meant by it, where you said you've had these core identities and rules that you've lived to for the competition today. I saw one looking at it going — well, the specific headline was: "The hundred's costly makeover still leaves English cricket playing a waiting game." I.e. what they were saying is we're still trying to understand what this actually is. Is that fair? Because I didn't feel immediately when I read that. I was like, well, I kind of know I think what it is.

Vik: I look — I think the core tenets that I mentioned and you referenced there is: it's always been about growth, new fans coming into the sport, establishing ourselves as this unmissable event of the summer that is designed to throw doors open. And that's what we've been about. Then you add on top of that it's around the gender parity and the men's and women's on one club, two teams, equal footing. And that DNA runs throughout, and has done, through that.

What we now need to do to go to the next level is to deepen fandom of the eight teams. I understand and appreciate the feedback of previous years, and probably still to this date: fans are coming because it's a great day out at the 100. We are now only starting to build a — "I'm coming because I'm a My London fan" or "I'm a Sunrisers Leeds fan." And that is the next step that we need to do to become where we want, to achieve our objectives. But that's not an overnight thing. That's years in the making to get to that point. I have no doubt we'll get there, but you can't just flick a switch and say "you're a deep-rooted Birmingham Phoenix fan, and that's it, that's who you are." That will take time.

商业升级：赞助商与投资人的网络效应

Host: Yeah. Commercially, to me, it looked like a real level up. And I mean that just purely as like the breadth of associations that you seem to have now part of this year. You had — I mean, well, you had Barclays, you had Soen, Sketchers, Vitality, DP World all on front of shirts. That's a huge part of developing value in emerging sports, but it's also a huge part in now creating more value, driving better business. And I would imagine the new ownership that you have being able to add some form of value and bring their networks and experiences into the —

Vik: Exactly. And you'd hope it's a bit of a virtuous cycle, right? You establish yourself, you've got massive brands there that are associated, and you'd hope this year then more massive brands go, "Well actually I'd like to be associated with this sport." And so it was — you'd think that as that grows, it was important for us to establish ourselves in that way and that will continue to build. It's one of the many areas — you think you've brought this caliber of people into our sport, the commercial side will see a series of step changes in the right direction. For a lot of them, this year was a lot about learning and understanding the UK sports ecosystem and how that works. And so I'm looking forward to another busy winter as we go again on that side of things.

Host: How are the deals done, and are they generally done annually? They longer term?

Vik: Yeah, it varies. Some of them are done three years, some of them were one-year deals. That's done by team by team. So front of shirt now — we're not involved in that, it is a team to do their relationship. So they vary across the different teams.

Host: Where's the big value you think now that you can build on after this year, now people have actually seen this product?

Vik: I think it's important. Yes, there's the revenue side of things, but if you look at our audience and those audiences that perhaps aren't as high affinity to cricket at the moment, I'd like to go where they are and what's relevant to them, what's important to them, what's cultural to them. And brand partnerships can really help with that because they give relevance to us, because that brand has gone there. And so that's something I'd like to explore through this winter, to see what we can bring in either centrally or for a team for next year.

Host: We always talk in sport about value-add investors, and I'd imagine when you were bringing people into the investment groups, that again was a huge part commercially — was, have you seen that has been an area where there's been a real opportunity to start moving everything on?

Vik: Yeah. The investors that we've got are definitely value-add investors. They're incredible. Each — in different ways and with their own ways — but the caliber and quality, whether that's conversations that you can have and kind of guidance that they can give to me in terms of "here's how I would do it, here's some ideas," or whether it's for their own team and, like you say, contacts and black books that they can open — they've added a lot of value already.

100 与 Blast 的共存关系

Host: A question I get asked a lot — whether it's associated with the show, or whether it's a conversation about what I actually enjoy — I enjoy it, I often get a: "Why couldn't they have done this with the Blast?"

Vik: Yeah.

Host: But it also isn't the Blast, and I wasn't — you know, it wasn't my decision. I don't know all the details of it. But one of the things I will say is that I think it's great for English cricket that there are two. There's not many sports or many even within the cricket ecosystem that has that opportunity to have the 100 and what the hundred can do and is doing, but also to have the Blast and what the Blast is for and what that's doing, which gives you a kind of a sum round suite of products that allows each to go in their own direction without everything falling on one thing and one thing only.

So what's the Blast for that the 100 isn't? What's the 100 for that the Blast isn't?

Vik: Well, I think what the Blast provides is 18. So every county, every venue has a number of games. It has attendance — and good attendance — at those games with those that have high affinity to those counties. And again, we're — while that serves as that, ours then becomes the growth product in those peak months. I'm sure lots of conversations we're having at the time, but that now for me fits really well for both products. And I genuinely believe that both products can and will thrive in years to come, almost because of each other. The hundred needs the Blast. It produces a whole host of players and fandoms that come across that way. And I would hope that the hundred, as the hundred grows in prominence and grows cricket's fandom, some of them will move to the Blast. And so that coexistence will be beneficial for both.

5 亿英镑：如何分配、意味着什么

Host: A huge part of the 100 and its formation was also its ability to support English cricket financially.

Vik: Yes.

Host: When we were talking about that previously, it was a hypothetical from a distribution point of a big pot of money. Hopefully, this will go down. But since we chatted two years ago, you've had 500 million in essence now distributed to the English game. Look, you can't underestimate the importance and the value of that in the sport. How do you see that making the difference?

Vik: Look, it's incredible and I — you know, I think it's generational change for the sport. But what's really important now is that money, which is huge sums of money, multiples of what an annual turnover is of some of the counties, is invested well. Because what now needs to happen is that all 18 counties can use that funding a little bit like a kind of seed funding to ensure that their business model now is robust and sustainable for the long term. If they do that, then set cricket up for generations to come which is unbelievable — regardless of your fandom of the sport. But that's — and what that means in each of the 18 counties varies and will vary based on where each of the counties. But I'm confident they will, and once it is invested well, it'll be unbelievable.

Host: And can you just quickly explain to those that may not know how the distribution worked? Because you only have eight teams, but as you said, there are previously — you know, there are 18 counties.

Vik: So the way that it works is that for every pound that comes in, 10p goes to the recreational game. So 10% to the recreational game. Regardless of — so all the sales, all the money — it's all brought into one central pot.

Host: Yeah. 10% to the recreational game. And recreational game is like grassroots.

Vik: Grassroots. So that's 50 million to grassroots. Grassroots — and then they have a board effectively that looks at that money and has distributed it to the different counties, county boards, and how that gets used, that 50 million.

For the remainder of the money, there is effectively quite a complicated formula that splits it amongst the 18 professional first-class counties. And what it ended up being is that if you were a host venue of the 100, then there's £18 million there and thereabouts. If you're a non-host, there's about £26 million that you had. On that capital sums there are some restrictions of what you can spend it on. But the interest of which — you can imagine is quite a substantial amount — is yours as a county to keep as well on top of that amount.

Host: So if you don't have a franchise — do you — the money generated centrally does — is there a pot of that that still gets distributed? I.e. is it a one-off payment, or is it — we made X amount, let's just say this year — a portion of that X amount, even if owned by the individual teams, gets recentralized into a pot and then distributed amongst 18?

Vik: Yeah. So effectively — my old team Gloucesters has £26 million available to it. The way they get access to that 26 million is effectively through a business case. So if they wanted to do capital expenditure, whether they wanted to — if they have debt that they need to refinance, whatever it may be, there's a business case that gives them access to that. While that money is sitting there, any interest goes — is it still belongs to Gloucester? So that 26 at some point will become 27, become 28 and so on and so forth. But that's theirs.

Host: Yeah, but it's stuff like infrastructure project, right? Long-term value building rather than plugging immediate holes, or being allowed to then go and spend more and lose more.

Vik: Analogously, it needs the business change. The business model needs to change or adapt or improve so that the club is then sustainable once they have spent some or all of that money.

Host: You can't go back to the world. You can't do this again. So it has to plug any holes it needs to for the long term.

5000 万给草根板球的意义

Host: Can you just drill home the importance of that grassroots piece? Because a 50 million injection into the system — I don't care where that comes from. If I'm a cricket fan, right, whether I like the hundred or not, I want the game to be as healthy as possible. The foundations of it are anyone's ability to get access to the game, to pick up a bat, to have a facility, right? So the importance of you being able to attribute some of that money directly to this, which feeds the county's future 100 players, test match players — what is —

Vik: It's so important, and it's something that I was personally very passionate about. Cricket's given me so much in my life. You just want as many boys and girls to have that opportunity to play the sport. And so with all that we're doing, we're trying to inspire them to fall in love with cricket. And that 50 million can be spent and will be spent on all sorts of things that's so important that sadly isn't there at the moment — things like places to play, and facilities, and access to sports and equipment and coaches, so that when someone's five or six years old, they can actually have some great experiences with our sport. And then who knows — some of them are going to go on to be the next Nat Sciver-Brunt, or whoever it might be. Some will just love the sport and start watching it on telly. Some will buy tickets and come to games. Some will turn up every Saturday afternoon and Thursday evening and train and play club cricket. How they love the sport is almost irrelevant. But to give them that opportunity is so important.

扩军？投标故事？

Host: Expansion franchises — is that on the agenda?

Vik: Not right now. But look, I've said before, if the tournament does really well and grows, and it's almost like a sign of success that there is room and scope for more teams, there's more demand, there's more passion for more teams. But we have to be careful that we do it for the right reasons, and that is the growth of the tournament. So in a few years time, absolutely, we want to be looking at it.

Host: Yeah. But when you went through the process, I guess you were buoyed by the interest that you received — and I mean, from the investment side, you were buoyed by the amount of people keen to pick this up.

Vik: In that first round, we had over a hundred people that put in bids and put in interest for teams. So very much buoyed by that.

Host: Over 100.

Vik: Yeah. Yes. For across the eight teams — which is great. And hopefully if we continue to show potential and show growth of the tournament, that number will continue to grow and we'll have more interest from different people. So I'm hopeful that the demand side stays positive. And that's not a barrier — I don't think it will be right now — but we just need to establish the tournament as it is at the moment first.

Host: How do you filter a hundred down to eight without giving away the real secrets?

Vik: The process was fascinating. It was really enjoyable. Some of it now in hindsight —

Host: Yeah. Exactly.

Vik: So the bids that came in were for individual teams, and we had some firms that were like, "I've got eight teams. Here are eight bids." Others were, "No, that is my team. That's the only one bid I'll have." Okay. We then, because of the JV, we then went to the venue. So take Notts for example, Trent Rockets, and said, "Look, here are the bids that have come in for you."

We reviewed paper bids and then it was October, November — it was about a month where we organized meetings. So on one side of the table was a venue, other side was a potential investor. I would give my vision for Trent Rockets and where I see it going. They would do the same. And you'd have these matchmaking sessions that were half a day to a day long. And off the end of it, we'd then work with the venue to go, "Okay, let's narrow those down."

You'd then have another round of bids and then — the final round was an auction. And at that point between us and the venue, the venue had to pick at least two, so you'd have some competitive tension. And they would say, "Well, we're happy with that. Any of those would be fine." And some were two, some were four or five. And then that final round of one auction — it's an auction, so it's whatever the number is.

Host: And there was a lot of commentary around the pricing — or sorry, pricing — should we say, the eventual value that was brought out of it. Was that the result purely of an auction rather than anything being set? And how did — because you know, some went for more money than others did, as you would anticipate. It all kind of contributed to that central pot, right?

Vik: Yeah. And part of the reason for the numbers was, we'd had three rounds of bids already, so we kind of knew where things were going. There's always going to be a premium on London cities over some others. Some was because of demand. Frankly, if you have lots of people demanding and wanting to be part of that city, then prices — it's basic economics. And then others — the counties themselves and the venues have done a great job in these meetings, selling their vision, how they're going to work with you, how that can work, and what they can bring. So they're also buying into that partnership, and that partnership works really well. So it was a combination of lots of different things that came together to help get us to where we are today.

短赛制的全球定位与球员经济学

Host: Yeah. When you were here last time, you were adamant, right, that this was — you wanted to build this into one of the top short-form franchises. And we talked about the level of competition that you have, even fitting into a calendar and getting the players involved and all of this. You've got the credibility that comes with major investment coming in. You've got a very good product which is succeeding. How do you look at the hundred now in the landscape of cricket and where you want to be versus the work that you still need to do to sit it right at that top table? But also, one thing you really tied into there was: you need to have the financial power to do it as well.

Vik: Yeah, even more bullish, even more confident, but excited as well that we can be an unmissable event of the sporting calendar. So cricket, yes, but just the sporting calendar this year. The thing that will set us up in my opinion for the long term is the quality of sport went up a massive level. And I, in my humble opinion, think we have now set ourselves apart from the chasing pack, with the IPL being kind of out there and the WPL on the women's side. So that will give us a really strong foundation.

We then have all the other things that go with it in terms of our investment in our board, the investors that come in, the venues that we've got, which are fantastic in their own right. And I think we have an amazing opportunity to become a real key moment for those that watch cricket but also watch a number of sports in this country. So hugely exciting.

Host: Yeah. What about the talent? Because getting the best talent — not just in cricket, across all sport — now for any competition is a huge driver. Great players on both sides on the men's and women's side in this edition, but again — sorry, just tap back into the piece you said last time — you also need to have the financials to attract the best players to the tournament. So where are we at from the talent perspective?

Vik: So what we did in the first thing was, we were able to increase the salary caps. So each team has a salary cap which they can spend up to. In the men's and the women's, that was hugely increased. We then reshuffled the teams so that there's an equality across all eight.

Host: What is that cap?

Vik: For the men it is £2.1 million. For the women it is £900,000.

Host: Up from — was that like increase?

Vik: No, no, it was huge. So the women were at 400 and the men was 1.2, 1.3 I think. So big jumps, for that very reason.

As you point out, I also think it's important that we look after our players as well, because these — not kind of — but the top players now get so many opportunities and so many chances to play around the world and earn huge sums of money, that it's those small things that almost in a weird way count for more. And so it's the team's responsibility, but we implore them, and they do buy in, that look after the players, their families, their children — all those sorts of things which all goes down really well. I think we've got a — we don't have to fly everywhere, that helps as well, and all those other things that come into it. So we try and create a really brilliant environment for the players on the basis that if they enjoy coming here, they'll come back again and they'll perform at their very best.

But that I think now we've got — there weren't many people that we kind of missed out on in this year's edition. Definitely on the women's side. And on the men's side, obviously we still can't have Indian male players, but apart from that we got a really good crop of both English and overseas players. So I think we're up there.

Host: Can you explain why you can't have Indian just people in?

Vik: So at the moment there is a rule from the BCCI that says that Indian male players are only allowed to play for India or for the IPL. They're not allowed in any other tournaments around the world.

商业治理：薪资帽与可持续性

Host: Yeah. On that business side, you mentioned there's a cost cap. How important is the revenue, the business models of these franchises? They've got good values attached to them. You want to make them really good businesses as well. And I'd imagine you have to give — and you do give — now the level of autonomy for the individuals to do that. But I'm sure there is also some form of governance on your side to make sure that the businesses are being run as you hope they are or should be.

Vik: Yeah. And look, I think it's important that this is a long-term tournament and these teams continue to thrive not just for one year but for many many years into the future. That's the only way we're going to achieve our ambitions. So the salary cap, learning from other sports, is one of those really important bits of governance. It helps the business model, it also helps the jeopardy of the tournament. The fact that not one club has got all the players — they are spread out — and we had a really — one of the things about this tournament this year is you couldn't have predicted who was going to win at the start of the tournament, both men's or women's. And that's brilliant from a league perspective — probably less so if you're a team owner, you'd like it to be obvious, but from a league perspective, it's brilliant.

But that then gives you a real — on the biggest line item you'd expect, there is a cap, which then allows teams to be sustainable not just this year but next year and going forward.

Host: Yeah. And there'll be a conversation, I'm sure, where the cap type thing can increase once the businesses mature and show themselves. You're just going to evolve it as per the success of the product rather than the unsustainable element which we talk about a lot right — which sports has an unfortunate habit of doing of overextending itself too early, and particularly when it comes down to wages and fees etc associated with talent, steps outside of the means of the actual business capability.

Vik: You can see how it happens. It's easy to do. But it's so important that we keep that salary cap model on and that control going through it.

Host: So where does that cap put you in comparison to other short-form competitions?

Vik: The IPL on the men's side is miles ahead. The WPL on the women's side is miles ahead for both men's and women's. We are now second, but not miles ahead of third, fourth and fifth — South Africa and Big Bash. But enough to mean that we can attract those players. We've also then got the window and the other things that come together. And also now, I'd like to think that because the quality was so good, other players now look at it and go, "I can earn equivalent, but that's where I want to be playing because it's a best-versus-best tournament."

球员体验与国际化增长

Host: The player experiences are a huge part of making any tournament attractive, because as you've just said, it also is the key part that they go back and say, "Hey, I had a great time playing for 100." But like, what have you heard back from the players?

Vik: No, I think they're in a really good place. We've worked hard and continue to work hard with them, either through the teams or with them directly, to make sure that they have a really good experience here. We want this tournament to be the one that they love the most. Sure, you can earn more money in India and that's great, and I'm sure they have a great time there. But we have an opportunity here to be the most loved. And so, as you mentioned there, they then become our biggest marketing tool for other players because they will bring in their mates and say, "Come play this tournament because it's brilliant." So at the moment — and some of them have talked about it publicly in terms of the experience they had, the quality they had, the way that they were looked after — I think we're in a really good place.

Host: What about the international element? Obviously on the players front is really important. What's the data like internationally for the attention around the tournament?

Vik: It's growing. It is growing, especially in India and in the US with some of our investors. And then the other market, South Africa and so on and so forth. What's important with that is that the hundred remains — while we want to grow globally, we have to make sure that we have really strong foundations in the UK. So our first and foremost priority is the UK sports fan base, because if we have strong foundations here, we can then go from this place.

And I think if you look at the very best sports products pretty much to a tee around the world — the IPL is so dominant in India, and then it's starting to grow overseas. The NFL is so dominant in the US, and now it's starting to grow overseas. The Premier League went on a similar journey — that's now massive overseas, but it spent the first, what, 20 years very much UK based. So we're in that early stages where our focus is very much on the UK and the UK fan, and then we'll start to build our growth in the other opportunities that we have.

Host: And your UK talent kind of reflects that, right? I mean, the involvement from — the growth of a team and the establishment of team — yes, the overseas are great. They're great kind of gold dust sprinkled on top. But it's the local UK talent that really is the backbone of any of those teams.

广播合作与直到 2028

Host: Yeah. Where are we at with broadcast? I know previously it was tied in with test matches. Does anything change as the competition develops? Does it separate? You know, such media is the huge business line that obviously everyone knows within sport.

Vik: We're partnered with Sky and BBC, through to 2028. Both of them have been brilliant partners for us so far, and the amount that they invest — both resource and time and cross-marketing through their own tools — has been brilliant. And hopefully we, as we grow, we will in time provide them with more and more value as the tournament grows, because they get what they want to get out of it. So that's our focus for now through to '28, and we'll see where it gets to.

男女并重：一场结构性变革

Host: We've touched on it a few times, but I do want to give it its individual focus. A huge part of this has been aligning the men's and women's game and creating like a day, if you want, of entertainment. What it looks like it's done from the outside for women's cricket is huge. Can you add some real context and value to what it actually has achieved and what you've seen running this over the last few years? Because I don't think that can be passed over.

Vik: No, we're proud of that, and it's something that we want to keep and keep going again. So you mentioned some record crowds — you know, once again this year we saw record crowds for women's cricket at 100 games, beating previous 100 games record crowds. So hugely proud of it. It's been a phenomenal summer full stop for women's cricket, with the World Cup happening just before. So if you zoom out and look at the sport and where it is and where it's come from and look at what this summer held — that is unbelievable progress. By no means the end of the road. There's a long way that we want to keep it going, but you know, we talked about previously a salary cap of nearly a million, players getting £200,000 plus individually. This year — when in previous years, when we first started, which wasn't that long ago, you know, the total cap was 60,000 — so that growth has been quite phenomenal.

The — I should say the Helix Trophy this year — was another step, an attempted step, in that direction of bringing the men's and women's closer together. Of kind of — you have the women's winners, you have the men's winners, well, who was the best franchise, who managed to do that the best. And that was again a real positive step. And so we'll try and take all of those things and build again. But yeah, some really positive movement.

为什么不是 T20？红鲱鱼与心理定价

Host: Yeah, what do you think of the view — and again, something I get asked about a lot — everyone just goes, "It's going to be a T20 competition soon. Why is it not?"

Vik: Why is it — go on.

Host: Exclusive — no, seriously, like why does the hundred exist outside of all of the other formats when — it, people do just look at this, and particularly now, as we've just highlighted with ownership groups coming in who own other T20 franchises, you can see where they get it. They just go: two years, T20.

Vik: Yeah, I think it's a strange one because I think it's a red herring. I genuinely do. I think if you go back to my previous point, the 100 — or any sporting competition — needs to have really strong roots in its domestic market. It needs to be really deeply embedded for it to be successful. And the hundred was born out of a lot of research, a lot of insight on the UK domestic market — which is very very different to the Indian market, where they have 1.4 people, all of them cricket fans, understand the intricacies of T20 cricket. We don't have that luxury here.

And so here, the research into the barriers of cricket from sports fans came up with time, complexity and perception. And that effectively is what we set about breaking down step by step to create the hundred. And almost the format kind of falls off the back of it rather than it being the driving force. It is shorter. We're able to present it in a very different way, we're able to present it in a way that pulls it apart from the Blast and those sorts of things. But for those that follow cricket and know cricket — I mean, my six-year-old gets it. It is effectively T20 but with five balls as opposed to six. It's similar enough. It's still the very best bowlers in the world steaming in against the very best batters in the world trying to hit them out the park. And so it's working at the moment in the UK, as can be seen this year and in previous years. And I think that's the focus that we've got to keep going towards and what we can improve, rather than a distraction on a format because of other countries and what they do in other countries.

100 球制的女性板球红利

Host: Well, Tamar Mills, when he came on here — played every season of the 100, was the leading wicket taker I think until this year, I'm not sure if he still is — he, when we were talking about this, said, look, a huge part of it, even from your viewership as a fan, right? "What happened when I went to that game? Well, actually, you know what, we were done by nine." And if you've got families in there as well, I would imagine that's influential. But he also said, look, if you're top-and-tailing and you're having men's and women's games next to each other, and you want to build this thing, if you add another let's say hour onto each, that's — that's yeah, a big part of it.

Vik: Whether — and that's actually whether you're on a broadcast audience watching on telly or you're in the ground, the double headers are so important to what we do, or the gender parity part of it, so important. 20 balls might not seem like a lot, but 20 balls in is 40 balls a match, that's 80 balls across the day — that is a decent chunk of time, that's an hour and a half, couple of hours. So if we want to keep that part that is so core to us and so important to us, then that really helps because a family attending a match, done at 9:00, it might be, depending on their age of their kids, might be still a late night but not too late. Whereas a T20, 10:30, you're then back closer to midnight, it becomes tricky. Or you start the game much earlier, the double-header is much earlier, and then there's then an impact on the women's game, because the day becomes quite long, whether you're watching or attending.

So there are some real big advantages that it does bring. And like I say, with that, in my opinion still working, and the quality is still great, players enjoying it — I think that's really important.

全局视野：跨领域学习

Host: How much do you look at everything else going on around cricket? Multi-formats with long form, short form, discussions over who can thrive and who can survive and how money's distributed etc. Now having such an influential role running one of these top franchise tournaments, how important is it for you to be across everything understanding all that's going on? How you can make sure that you can apply the best bits of what's happening in global cricket to the hundred? How you can understand how to best speak to the players — because yes, you joked, your wife said that you work for one month — while I'm sure she may believe that, I'd imagine it's not true.

Vik: Yeah, look, I think the world of cricket full stop — whether it's franchise cricket or bilateral cricket or the ICC — is in a massive change period. Which if nothing else is fascinating just to observe and watch. In our role, the privilege that you have is that you're able, or you try, to pick and magpie the best bits of it and adapt as quickly as you can to that changing world.

But then that, and the combination — again I come back to the investors we've got — we can magpie from all different sports. What is it that football is doing so well that we can grow from? You talk about fan engagement with young kids and how we can build that — well, CFF YouTube's part of an investment committee at the London Spirit, so let's just go and speak to them directly. There's lots of things that you can bring in.

And yes, there's a lot to learn in cricket, but then you can go even broader than that — about sport and fan engagement and entertainment. What is it that we can continue to do? And so at the 100, we want to yes grow the fandom, deepen the fandom, deepen the high-quality cricket, but we want to also make sure it is sport and entertainment and people that can come. Even if you — you know, we were joking about the football before — even if your team gets battered, you have a great day, and it's a really fun day out with the family. And can you build both of those?

Host: That's a lie, by the way. He told me that he turned Aston Villa off yesterday, just before Halftime. So, did you have a good day for the rest of the day yesterday?

Vik: I did. I watched the Grand Prix. It was great.

Host: So yeah — okay, found it somewhere else. But the binary nature — right, and that's your word that you use and I think it's spot on — in how we generally approach as fans sport today, that's a really challenging environment to operate within.

Vik: It is challenging, but it's also a privilege, right? That sport is so — so many people are so passionate about sport. Sport means so much and so many different things to so many different people. If we can influence that just 1%, that's not to be taken lightly. I certainly don't take it lightly. I could be, you know, working behind a desk in an office somewhere doing something that I don't really care about. I care about this sport. I really care about cricket, about team sports and what it can do, and therefore to be able to be involved in that and to influence it is incredible. And that is what gets you out of bed every morning and means you do your best with the hundred.

Jude Bellingham 与年轻观众

Host: No, completely. And seeing young people engage with it, I'd imagine, is a huge part of it because obviously they are the audience now, everyone's trying to capture. Seeing Jude Bellingham come in — you know, it's so easy now for names just to turn up at sports events and just to be associated, and everyone questions whether it's genuine, whether it's real, whether they want to be there, whether there's some other reason. But I think, you know, as anyone that was there, as we saw, he actually really wants to be there. He's part of an ownership group. It's not just, "Oh, okay, you know, I'll put a bit of money."

Vik: It's brilliantly authentic. It's great. It doesn't seem to be, but I'm pretty sure it's not just a bit of money and there you go. He was there all day. He seemed to really enjoy his cricket. He enjoyed spending some time with the Phoenix players — which is great, and it's great for our competition to have someone like that involved in it, is unbelievable.

目标、北极星与故事

Host: Okay. So we've had five years, we've now had the first year of brand new. Looking ahead, how do you set your targets? Do you go year by year? Do you go, we would like to be here in five years time? What does success for this really look like?

Vik: I think success in the long term is huge. Really exciting. The ceiling is now very very high from a sports product full stop. And therefore to your point around how you set it, you then will set our target with the ambition and the passion of the teams that we've now got around that table — very high, five, ten years down the line. Okay. Well, to get there, the first step we need to do is X, and then we need to do Y, and you go step by step, but you have a north star that means that we are in that sporting calendar, an unmissable part of that sporting calendar in August. And so yeah, hugely exciting.

Host: If sport is all now stories, right? Is that the story you're really trying to tell?

Vik: I think — yeah. Well, people engage with stories. They engage with human stories. And I hope that fans can engage with the human side of the competition. We're going to sit here on a Business of Sport podcast and talk about the business. But the story that I'd hope they'd like to see is Phoebe Litchfield's superb batting, or Tim David's amazing catch, or Ciphert winning the game for the Manchester Super Giants. Those are the stories that I'd like to live and be in people's memories for a while to come. There'll inevitably be a lot of challenges ahead. There'll be ups and downs throughout that. But to your point, we have a great product. We have a great set of investors. And we've got people up and down the country that are passionate about what we've got, that want to try and improve it on a day-by-day basis. So yeah, an exciting time ahead.

Host: Awesome. All right. Now I will shut up. Thank you so much for coming back in. It's great. And congratulations to you and all the team putting it together. I think it's been really cool to watch it grow.

Vik: Oh, brilliant. Thank you very much.

## 一场被伪装成"体育联赛"的风险投资实验
表面上，Vik 谈的是板球联赛"The Hundred"的第一个新赛季。但如果把耳朵贴近他的措辞，你会听到一个更陌生的声音——**这其实是一场用"体育 IP"作为标的物的种子轮融资仪式**。
100 多个买家竞投 8 支队伍、"venue + investor"的相亲式配对会议、最后一轮拍卖定价、5 亿英镑分配给英格兰板球生态——这些不是传统体育联盟的语言，而是 YC Demo Day 的语言。ECB 不像在办联赛，更像在做一个 **"体育资产孵化器"**：中央先用 5 年建立最小可行产品（MVP），达到"因成功而触及天花板"的临界点，再把 8 个"子公司"拆出去独立融资，让每支队伍在下一阶段各自跑增长。
这里有一个**让人意外的观察**：Vik 反复强调"我们没有印度球员，但除此之外都有了"——听起来是限制，其实是**结构性护城河**。IPL 靠垄断印度男球员保住了金字塔尖；The Hundred 恰恰因为"抢不到 IPL 球员"，才被迫把资源、叙事、球员体验、女子板球溢价全部拉高到最大值。**限制反过来成了产品定义**。这和 Ne

item.title: [a16z] The Evolution of Computers & Abdication of Reasoning
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽略的相变：这一次抽象跃迁，方向反了

Steven 与 Ben 争论的核心其实是一个隐藏的相位反转——过去七十年的每一次抽象上移（晶体管→逻辑门→OS→应用→平台），人始终"在机器之上"下达指令，机器只负责执行。但 LLM 是历史上第一次让人"退到机器之下"——你不再规定端状态，你祈祷一个模型给你端状态。Ben 反复说的 "abdication of logic" 不是又一层抽象，而是抽象堆栈的方向倒转。

这里有个让人意外的观察：四色定理其实在 1976 年就已经完成了同样的"退位"——那不是一个人类能理解的证明，而是让计算机穷举 1936 种构型的 200 页黑箱结论。数学界当年也吵过一模一样的问题（"这算证明吗？"）。也就是说，"推理外包"并不是 AI 时代的独创，只是从边缘学科的一次事件，变成了所有认知工作的默认基础设施。这才是真正惊人的地方。

二、数学家为什么最兴奋？——一个反直觉的"存在主义分层"

被 AI 冲击最狠的群体，反而最兴奋。Ben 半开玩笑地抛出一个残忍的诊断："如果一件事被解决你反而抑郁，说明这件事本身可能不值得做。" 这句话表面刻薄，但它揭示了一个跨领域的普适规律——

任何长期缺乏经济外部性的智力活动，会把"过程"内化为"目的"。禅宗僧侣画沙曼陀罗、学院派研究后现代文学、加密圈研究拜占庭容错——这些活动的价值一部分（有时是大部分）来自"从事该活动的人的自我意义"。而癌症研究、材料科学、蛋白质折叠这类有明确外部端状态的领域，AI 帮忙推进只会让人狂喜。

由此可以做一个大胆的预测式判断：未来五年，AI 冲击带来的"存在危机烈度"，将是一个学科"内部意义 / 外部效用"比值的精确函数。你甚至可以用这个比值给学科排序，谁最痛苦，谁最快乐——这比"哪些工作会被替代"是一个更根本、也更预测力的问题。

三、资本-工程的百年反转：一个被大多数人忽略的康德拉季耶夫波

Ben 讲的这个数字最震撼："20 年前给 10 个人 10 亿美金，他们不知道该怎么花；今天给 20 个人 10 亿美金，他们能有效地用掉。"

这不是一句金句，这是行业物理定律的翻转。让我把它往回推，你会看到一个精确的三段式循环：

  • 1945–1985：资本约束（你首先得买得起一台机器）
  • 1985–2023：工程约束（Brooks 定律主宰，加人不减速，只增速）
  • 2023– ：资本约束（模型训练、GPU、数据中心，钱直接换算成能力）

这是同一维度上四十年后的镜像回归。跨领域看，这几乎精确对应能源行业的历史节律：铁路时代（资本）→ 内燃机时代（工程/工艺）→ 核电与超大规模电网时代（资本）。当一个行业进入"用钱买物理约束"的阶段，赢家标准就从'谁最聪明'变成'谁最能募资 + 最能配置资本 + 最能承担系统性风险'。

一个几乎没人明说的推论：既然行业物理反转了，风险投资的"精益创业"叙事（Eric Ries）在 AI 底层就彻底失效了，而"胖创业"（Ben Horowitz 的老论调）意外地重新成为默认路径。更微妙的是——这一次不是选择，而是必需。你不下注 200 亿美金去训练下一代模型，就没有下一代模型可谈。这也是为什么 Google 要走债券脱表、微软要给内部产品"限令牌"——巨头第一次尝到了"资本不够用"的味道，而这恰恰是过去四十年他们从未体会过的痛。

四、被埋在最后的洞见：AI 解决了分发问题

Ben 顺口提到但没展开的一句话，我认为是整期最被低估的洞见："AI 一并解决了分发问题——因为对 token 和 GPU 的需求是无限的，你可以把营销当作纯粹的资本投入。"

翻译一下：过去创业公司死于分发（distribution），不是死于产品。Clayton Christensen 的颠覆理论之所以成立，一半是因为大公司的销售渠道无法被撬动。而现在，Cursor / Anthropic / OpenAI 的火箭式增长，本质上是用无限的推理需求 + 无限的资本 = 无限的漏斗顶端——历史上第一次，一家 100 人公司能和微软在分发上正面对撞。

这才是真正颠覆'创新者的窘境'的东西。不是模型能力，不是团队规模，而是分发经济学的物理变化。老巨头擅长的所有护城河（销售、渠道、合作伙伴生态、政企关系），突然被一个"你想要多少 token 就买多少 token"的粗暴逻辑绕过了。这才是 Microsoft 焦虑的真正原因——不是 OpenAI 更聪明，而是它可以在没有销售队伍的情况下达到分发规模。

四、四色定理：算力驱动的证明先例

Steven: Yeah, but so those of you that don't know—we had to take a whole course in college on that, basically boiled down to this problem. And the interesting thing is why: it was because the theoreticians had postulated that if you can solve this problem in non-exponential time, in polynomial time, then you could solve all these other problems like the traveling salesperson problem, and all these other problems much much faster—which mattered because all of our computers were just so compute-bound. So if you were the AT&T people that gave, you know, "here's our node of 6,000 switches, how do you route optimally?" You'd be like, "Well, we don't have enough. That's like two years of running the simulation to solve this."

And so it turns out that one of the interesting things was they proved the four-color theorem.

Ben: Yeah.

Steven: But they did it—which, by the way, I mean, just—the four-color theorem says for any 2D planar map, you can color it, you can use only four colors such that no two adjacent areas have the same color, right? And you only need four colors, you'll never need five colors. And we learned it just so people—like, you kids know—that's literally how we learned it, and we could all repeat it like that. It's this very weird imprint over this problem.

And so what sort of happened was, no one ever arrived at basically what you could think of as a proof that looked like calculus. Instead what they did is they actually proved that the number of potential solutions was finite.

Ben: Have you actually seen the proof?

Steven: Yeah. Yeah. 200 pages of combinations. But they basically proved there's a finite number of them, and then they just computed all of them and said, "Look, it's only four colors." And so it's this sort of bankshot proof, but it was only possible because of compute.

Ben: And to your point, that was actually very very useful in the practical applications.

Steven: Right. And certainly as a topology person, setting strong bounds and things like that. So actually I see—I think that to me was just a really good lesson in when you have a new level of abstraction that says this is a whole class of problems that can be solved, you can then build tools working at that level of abstraction, and everybody doesn't have to start from "okay, what's the two-three tree representation of what we're doing?"

And they just never felt that that was going to—that was like a chip used in a printer, and also they looked at me like, "we're ARM licensees, we knew all"—and I'm like, "but it's the power, it's the graphics, it's the always-connected, all of this stuff." And the culture was—they do Moore's law at Intel—and just like with Google, they do hyperscale. So if AI moves on device—

Steven: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Of course. Like that's not what they do.

Ben: Yeah. And with Microsoft, they were squeezed. They're squeezed now. And I think you raise super interesting points about the opportunity though for startups with this capital inversion kind of thing.

Steven: Go raise capital and go after the—

Ben: Well, and it's not just—it's like you're also saying, "we're actually not going to question you if you're trying to raise that capital." Like, we're not going to look at you like you're crazy. And you just look at the raises that are happening right now, and these companies have been quite successful as a result.

十五、模型作为 200 亿美元数字艺术品：能力预测的失效

Host: The last thing—when Vinod Khosla came in and we had him on the podcast, he was sort of—he thought LLMs were a great achievement but he was bearish on their ability to invent new discoveries, particularly like scientific breakthroughs or things like that. And I'm curious if you think the math progress is consistent with that, or what is your latest thinking on sort of the limitations of the current model architecture versus, like, well, we need more—

Ben: So here's kind of my new view, which is: I think we know exactly how these things work. You put a bunch of data in them, they're stuck to that data, they can only do distribution stuff, and they can move along that manifold in a perfectly Bayesian way. So, okay, so we can say these words. And then the question is: okay, but what are the implications of that? What problems can it solve?

I think it's just so hard for a human being to reason about a digital artifact—in this case the model—that was built with $5 billion. So in the history of humanity, we've never created a single digital artifact that had that many flops and that much data in it. So on one hand, we know exactly how it works from a mechanic standpoint. On the other hand, that is so much data and that is so much compute, maybe all of that stuff's already in there and it can solve anything that you want.

And so the conversation has moved from "how do these things work?" We know. Can it do out-of-distribution stuff? No. Does—is there transfer learning? Probably not. Is the singularity here? Probably not. I think most people kind of agree—we're not in fast takeoff, we're stuck to it being in distribution, we haven't closed—we all agree about that. But what I don't think anybody knows is: okay, but you're still putting tens of billions of dollars in that thing. What's it capable of now? And if you consider this meta-economic machinery, which means the ability from Anthropic to raise lots of money, then pour all of that money into this thing to create this super powerful thing—I don't think any of us can predict what that means and where that goes.

And so it's a different conversation, but the question is the same. It's like, will that be able to cure cancer? Maybe. But if you put $20 billion into something, maybe it can cure cancer effectively. And that's where I think the discourse has evolved, and where it is now. And I honestly have decided that I cannot predict what an artifact worth that was—that you used $20 billion to create—is capable of.

Steven: Look, I think it's just so important. It's important for people who are deep in watching everything that's new to admit that they can't predict. And I think that's great, because it turns out I wrote 58 memos on what the internet was going to be, and I was wrong on a lot of them by far.

Ben: But even this one is a little different. This is like—I take $20 billion and I put it into a model, right? And then you and I look at that model, and we can do whatever we want. I don't think we can comprehend what that even means. It's so many flops and so much data. Like, I don't know what that's capable of.

Steven: I think we are—I think that that's really true. And on biomedicine in particular—look, the other half of my household is a research doctor who uses AI. We have a Spark at home, and she's loaded—

Ben: Like a ton?

Steven: Like a Sun Spark. No, no. Nvidia Spark.

Ben: Oh, yeah. No, no, no. Not with a C or with a K. Oh, yeah.

Steven: Not a Scott McNealy Spark. A relic.

Ben: No, no.

Steven: And it's all AI. She does brain stuff and surgical brain stuff. All AI. And it's so interesting to see, because what it really can do is—it sees the patterns that you can't, that only experience could tell somebody. But if there's 10,000 papers on a topic that's part of her model, then it's just finding the patterns that no one has. And that's a pretty basic AI capability at this point, but it's actually opening up solutions or problems or research directions and things like that.

I will say, just for the—this is not magic to discover drugs, because the hard part of drugs has always been candidates—not candidate. It's always been efficacy and safety. The candidates have, since the 80s, been able to develop more than we could test. It's human patients and it's very very very hard.

Ben: Can I just tell you something that I got wrong on this? So I love the question that you asked, which is: how has our thinking evolved on whether these things—their capabilities in generality—

I was responding to this Bostrom notion of recursive self-improvement fast takeoff. You create one of these things, you step back, and it takes over the world, right? And so I kind of poo-poohed that, because that's clearly not what's happening. And I think most people—a lot of people agree that that's the case. Right?

But here's what I got wrong. What I got wrong is: I did not know that we could effectively just continue to pour money in this. Like, the scaling laws are holding. And I don't know what it means to—let's say we do a $100 billion training run to have this thing that you're putting $100 billion in. And then that money comes from this meta-economic machinery that may be able—want to solve whatever they may want to solve—cancer, but they may also want to create a weapon, who knows. And so this concentration of this many resources in a useful way, I think is very new. I don't think we understand the implications. I think you could reasonably argue that that's very dangerous if you kind of apply that $100 billion in the wrong way.

So I think that's kind of where this conversation needs to evolve to. So less the FOOM, and more the: what does it mean to be able to concentrate resources?

Steven: Which also was in all—I mean, this is—you're basically talking about exponential growth. And this is just exponential in dollars. And we all know none of us can model exponential very well.

Ben: Yeah, we've never been able to do that. Like, complex engineering projects—you were not tackling one problem with a lot of money—or just kind of building this machine.

Steven: Well, you're right. You're 100% right, and I completely agree. But I remember just sitting in meeting after meeting at Intel saying, "we have 5 gigahertz, we have this many gigahertz, this many transistors," and literally nobody knows what we're going to do with them all.

Ben: No, no, you're building the machinery. I'm saying, in this case, if you're like, "I want to exhaustively explore every protein combination," right? We can just turn that into a money problem.

Steven: Yes. Got it.

Ben: A very strange—

Steven: Which is a great way to say it. That we can take previously infinite problems and apply capital, and it becomes finite.

Ben: Just makes it a capital problem and not an engineering problem. Yeah. Which is just a very different laws of physics.

Steven: Yeah. Yeah.

Host: Let's wrap on that, because it's 2:30. This has been a great episode. Thank you guys.

Steven & Ben: Thank you.
